topics.title: Economics all around us: economic activities and roles

learn.hook: Walk through any sabzi mandi at 7 a.m. and you can watch economics happen live: someone grows, someone sells, someone buys, someone carries the crates for a wage.
points: Economics studies the everyday activities people carry out to earn a living and to meet their needs: buying, selling, producing, working and hiring.
A consumer buys goods and services to satisfy wants; a seller sells goods; a producer makes goods or provides services.
An employee (worker) sells labour for wages or salary; an employer hires workers and pays them.
Services are produced too: a doctor produces health services, a teacher produces education services, a taxi driver provides transport services.
Economic activities are done for money or a livelihood; non-economic activities (helping a friend, praying, playing for fun) are not done to earn income.

example.q: At a bus stand you see: (a) a vendor selling chai, (b) a girl waiting for her bus to school, (c) a conductor issuing tickets, (d) two friends chatting. Which are economic activities?
steps: Ask of each: is someone earning a living or buying/selling a good or service?
(a) The vendor sells chai to earn income: economic.
(c) The conductor works for a salary from the transport undertaking: economic.
(b) Waiting for a bus and (d) chatting earn nobody any income: non-economic.

learn.reallife: When you buy a metro card you are a consumer; the Delhi Metro is a service producer; the ticket clerk is an employee; DMRC is the employer. One trip, four economic roles.

quiz.q: Which one of these is an economic activity?
options: A student watching a cricket match for fun
A plumber repairing a pipe for a fee
A boy helping his grandmother cross the road
quiz.explain: The plumber provides a service in return for payment, so it is done to earn a living.
quiz.mistake: Treats any useful or busy activity as economic, even when no income is involved

quiz.q: A doctor treating patients at a clinic for a fee is best described as a:
quiz.explain: The doctor produces a service (health care) that patients pay for.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that services are produced just like goods

quiz.q: Raju works in a garment factory and receives ₹15,000 every month. In this role he is an:
quiz.explain: Raju sells his labour to the factory owner for wages, so he is an employee.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the person who hires (employer) with the person hired (employee)

quiz.q: When the same Raju spends part of his wage on vegetables, he acts as a:
quiz.explain: Buying goods to satisfy his wants makes him a consumer. One person can play several economic roles.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a person can have only one economic role

quiz.q: Which statement about economics is correct?
options: It only studies big companies and the stock market
It studies how people earn and spend to meet their needs in everyday life
It only studies money kept in banks
quiz.explain: Economics begins with everyday activities: consumption, production, work, buying and selling.
quiz.mistake: Thinks economics is only about money, banks or big business

quiz.q: A taxi driver who drives his own car and charges passengers a fare is mainly a:
quiz.explain: He provides a transport service and earns income from it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only people who make physical goods are producers

quiz.q: At a market you observe four things. Which one is NOT an economic activity?
options: A porter carrying sacks for ₹50 a trip
A trader buying apples in bulk to resell
A shopper paying for a shirt
A child feeding stray dogs out of kindness
quiz.explain: Feeding animals out of kindness earns no income and involves no buying or selling.
quiz.mistake: Counts any good deed as an economic activity

quiz.q: A shopkeeper who employs two helpers is, at the same time, a:
options: Employee and a producer of goods
quiz.explain: He sells goods to customers (seller) and pays wages to helpers (employer).
quiz.mistake: Ignores that one person can hold more than one economic role

teach.ask: Gappu flaps in: 'My uncle is a bus conductor and buys a new phone. Is he doing economics? What role does he play?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Conductor = employee earning a living, phone buyer = consumer. One person, many roles!
teach.nudge: Good start! But which role is he in when he buys the phone, and which when he works for a salary?

topics.title: Scarcity and choice: we cannot get something for nothing

learn.hook: You have ₹500 for the month. The new cricket bat costs ₹450, the concert ticket ₹300 and the online course ₹250. Welcome to the oldest problem in economics.
points: Human wants are unlimited, but the income and resources available to satisfy them are limited. At given prices, you cannot buy everything you want.
This gap between wants and means is called scarcity. Scarcity is the root of all economic problems.
Resources have alternative uses: a plot of land can grow food crops or cash crops; a rupee can buy a book or a burger. So every use means giving up another.
Because of scarcity, individuals and society must choose which wants to satisfy and which to postpone.
Signs of scarcity are everywhere: long queues for gas cylinders, crowded local trains, shortages of seats in good colleges.

example.q: Anjali has ₹600. She wants a book (₹400), shoes (₹500) and a movie outing (₹200). What can she afford, and what does this show?
steps: Total cost of all three = 400 + 500 + 200 = ₹1,100, which is more than ₹600.
Affordable sets within ₹600: book + movie (₹600), shoes alone (₹500), book alone, or movie alone.
She must rank her wants and give up something.
example.answer: She cannot buy all three; she must choose, for example book + movie. This is scarcity forcing a choice.

learn.reallife: During the 2023 tomato price spike, many families shifted to other vegetables. Limited budgets plus higher prices forced choices, exactly what scarcity means.

games.title: Scarcity check
items: Scarcity means a good is not available anywhere at all.
Scarcity means resources are limited relative to wants, not that a thing is totally absent.
Even a very rich country faces scarcity.
Its wants still exceed its resources, so it too must choose.
A piece of land that can grow either rice or cotton shows resources have alternative uses.
Using it for one crop means giving up the other.
If wants were limited and resources unlimited, there would be no economic problem.
Choice is needed only because of scarcity.
Queues at a ration shop are a sign of scarcity.
More people want the goods than can be served at once.
Scarcity is a problem only for poor people.
Every individual, firm and government faces limited means.

games.title: How a choice is made under scarcity
games.prompt: Arrange the steps of a sensible choice
items: List all your wants
Find the price of each want
Compare the total with your income
Rank the wants by importance
Satisfy the most urgent wants first and postpone the rest

quiz.q: The basic economic problem arises because:
options: Wants are limited and resources are unlimited
Wants are unlimited and resources are limited
People do not like to work
quiz.explain: The mismatch between unlimited wants and limited means is scarcity, the root of the economic problem.
quiz.mistake: Reverses which side is limited

quiz.q: Which of these is the best example of a resource with alternative uses?
options: A farm that can grow wheat or sugarcane
A painting that has already been sold
quiz.explain: The farm can be put to one use or another; choosing one means giving up the other.
quiz.mistake: Picks a free or used-up resource that has no real alternative economic use

quiz.q: Meera has ₹1,000. A phone cover costs ₹300, earphones ₹800 and a book ₹400. Which set can she buy?
quiz.explain: 300 + 400 = ₹700, which fits in ₹1,000. Every set with the earphones costs more than ₹1,000.
quiz.mistake: Adds prices carelessly and ignores the budget limit

quiz.q: A long queue outside a railway reservation counter during Diwali is mainly a sign of:
quiz.explain: Many more people want tickets than there are seats, so seats are scarce.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a crowd with plenty

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Every society has to make choices about the use of its resources.
Reason (R): Resources are limited and have alternative uses.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Limited resources with alternative uses are exactly why choice becomes unavoidable.
quiz.mistake: Sees both as true but misses the cause-and-effect link

quiz.q: Which statement best expresses 'we cannot get something for nothing'?
options: Everything we get has a cost in terms of money or something given up
Goods are always free in a market
Only the government pays for goods
quiz.explain: With limited means, getting one thing means paying for it or giving up something else.
quiz.mistake: Takes the phrase literally as being about gifts only

quiz.q: Rahul's income is ₹20,000 a month and the goods he wants cost ₹35,000. What is the shortfall he must manage by choosing?
quiz.explain: Wants exceed means by 35,000 − 20,000 = ₹15,000, so he must give up wants worth at least that much.
quiz.mistake: Adds income and wants instead of finding the gap

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a sign of scarcity?
options: Seats filling up quickly in good colleges
A shop with plenty of unsold stock and no buyers
Overcrowded buses in the rush hour
quiz.explain: Unsold stock with no buyers is excess supply, the opposite of scarcity.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every market situation shows scarcity

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'Why can't I just have every toy I want? Explain scarcity to me!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Wants are unlimited, means are limited, so I must choose. That is scarcity!
teach.nudge: Nearly! But what about money and resources: are they unlimited too? And what does that force me to do?

topics.title: Consumption, production, distribution and the definition of economics

learn.hook: Every rupee of India's national income ends up in someone's pocket as wages, rent, interest or profit. Who gets what is one of economics' biggest questions.
points: Consumption: how consumers decide what to buy with their income, given prices, to satisfy their wants.
Production: how producers decide what to produce, how much, and with which inputs, given costs and market demand.
Distribution: how national income is shared among the factors of production as wages (labour), rent (land), interest (capital) and profit (entrepreneurship).
Definition: economics is the study of how people and society choose to use scarce resources that have alternative uses, to produce goods and services and distribute them for consumption.
Modern economics also studies poverty, unemployment, inequality, education, health and disasters, and these questions need statistical data.

example.q: A sugar mill pays ₹40 lakh in wages, ₹10 lakh as rent for land, ₹15 lakh as interest on a loan, and keeps ₹35 lakh as profit. Which factor earns what?
steps: Rent goes to the owner of land.
Interest goes to the supplier of capital (the lender).
Profit goes to the entrepreneur (the mill owner).
example.answer: Labour ₹40 lakh, land ₹10 lakh, capital ₹15 lakh, entrepreneur ₹35 lakh; total ₹100 lakh. This is distribution.

learn.reallife: When the government debates raising the minimum wage for construction workers or tax on company profits, it is debating distribution of national income.

games.title: Match factor income to its factor
Consumption, production or distribution?
items: A family deciding between a scooter and a fridge
A firm choosing machines or more workers
A debate on how much of national income goes as wages
A student choosing which snacks to buy with pocket money

A bakery deciding how many loaves to bake each morning

quiz.q: The branch of economics that studies how national income is shared as wages, rent, interest and profit is:
quiz.explain: Distribution studies how income is divided among the factors of production.
quiz.mistake: Confuses distribution of income with distribution (transport) of goods to shops

quiz.q: Interest is the reward for which factor of production?
quiz.explain: Interest is paid to the owner of capital for its use.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up rent (land) and interest (capital)

quiz.q: Which is the best definition of economics?
options: The study of money and banks only
The study of prices in the stock market
The study of how to become rich quickly
The study of how society uses scarce resources with alternative uses to produce and distribute goods and services
quiz.explain: This definition captures scarcity, alternative uses, production and distribution.
quiz.mistake: Picks a narrow money-only definition

quiz.q: A mill's factor payments are wages ₹60 lakh, rent ₹15 lakh, interest ₹10 lakh and profit ₹25 lakh. What is the total income distributed (in ₹ lakh)?
quiz.explain: Total factor income = 60 + 15 + 10 + 25 = ₹110 lakh.
quiz.mistake: Leaves out one factor payment, often profit

quiz.q: Using the same mill (wages ₹60 lakh out of ₹110 lakh total), what percentage of the income goes to labour? (Round to two decimals.)
quiz.mistake: Treats ₹60 lakh as 60% without dividing by the total

quiz.q: A producer deciding whether to make 100 or 200 bicycles a day, using more workers or more machines, is dealing with:
quiz.explain: Deciding how much to produce and with what inputs is the study of production.
quiz.mistake: Thinks hiring workers is about distribution because wages are involved

quiz.q: Why does modern economics need statistics more than ever?
options: Because only numbers matter and ideas do not
Because it studies issues like poverty, unemployment and inequality that must be measured with data
quiz.explain: Measuring and analysing these issues requires reliable numerical data.
quiz.mistake: Thinks statistics replaces reasoning instead of supporting it

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Economics studies only the behaviour of producers.
Reason (R): Consumers do not face scarcity.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are false
quiz.explain: Economics studies consumers, producers and distribution, and consumers certainly face scarcity of income.
quiz.mistake: Accepts a narrow view of economics

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: 'Economics is just about money, right? Tell me what economics actually studies.'
teach.praise: Tweet! Scarce resources, used for consumption and production, and income distributed as wages, rent, interest and profit!
teach.nudge: Good! You mentioned some parts. What about how income is shared, and why resources must be chosen carefully?

topics.title: Economic data, analysis and policy

learn.hook: Before launching free cooking-gas connections for poor families, planners needed to know how many households still cooked on firewood. No numbers, no plan.
points: Economic facts expressed in numbers, such as rice output, prices or the number of unemployed, are called economic data.
The chain is: data → analysis (finding the causes of a problem) → policy (measures to solve it).
Without data there can be no proper analysis, and without analysis there can be no sound policy. This is why economics and statistics are linked.
Governments use data such as the Census, NSS surveys and price indices to design and review policies on food, health, jobs and education.

example.q: The government wants to reduce child malnutrition in a district. Put the steps in order using the data-analysis-policy chain.
steps: Data: survey children's height and weight and families' food intake.
Analysis: find the causes, e.g. low protein in diet, poor sanitation.
Policy: add eggs or pulses to mid-day meals and improve sanitation.
Review: collect fresh data to check whether malnutrition has fallen.
example.answer: Data → analysis → policy → review with new data.

learn.reallife: The Public Distribution System uses data on household numbers and incomes to decide how much grain each state is allotted.

games.title: From numbers to action

Analyse the data to find causes

games.title: Data and policy
items: Economic facts stated in numbers are called economic data.
Numbers such as output, prices and employment are economic data.
A good policy can be made without any information about the problem.
Without data the causes cannot be analysed, so policy would be guesswork.
Analysis means finding the causes of an economic problem.
Analysis comes after data and before policy.
Statistics has no role in economics.
Economics needs statistics to collect and analyse data.
Data on births and deaths can help plan hospital capacity.

quiz.q: Which of the following is an example of economic data?
quiz.explain: Economic data are facts expressed as numbers.
quiz.mistake: Accepts a vague verbal statement as data

quiz.q: The correct sequence for tackling an economic problem is:
quiz.explain: First collect data, then analyse causes, then design policy.
quiz.mistake: Jumps to policy before knowing the facts

quiz.q: Analysis of economic data mainly aims to:
options: Find the causes of a problem
quiz.explain: Analysis identifies the causes, which then guide policy.
quiz.mistake: Confuses analysis with data collection

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Economic policy depends on statistical data.
Reason (R): Without data, the causes of a problem cannot be analysed.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Policy needs analysis, and analysis needs data, so R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Fails to see the data → analysis → policy link

quiz.q: A state finds from survey data that 30% of 2,000 sampled villages lack a primary health centre. How many sampled villages lack one?
quiz.mistake: Divides by 10 instead of finding 30%, or finds the villages that do have one

quiz.q: Which is the best example of the government using statistical data for development policy?
options: Using Census data on literacy to decide where to open new schools
Choosing a colour for new currency notes
quiz.explain: Literacy data show where schools are most needed, guiding the policy.
quiz.mistake: Picks an action that does not depend on economic data

quiz.q: After a new irrigation scheme, a district's crop yield rose from 2,000 kg to 2,500 kg per hectare. By what percentage did the yield rise?
quiz.explain: Rise = 500 kg on a base of 2,000 kg: 500/2,000 × 100 = 25%. Such numbers help evaluate a policy.
quiz.mistake: Divides by the new value (2,500) instead of the old value

quiz.q: Why is statistics called a tool of economics?
options: It decides what people should want
It helps collect, organise and analyse economic data for theory and policy
quiz.explain: Statistics supplies and processes the data that economic analysis and policy need.
quiz.mistake: Thinks statistics itself solves economic problems

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Why does the government keep counting things? How do numbers help make rules?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Data first, analysis of causes next, and then the policy. Counting is the first step to solving!
teach.nudge: Good thinking! But what happens between collecting numbers and making a policy?

topics.title: Meaning of statistics and kinds of data

learn.hook: 'India produced over 130 million tonnes of rice' and 'Statistics helps us compare states' use the word statistics in two different senses. Can you spot them?
points: Plural sense: statistics means numerical facts or data, e.g. statistics of exports or crop output.
Singular sense: statistics is the science of collecting, organising, presenting, analysing and interpreting data.
Quantitative data are characteristics measured in numbers: income, marks, height, output of rice.
Qualitative data are attributes that cannot be measured directly in numbers: gender, beauty, honesty, skill, health. They are often described in degrees (good, average, poor).
Stages of a statistical study: collection → organisation → presentation (tables, diagrams, graphs) → summarising (averages etc.) → analysis → interpretation.

example.q: Classify: (i) beauty, (ii) monthly income, (iii) marks in an exam, (iv) singing ability, (v) intelligence.
steps: Ask: can it be measured directly as a number with a unit or count?
Income (₹) and marks (out of 100) are numbers: quantitative.
Beauty, singing ability and intelligence are attributes: qualitative.
example.answer: Quantitative: income, marks. Qualitative: beauty, singing ability, intelligence.

learn.reallife: The Census of India records quantitative data (age, number of rooms) as well as qualitative data (religion, mother tongue, type of roof) about every household.

games.title: Quantitative or qualitative?
items: Height of students in cm
Honesty
Daily wage in ₹
Gender
Rainfall in mm
Skill in painting
Marital status
Number of children in a family

games.title: Stages of a statistical study
items: Collection of data
Organisation of data
Presentation in tables and diagrams
Analysis using summary measures
Interpretation of results

quiz.q: In the sentence 'Statistics of rice production show a rising trend', the word statistics is used in the:
quiz.explain: Here statistics refers to the numbers on rice production, i.e. data.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the plural (data) and singular (method) senses

quiz.q: Statistics in the singular sense refers to:
options: Methods of collecting, presenting, analysing and interpreting data
Only the numbers in a table
quiz.explain: The singular sense is the science or set of methods for dealing with data.
quiz.mistake: Thinks statistics only means the numbers

quiz.q: Which of these is qualitative data?
quiz.explain: Honesty is an attribute and cannot be directly measured in numbers.
quiz.mistake: Assumes anything that can be ranked is quantitative

quiz.q: Which of these is quantitative data?
quiz.explain: Output in million tonnes is measured in numbers with a unit.
quiz.mistake: Thinks attributes with labels are numbers

quiz.q: What is the correct order of the first three stages of a statistical study?
quiz.explain: You must first collect data, then organise it, then present it.
quiz.mistake: Tries to present or analyse data before collecting it

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Statistics deals with both quantitative and qualitative data.
Reason (R): Attributes like gender can be counted, for example the number of females in a class.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Qualitative data become usable in statistics by counting how many units have each attribute.
quiz.mistake: Believes statistics can never handle attributes

quiz.q: In a class of 40 students, 18 are girls. What percentage of the class are boys?
quiz.explain: Boys = 40 − 18 = 22. Percentage = 22/40 × 100 = 55%. A qualitative attribute (gender) turned into numbers by counting.
quiz.mistake: Gives the girls' percentage instead of the boys'

quiz.q: Statement: 'Statistics can be used only for quantitative data and never for any attribute.' This statement is:
options: True, because attributes have no numbers
True, because qualitative data are useless
False, because attributes can be counted and classified
False, because all data are qualitative
quiz.explain: Qualitative characteristics can be classified and counted, so statistics handles them too.
quiz.mistake: Overlooks counting as a way to quantify attributes

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'Statistics is just a pile of numbers, isn't it? Teach me both its meanings and the kinds of data.'
teach.praise: Tweet! Plural = data, singular = methods, and data can be quantitative or qualitative. Got it!
teach.nudge: Close! Statistics also has a singular meaning. And what about data like gender or honesty?

topics.title: Why statistics matters, and where it falls short

learn.hook: A family of four heard the river's average depth was 3 feet, so they all waded across. The average was right; the middle was 7 feet deep. Statistics is powerful, but it needs common sense.
points: Precision: statistics states facts exactly. 'Rice output rose by 8%' says more than 'output went up a lot'.
Condensation: it reduces masses of data to a few summary figures such as averages and percentages.
Relationships: it helps find and test links between variables, e.g. price and demand, income and consumption.
Forecasting and policy: it helps estimate future values (food demand, oil imports) and check whether a policy works and what causes a problem.
Limitations: it studies aggregates, not single individuals; it can be misused or misread (e.g. averages hiding extremes); it is no substitute for common sense.

example.q: A town's average monthly income is ₹50,000. Nine people earn ₹10,000 each and one earns ₹4,10,000. Does the average describe a typical person?
steps: One extreme value has pulled the average up.
example.answer: No. The average is misleading here; common sense says most people earn ₹10,000.

learn.reallife: The RBI forecasts inflation each quarter from price data before deciding interest rates: statistics used for forecasting and policy.

games.title: Use or limitation?
items: Condenses huge data into an average
Helps forecast demand for electricity
Cannot describe one particular individual
States facts precisely in numbers
Can be misused to mislead
Is no substitute for common sense
Helps test if price and demand are related

games.title: Common sense test
items: A river with an average depth of 3 feet is safe to wade across at every point.
An average hides the deep parts; some spots may be much deeper.
Statistics deals with groups of observations rather than one single observation.
Statistics studies aggregates.
Exact figures are generally more convincing than vague statements.
Precision is a key use of statistics.
Statistics can prove anything, so it is never misleading.
Data can be misused or misinterpreted if handled carelessly.
Statistics helps evaluate whether a government policy is working.
Comparing data before and after a policy shows its effect.

quiz.q: Which function of statistics is shown when the average income of 10 crore households is reported as one figure?
quiz.explain: Reducing a mass of data to one summary figure is condensation.
quiz.mistake: Confuses summarising with stating facts precisely

quiz.q: An economist checks whether higher income leads to higher spending on food. Which use of statistics is this?
quiz.explain: Testing how income and spending move together is finding a relationship.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any use of data is just condensation

quiz.q: Which is a limitation of statistics?
options: It studies aggregates and not individuals
quiz.explain: Statistics deals with groups; it cannot describe a single unit by itself.
quiz.mistake: Mistakes a use for a limitation

quiz.q: Five workers earn ₹8,000, ₹8,000, ₹9,000, ₹10,000 and ₹65,000. What is their average wage?
quiz.explain: Average = total / number = 1,00,000 / 5 = ₹20,000. Note how one high wage lifts the average far above most workers.
quiz.mistake: Picks the middle value or forgets the extreme value

quiz.q: In the previous data (₹8,000, ₹8,000, ₹9,000, ₹10,000, ₹65,000), how many workers earn LESS than the average of ₹20,000?
quiz.explain: Four of the five earn below ₹20,000; only one earns more. The average misleads about the typical worker.
quiz.mistake: Assumes about half the values must lie below the average

quiz.q: The 'average depth of a river' story is used to show that:
options: Statistical methods are no substitute for common sense
quiz.explain: The average was correct but hid dangerous deep parts. Judgement is still needed.
quiz.mistake: Concludes that statistics is useless rather than that it must be used wisely

quiz.q: A ministry projects next year's crude oil imports from past data. Which use of statistics is this?
quiz.explain: Estimating future values from past data is forecasting, which supports planning.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up forecasting with simply stating a fact

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Statistics can be misused.
Reason (R): Statistics is a precise science, so its results never depend on how data are chosen or presented.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Statistics can be misused precisely because results depend on how data are selected and presented, so R is false.
quiz.mistake: Believes numbers always speak the truth on their own

teach.ask: Gappu worries: 'If statistics is so clever, can it ever fool me? Tell me what it is good for and where it fails.'
teach.praise: Tweet! It is precise, condenses data and helps forecast, but it can mislead without common sense!
teach.nudge: Good list of uses! Now, what can go wrong? Think about the river with an average depth of 3 feet.

topics.title: Data: primary and secondary

learn.hook: A student who interviews 50 chaiwalas about their earnings has primary data. The student who later reads her report has secondary data. Same numbers, different labels!
points: Data are the values of variables; each recorded value is an observation. Data help explain economic problems such as low farm income.
Primary data are collected first-hand by the investigator for the purpose of the enquiry, e.g. through a survey or interview.
Secondary data have already been collected and processed by another agency, e.g. Census reports or RBI publications. They save time and money.
The same data are primary for the agency that collected them and secondary for anyone who uses them later.
Choice depends on purpose, time and money: primary data are original and suited to the purpose but costly; secondary data are cheap but must be checked for suitability and reliability.

example.q: A student wants to know the average pocket money in her school. She (a) surveys 60 classmates herself, and (b) also reads a newspaper report on teenagers' spending. Classify each source.
steps: (a) She collects the data first-hand for her enquiry: primary data.
(b) The newspaper collected and published the figures earlier: secondary data for her.

learn.reallife: NSO publishes the Periodic Labour Force Survey. For NSO it is primary data; for a journalist writing about jobs from that report it is secondary data.

games.title: Primary or secondary (for the person using it)?

topics.title: Framing a good questionnaire

learn.hook: 'Don't you think our tasty noodles are better than other brands?' That one question breaks at least two rules of survey design. Let's learn to spot them.
points: A survey collects information from individuals using an instrument: a questionnaire (filled by the respondent) or an interview schedule (filled by the interviewer).
A good questionnaire is short, clear and precise, and moves logically from general to specific questions.
Avoid: ambiguous words ('often', 'regularly'), double negatives ('Don't you not…'), leading questions that hint at an answer, and questions that need calculations.
Closed-ended questions give fixed choices: two-way (yes/no) or multiple-choice. They are easy to tabulate but harder to frame well.
Open-ended questions allow free answers ('What do you think of…?'). They give rich detail but are hard to compare and interpret.

example.q: Improve this question: 'You don't think smoking is not harmful, do you?'
steps: Problem 1: double negative ('don't… not') confuses the respondent.
Problem 2: it leads the respondent towards an answer.
Rewrite as a neutral closed question: 'In your opinion, is smoking harmful to health?' (Yes / No / Can't say).
example.answer: 'In your opinion, is smoking harmful to health? Yes / No / Can't say'

learn.reallife: Before every big election, survey agencies frame neutral, short questions so that responses from lakhs of voters can be compared quickly.

games.title: Good or bad question?
items: What is your age in completed years?
Don't you think this soap is the best?
Do you own a two-wheeler? Yes / No
How much did your family spend on food per day last year, multiplied by 365?
Do you watch TV often?
Which brand of noodles do you buy most? A / B / C / Other
Are you not unhappy with the bus service?

games.title: Match the flaw to the question
pairs: 'Wouldn't you agree prices are too high?'
'What is your yearly income if your monthly income is ₹18,500?'
'Do you own a bicycle? Yes / No'

quiz.q: Which of the following is a two-way question?
options: Do you have a bank account? Yes / No
What is your opinion of online classes?
Which of these four brands do you prefer?
How can the bus service be improved?
quiz.explain: A two-way question offers exactly two possible answers, such as yes or no.
quiz.mistake: Confuses two-way with multiple-choice

quiz.q: 'Don't you agree that our new phone is the best in the market?' is a poor question mainly because it is:
quiz.explain: It pushes the respondent towards agreeing.
quiz.mistake: Notices the question but not the hint built into it

quiz.q: A questionnaire should generally move from:
quiz.explain: Starting with general questions eases the respondent into the specific ones.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the logical order

quiz.q: The main disadvantage of open-ended questions is that the answers are:
quiz.explain: Free answers vary widely in content and wording, so they are hard to tabulate and compare.
quiz.mistake: Confuses open-ended with closed-ended questions

quiz.q: Which question avoids ambiguity best?
options: How many hours did you study yesterday?
Do you often go to the library?
quiz.explain: It asks for a precise, measurable answer about a fixed time.
quiz.mistake: Accepts vague words like 'a lot' or 'often'

quiz.q: Which question should NOT be put in a questionnaire?

Do you use a smartphone? Yes / No
If you spend ₹45 a day on travel, what do you spend in a leap year?
quiz.explain: Questions that require calculation burden the respondent and cause errors.

quiz.q: A firm surveying the popularity of its noodles wants answers it can tabulate easily. It should mostly use:
quiz.explain: Closed-ended questions give fixed options that are quick to count and compare.
quiz.mistake: Thinks open-ended questions are easier to tabulate

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Closed-ended questions are easy to analyse.
Reason (R): Closed-ended questions are always easy to frame.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Closed questions are easy to analyse, but framing complete and unbiased options is actually difficult.
quiz.mistake: Assumes ease of analysis means ease of framing

teach.ask: Gappu wants to survey his flock: 'Isn't my song the best, don't you think?' Teach me how to write good survey questions.
teach.praise: Tweet! Short, clear, no leading hints, no double negatives, and choose closed or open questions wisely!
teach.nudge: Good! But my question hints at the answer. What is that flaw called, and what other traps should I avoid?

topics.title: Modes of data collection and the pilot survey

learn.hook: Want to survey tribal households in remote Bastar, college students in Pune, and shoppers at a Delhi mall? One method will not fit all three.
points: Personal interview: face-to-face questioning. Highest response, allows clarification and observation, but costly, slow, needs trained interviewers, and the interviewer may influence answers.

Mailing questionnaire (post, email, online form, SMS): cheapest, covers wide and remote areas, respondents answer privately, but response is low, no one can clarify doubts, and it needs literate respondents.
Telephone interview: cheaper and quicker than personal visits, allows some clarification, but reaches only people with phones and loses face-to-face cues like body language.
Pilot survey: a small trial survey before the main one. It tests the questionnaire's clarity, the instructions, the enumerators' performance, and estimates cost and time.

example.q: Choose a mode: a researcher must survey 5,000 graduates across India within a week and with a small budget.
steps: Personal interviews across India in a week: too slow and costly.
Telephone: possible but costly for 5,000 people in a week.
Online/mailed questionnaire: cheap, fast and graduates are literate and connected.
example.answer: An online (mailed) questionnaire, perhaps with phone follow-ups for non-response.

learn.reallife: Before Census operations, enumerators run a pre-test (a pilot) in selected areas to see which questions confuse people, and the forms are revised.

games.title: Match the mode to its feature
pairs: Interviewer can observe and clarify, but costly
Cheapest and wide coverage, but low response
Quick, but only reaches people with phones
Small trial to test the questionnaire

games.title: Which mode suits best?
items: Survey of non-literate farm workers in a village
Survey of 10,000 software engineers across cities
Quick follow-up with 200 known customers who own phones
Detailed study needing observation of living conditions
Low-budget survey of literate people in remote areas
Calling 300 shopkeepers who have phones but no internet for a same-day opinion poll

quiz.q: Which method of data collection gives the highest response rate?
quiz.explain: Face-to-face contact makes refusals less likely and lets the interviewer clarify questions.
quiz.mistake: Thinks cheaper methods give better response

quiz.q: A major disadvantage of the mailing questionnaire method is:
quiz.explain: Many people do not return mailed or emailed questionnaires.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the disadvantages of different modes

quiz.q: The telephone interview method cannot be used for people who:
options: Do not have access to a phone
quiz.explain: Only people with phones can be reached.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the access limitation of phone surveys

quiz.q: Which mode is most suitable for a survey of non-literate respondents?
quiz.explain: An interviewer can read the questions aloud and record answers.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that mailed questionnaires need literate respondents

quiz.q: A pilot survey is conducted:
options: Before the main survey as a small trial
After the main survey to check results
quiz.explain: It is a trial run to test the questionnaire and estimate cost and time.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a pilot survey is done after the main survey

quiz.q: Which is NOT a purpose of a pilot survey?
options: Estimating the cost and time of the main survey
Replacing the need for a main survey
quiz.explain: A pilot survey prepares for the main survey; it does not replace it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the trial results are enough

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): In a personal interview, the respondent's answers may be influenced by the interviewer.
Reason (R): The interviewer is physically present and may unintentionally suggest answers.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The interviewer's presence, tone or expressions can bias answers.
quiz.mistake: Assumes personal interviews have no drawbacks

quiz.q: A survey team mails 800 questionnaires and gets 200 back. What is the response rate?
quiz.explain: Response rate = 200/800 × 100 = 25%. Low response is typical of mailed surveys.
quiz.mistake: Divides 800 by 200 or reports the non-response

teach.ask: Gappu must survey birds all over the forest with very little money. 'Which method should I choose? Teach me the modes!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Personal, mailed or phone, each with pros and cons, and a pilot survey first to test my questions!
teach.nudge: Good! You named some methods. What about a small test run before the real survey?

topics.title: Census and sample survey

learn.hook: To know if the dal is cooked, you taste one spoonful, not the whole pot. That spoonful is a sample.
points: Population (universe): all the items or units under study, e.g. all farms in a district.
Census (complete enumeration): data collected from every unit of the population. The Census of India is held every 10 years and counts every person.
Sample: a group of units drawn from the population that represents it. A good sample is representative.
Advantages of a sample survey: cheaper, quicker, needs fewer staff, allows more detailed questions, and can give reasonably accurate results.
A census is preferred when every unit matters (e.g. population count, voter lists) or when the population is small; a sample is needed when testing destroys items (e.g. testing bulbs).

example.q: A researcher studies 50 out of 200 farms in a village to estimate average yield of wheat per acre. Identify the population, sample and variable.
steps: Population = all units under study = 200 farms.
Variable = the characteristic measured = wheat yield per acre.
example.answer: Population: 200 farms; sample: 50 farms; variable: yield per acre.

learn.reallife: India's population grew from about 23.8 crore in 1901 to about 121 crore in 2011, a fact known only because the Census counted everyone.

options: Only the people living in a country
A part of the units under study
Only the units with data errors
quiz.explain: Population (universe) is the complete set of items being studied.
quiz.mistake: Uses the everyday meaning of population

quiz.q: Complete enumeration of every unit of the population is called:
quiz.explain: A census covers every unit.
quiz.mistake: Confuses census with sampling

quiz.mistake: Divides the wrong way or slips a decimal

quiz.explain: The variable is the characteristic being measured: monthly expenditure.

quiz.q: Which situation requires a sample rather than a census?

Counting students present in class today
Listing all bank branches in a city
quiz.explain: Testing destroys matchsticks, so only a sample can be tested.
quiz.mistake: Does not see destructive testing as a reason to sample

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A sample survey can collect more detailed information than a census with the same budget.
Reason (R): A sample covers fewer units, so more time and money can be spent on each unit.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: With fewer units, resources can go into detailed, careful questioning.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a census always gives more detail

quiz.q: A good sample should be:
quiz.explain: It must reflect the features of the population to give reliable estimates.
quiz.mistake: Thinks convenience is enough for a sample

quiz.q: India's population was about 23.8 crore in 1901 and about 121 crore in 2011. Roughly how many times did it grow?
quiz.explain: 121 ÷ 23.8 ≈ 5.1, so about five times in 110 years.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts instead of dividing, or misreads the units

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know how sweet all the mangoes on a tree are. 'Must I eat every mango? Teach me census and sample!'
teach.praise: Tweet! A census checks every mango; a representative sample checks a few, cheaper and quicker!
teach.nudge: Good! But what makes a sample trustworthy? And why not just check every mango?

topics.title: Sampling methods: random and non-random

learn.hook: Exit polls on election day interview a few thousand voters and try to predict the votes of crores. Sometimes they nail it; sometimes they miss badly. Sampling method makes the difference.
points: Random sampling: every unit of the population has an equal chance of being selected. The investigator has no say in who is chosen.
Lottery method: write each unit's name on a slip, mix well, draw the required number. Random number tables or computer-generated random numbers do the same for large populations.
Sampling frame: the complete list of units of the population from which the sample is drawn (e.g. a voters' list).

Non-random sampling: units do not have an equal chance of selection. Types: judgement/purposive (investigator's choice), convenience (easy to reach) and quota (fixed numbers from each group). Bias is likely.
The number of ways of choosing r units from N is ᴺCᵣ = N! / (r!(N − r)!), e.g. 3 students out of 10 can be chosen in 120 ways.

example.q: How many different samples of 3 students can be drawn from a class of 10?

learn.reallife: Exit polls sample voters at chosen booths. If the booths or voters chosen are not representative, or people do not answer honestly, the prediction can go wrong.

games.title: Random or non-random?
items: Drawing names from a box after mixing slips
Interviewing whoever is standing near the college gate
Using a computer to pick 50 roll numbers at random
Choosing the 'most typical' villages by the researcher's judgement
Selecting exactly 20 men and 20 women as they come
Using random number tables to pick households

games.title: Match the method to its description
pairs: Units easiest to reach are chosen
Investigator picks units he thinks typical
Fixed number of units from each group

quiz.q: In random sampling:
options: Every unit has an equal chance of being selected
The investigator chooses the units he likes
Only the largest units are selected
quiz.explain: Equal chance of selection is the defining feature of random sampling.
quiz.mistake: Confuses random with haphazard or convenient selection

quiz.q: How many different samples of 2 can be drawn from 6 households?
quiz.mistake: Uses 6 × 5 = 30 and forgets that order does not matter

quiz.q: How many different samples of 3 students can be chosen from 10 students?
quiz.mistake: Stops at 10 × 9 × 8 = 720 and forgets to divide by 3!

quiz.q: The list of all units of the population from which a sample is drawn is called the:
quiz.explain: A sampling frame is the full list, like a voters' list or school register.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the list of units with the survey instrument

quiz.q: Choosing respondents simply because they are easy to reach is:
quiz.explain: Convenience sampling picks easily accessible units, so bias is likely.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any unplanned selection is random

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Non-random sampling may give biased results.
Reason (R): In non-random sampling, all units do not have an equal chance of being selected.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Unequal chances let the investigator's choice or convenience distort the sample.
quiz.mistake: Misses the link between unequal chance and bias

quiz.q: A lottery is drawn, but the slips for some names are folded differently and are easier to pick. Is the sample still random?
options: Yes, because a lottery always gives a random sample
Yes, if the box is large
No, because the units no longer have an equal chance of selection
No, because lotteries are never random
quiz.explain: A lottery is random only if every slip is identical and well mixed, giving each unit an equal chance.
quiz.mistake: Believes the lottery method guarantees randomness automatically

quiz.q: Why can an exit poll go wrong?
options: The sample of voters may not represent all voters, or voters may not answer honestly
quiz.explain: Unrepresentative booths or untruthful answers bias the estimate.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a sample-based prediction must always be right or always wrong

teach.ask: Gappu must pick 5 birds out of 30 for a choir test. 'How do I pick fairly? Teach me random sampling!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Give every bird an equal chance, using a lottery or random numbers, and avoid biased judgement picks!
teach.nudge: Nice! But how exactly would you make sure each bird has the same chance? Name a method.

topics.title: Sampling and non-sampling errors

learn.hook: Your sample says farmers in a village earn ₹600 a day on average. The truth is ₹580. That ₹20 gap has a name, and so do the much nastier errors that no sample size can fix.
points: Sampling error = sample estimate − true population value (the gap is often stated as a size). It arises because only part of the population is observed.
Sampling error falls as the sample size rises; it disappears in a census.
Non-sampling errors can occur in both a census and a sample survey, are more serious, and are harder to detect and control.

Types: sampling bias (the sampling method excludes some units, e.g. a phone survey missing people without phones); non-response (people do not reply); errors in data acquisition (wrong recording, measurement mistakes, misunderstood questions, false answers).
Non-sampling errors can be reduced by careful questionnaire design, training enumerators and follow-ups, but not by simply enlarging the sample.

example.q: Five farmers earn ₹500, ₹550, ₹600, ₹650 and ₹700 a day. A sample of two picks ₹600 and ₹700. Find the sampling error.

learn.reallife: Surveys on household spending face non-response when wealthy households refuse to take part, which can understate average consumption, an error a bigger sample alone cannot fix.

games.title: Sampling or non-sampling error?
items: Sample mean differs from population mean by chance
Enumerator writes 45 instead of 54
Many households refuse to answer
A phone survey misses people without phones
Estimate changes when a different random sample is drawn
Respondent misunderstands a question

games.title: Errors true or false
items: Sampling error can be reduced by increasing sample size.
Larger samples give estimates closer to the true value.
Non-sampling errors occur only in sample surveys.
They occur in census too, e.g. recording mistakes.
A census has no sampling error.
Every unit is covered, so there is no sample-population gap.
Non-sampling errors are usually easier to control than sampling errors.
They are harder to detect and control.
Non-response is a type of non-sampling error.
Missing replies can bias results.

quiz.q: Sampling error is the difference between:
options: The sample estimate and the actual population value
quiz.explain: It is the gap between what the sample says and the true population value.
quiz.mistake: Thinks sampling error means a mistake by the enumerator

quiz.q: Population of 5 incomes: ₹200, ₹300, ₹400, ₹500, ₹600. A sample picks ₹200 and ₹300. By how much does the sample mean underestimate the population mean?
quiz.explain: Population mean = 2,000/5 = ₹400. Sample mean = ₹250. The sample falls short by 400 − 250 = ₹150; this gap is the sampling error.
quiz.mistake: Reports the sample mean or the population mean instead of the gap

quiz.q: Population of 4 marks: 40, 50, 60, 70. A sample picks 60 and 70. What is the sampling error of the sample mean?
quiz.explain: Population mean = 55, sample mean = 65, so error = 65 − 55 = 10 (an overestimate).
quiz.mistake: Reports the sample mean or flips the sign

quiz.q: Which of the following is a non-sampling error?
options: The sample mean differs from the population mean by chance
An enumerator records the wrong age
A larger sample gives a different estimate
Two random samples give slightly different means
quiz.explain: Recording mistakes are errors in data acquisition, a non-sampling error.
quiz.mistake: Confuses chance sampling variation with human errors

quiz.q: Sampling error can be reduced by:
options: Increasing the size of the sample
quiz.explain: Larger samples represent the population better.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a smaller sample is more accurate

quiz.q: A telephone survey about internet use in a district misses all households without phones. This is:
quiz.explain: The method systematically excludes part of the population: sampling bias.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any wrong estimate is just random sampling error

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Non-sampling errors can occur even in a census.
Reason (R): A census covers every unit of the population.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but covering every unit does not explain the errors; they come from recording, non-response and similar problems.
quiz.mistake: Thinks complete coverage causes or removes non-sampling errors

quiz.q: Why are non-sampling errors considered more serious than sampling errors?
options: They occur only in small samples
They are harder to detect and do not fall just by increasing sample size
They can be calculated exactly by formula
quiz.explain: They arise from bias, non-response and recording errors, which a bigger sample does not remove.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a larger sample fixes all errors

teach.ask: Gappu counted 10 nests and found the average eggs to be 4, but the forest's true average is 3. 'Did I make a mistake? Teach me about errors!'
teach.praise: Tweet! The gap between sample and truth is sampling error, which falls with a bigger sample; non-sampling errors are trickier!
teach.nudge: Good! Can a bigger sample cure every error? What about birds who refuse to answer or wrong records?

topics.title: Census of India, NSSO and other data agencies

learn.hook: Every 10 years, lakhs of enumerators knock on every door in India, from Ladakh to Lakshadweep. It is one of the largest data operations on the planet.
points: Major national agencies: Census of India, National Sample Survey Office (NSSO), Central Statistical Office (CSO), Registrar General of India (RGI), Directorate General of Commercial Intelligence and Statistics (DGCIS), and the Labour Bureau.

Census of India: the most complete source of demographic data (population size, density, sex ratio, literacy, migration). Held regularly every 10 years since 1881; the first Census after independence was in 1951.

NSSO (set up in 1950) runs nationwide sample surveys in 'rounds' on socio-economic issues such as consumer expenditure, employment, literacy and health. Results appear in reports and its journal 'Sarvekshana'. In 2019, NSSO and CSO were merged to form the National Statistical Office (NSO).
Other sources: CSO (national income), RGI (births and deaths), DGCIS (foreign trade), Labour Bureau (labour data); also the Economic Survey, RBI publications and international bodies.

example.q: A student needs data on (i) India's sex ratio, (ii) household consumption expenditure, (iii) India's exports. Which source fits each?
steps: (i) Sex ratio is demographic: Census of India.
(ii) Consumer expenditure surveys are run by NSSO (now NSO) in rounds.

learn.reallife: Census 2011 was the 15th Census of India and the 7th after independence. Census data guide everything from seat allocation to planning schools and hospitals.

A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because it enumerates everyone, it gives the fullest population data.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect complete coverage with completeness of data

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Who counts all the people in India, and who asks families how much they spend? Teach me the data agencies!'
teach.praise: Tweet! The Census counts everyone every 10 years; NSSO runs sample surveys in rounds. India runs on data!
teach.nudge: Good! You named one agency. Who runs the sample surveys on spending and jobs, and how often is the Census held?

topics.title: Why classify data? Raw data and classification

learn.hook: A kabadiwala's cart is a jumble of newspapers, bottles, tins and plastic. Within minutes he sorts it into neat heaps, because sorted scrap is easy to price and sell. Data work the same way.
points: Raw (unclassified) data are data in the form they were collected: large, disorganised and hard to handle. Even finding the highest value or the average is tedious.
Classification arranges data into groups or classes according to some common feature, so the data become easy to understand, compare and analyse.
Each classification must follow a clear criterion (basis), e.g. by year, by state, by gender or by income range.
Advantages: brings order, highlights similarities and differences, makes comparison possible, and prepares data for tabulation and analysis.

example.q: Marks of 20 students are recorded in roll-number order: 47, 85, 32, 61, 75, 52, 90, 38, 64, 71, 29, 55, 83, 49, 66, 78, 41, 58, 69, 93. How many scored 60 or more? Why is this slow?
steps: We had to check every value because the data are raw and unordered.
example.answer: 11 students; raw data force us to inspect every value, which classification avoids.

learn.reallife: The RBI classifies bank loans by sector (agriculture, industry, services, personal loans) so it can quickly see where credit is flowing.

Finding the highest value in raw data is always quick.
With large raw data you must scan every value.
A kabadiwala sorting scrap is an analogy for classification.
Grouping like items together is exactly what classification does.

quiz.mistake: Sees no benefit in classification

teach.praise: Tweet! Raw data are messy; grouping by a clear basis makes them easy to compare and analyse!

topics.title: Kinds of classification

learn.hook: India's GDP by year, rainfall by state, workers by gender, and students by marks are four different ways to slice data. Each answers a different question.
points: Chronological (temporal): by time, such as years or months. Such data form a time series (e.g. India's population 1951–2011).
Spatial (geographical): by place, such as country, state, district (e.g. wheat output by state).
Qualitative: by attributes that cannot be measured, such as gender, marital status, religion. Classifying by several attributes at once (e.g. sex, then married/unmarried) is manifold classification.
Quantitative: by measurable characteristics such as marks, height, income, grouped into classes like 0–10, 10–20.
Relative frequency of a class = class frequency ÷ total frequency; it can be shown as a percentage (× 100).

example.q: In a class of 50, the 30–40 marks class has 15 students. Find its relative frequency and percentage.

learn.reallife: The Economic Survey shows exports by year (chronological), by destination country (spatial) and by commodity group (qualitative), all from the same trade data.

games.title: Which kind of classification?

Monthly sales of a shop for 12 months
Population classified by marital status
Foreign tourist arrivals by country of origin
Patients classified by blood group

quiz.q: Classification of data according to time is called:
quiz.explain: Classifying by years, months or days is chronological (temporal).
quiz.mistake: Mixes up chronological with spatial

quiz.q: Data on cotton production in Gujarat, Maharashtra and Telangana are an example of:
quiz.explain: Classifying by place (states) is spatial or geographical.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any data with names is qualitative

quiz.q: Classifying a population first by sex, then each group by literate/illiterate, is called:
quiz.explain: Classification by more than one attribute is manifold classification.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the term for multi-attribute classification

quiz.q: Grouping workers by their daily wages into ₹200–300, ₹300–400 and so on is:
quiz.explain: Wages are measurable, so this is quantitative classification.
quiz.mistake: Confuses measurable characteristics with attributes

quiz.q: Out of 80 households, 20 fall in the income class ₹20,000–30,000. What is the relative frequency of this class?
quiz.mistake: Divides the total by the class frequency (80/20 = 4)

quiz.mistake: Treats the class frequency itself as a percentage

quiz.q: A time series is produced by which type of classification?
quiz.explain: Arranging values by time gives a time series.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a time series is arranged by place

quiz.q: The relative frequencies of all classes in a distribution add up to:
quiz.explain: Each is class frequency ÷ total, so together they sum to total ÷ total = 1 (or 100%).
quiz.mistake: Confuses proportions with percentages or counts

teach.ask: Gappu has data on bird counts by year, by forest, by colour and by weight. 'Are these different kinds of classification? Teach me!'
teach.praise: Tweet! By time, by place, by attribute, and by measurable value: four kinds of classification!
teach.nudge: Good! You listed some kinds. What do we call classification by place, or by a feature like colour?

topics.title: Variables: continuous and discrete

learn.hook: Your height can be 162.37 cm, but the number of siblings you have can never be 2.5. That difference decides how data are grouped.
points: A variable is a characteristic whose value changes from unit to unit and can be measured, e.g. income, height, marks. An attribute (like gender) is qualitative and is not measured in numbers.
A continuous variable can take any value within a range, including fractions and decimals: height, weight, time, temperature, rainfall, area, age.
A discrete variable takes only certain values (usually whole numbers) and changes in jumps: number of students, cars, children, the number on a dice.
Tip: if you measure it, it is usually continuous; if you count it, it is usually discrete.

example.q: Classify: (a) area of a farm, (b) number on a rolled dice, (c) population of a city, (d) rainfall in a month, (e) age.
steps: Population is a count of people: discrete.
Age can be 15 years 4 months: continuous.
example.answer: Continuous: area, rainfall, age. Discrete: dice number, population.

learn.reallife: IMD reports rainfall to the nearest millimetre (a continuous variable), while Indian Railways counts passengers (a discrete variable).

options: A variable can be measured numerically; an attribute is a quality that cannot be directly measured
quiz.explain: Variables (income, height) are quantitative; attributes (gender, honesty) are qualitative.
quiz.mistake: Treats attributes and variables as the same thing

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'My feather length and my number of eggs: are they the same kind of variable? Teach me!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Feather length can be any value: continuous. Eggs are counted in whole numbers: discrete!
teach.nudge: Good! But can I lay 2.5 eggs? Which kind of variable takes only whole-number values?

topics.title: Frequency distribution: the key terms

learn.hook: The marks of 1,000 board candidates fit on one small table once you group them into classes like 40–50 and 50–60. That table is a frequency distribution.
points: A frequency distribution shows how the values of a variable are spread across classes, with the number of values (frequency) in each class.
Class: a group of values such as 20–30. Class limits: the lowest (lower limit) and highest (upper limit) values of a class. Class frequency: the number of observations in the class.
Class interval (class width) = upper class limit − lower class limit, e.g. 30 − 20 = 10.
Class mark (mid-point) = (upper limit + lower limit) / 2. It represents the whole class in calculations.
Range = largest value − smallest value. A frequency curve is drawn by plotting frequencies against class marks and joining the points smoothly.

example.q: For the class 40–60: find the class width and class mark. If the data range from 12 to 97, find the range.

learn.reallife: Pay commissions publish salary bands like ₹25,000–35,000; HR teams use the band's mid-point to estimate average pay.

games.title: Match the term to its meaning
pairs: Number of observations in a class
Smallest value a class can hold

items.q: Range if max is 88 and min is 23

quiz.q: The class mark of the class 30–50 is:
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the limits (gives width 20) instead of averaging

quiz.q: The class interval (width) of the class 15–25 is:
quiz.mistake: Adds the limits or gives the mid-point

quiz.q: The lowest value in a data set is 18 and the highest is 96. What is the range?
quiz.mistake: Adds the extremes instead of subtracting

quiz.q: The mid-point of a class is 45 and its lower limit is 40. What is the upper limit?
quiz.mistake: Adds the mid-point and lower limit directly

quiz.q: The class mark of a class is used in calculations because:
options: It is the largest value in the class
It represents all the values in that class
quiz.explain: Once data are grouped, each value in a class is represented by the mid-point.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the class mark is a frequency

quiz.q: A frequency curve is obtained by plotting:
options: Frequencies against class marks and joining them by a smooth curve
quiz.explain: Frequencies are plotted against class marks and joined smoothly.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the frequency curve with an ogive

quiz.q: The class marks of consecutive equal classes are 25, 35, 45. What is the class width?
quiz.explain: With equal classes, the gap between consecutive class marks equals the class width: 35 − 25 = 10.
quiz.mistake: Takes the first class mark as the width

quiz.q: Consecutive class marks are 25, 35, 45 and the class width is 10. What are the limits of the first class?
quiz.mistake: Uses the class mark as the lower limit

teach.ask: Gappu sees '20–30: 12 birds' and asks: 'What are the class limits, the class mark and the frequency here?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Limits 20 and 30, width 10, class mark 25, frequency 12. I can read a frequency table now!
teach.nudge: Good! Can you also tell me the middle value of the class, and how wide it is?

topics.title: Building a frequency distribution

learn.hook: Too few classes and you lose the shape of the data; too many and the table is as messy as the raw data. The art is choosing the right classes.
points: Decide equal or unequal classes: equal classes are usual; unequal classes suit data with a very wide range or values bunched in one area (e.g. incomes).
Number of classes is usually between 6 and 15. Number of classes = range ÷ class width (round up to a whole number).
Class limits should be clear and avoid gaps or overlaps. Open-ended classes (like 'below 10' or '90 and above') are avoided where possible because they have no mid-point.
Tally marks count frequencies in groups of five: four strokes and a fifth crossing them (𝍸).
Grouping causes loss of information: once grouped, every value in a class is treated as if it were equal to the class mark.

example.q: Marks range from 30 to 99. You want exclusive classes of width 10. How many classes are needed, and what are they?
steps: Number of classes = 69 / 10 = 6.9, round up to 7

learn.reallife: Income tax slabs are a frequency-style grouping with unequal classes, because incomes are spread over a very wide range.

games.title: Building classes
items: The number of classes is usually between 6 and 15.
This keeps the table readable without losing too much detail.
Open-ended classes are preferred because they have clear mid-points.
Open-ended classes have no defined mid-point, so they are avoided.
Grouping data causes some loss of information.
Individual values are replaced by the class mark.
Unequal classes may suit income data with a very wide range.
They avoid many near-empty classes.
A tally mark group shows ten observations.
Each tally group shows five observations.

quiz.q: Data range from 10 to 89. With a class width of 10, how many classes are needed?
quiz.explain: Range = 89 − 10 = 79, and 79/10 = 7.9, which is rounded up to 8 classes (10–20 up to 80–90).
quiz.mistake: Rounds 7.9 down, or forgets to divide the range by the width

options: Marks of a class test out of 50
Heights of students between 140 and 180 cm

quiz.explain: A huge range with bunching at one end is better shown with unequal classes.
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal classes always work

quiz.q: Open-ended classes such as 'Above 80' are generally avoided because:
options: They make the table too long
quiz.explain: Without an upper limit, the class mark cannot be found, which hampers calculations.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the problem with missing limits

options: A stroke crossing the previous four

quiz.mistake: Does not know the convention for groups of five

quiz.q: If 4 complete tally groups and 3 extra strokes are marked against a class, its frequency is:
quiz.mistake: Counts each tally group as one or adds 4 and 3

quiz.q: The values 21, 22, 23 and 28 fall in the class 20–30. After grouping, what single value represents each of them?
quiz.explain: Every value in the class is represented by the class mark (20 + 30)/2 = 25. This is the loss of information in grouping.
quiz.mistake: Uses a class limit, or the actual average of the values (23.5), instead of the class mark

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Grouping data into classes leads to some loss of information.
Reason (R): After grouping, individual values are replaced by the class mark.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Replacing actual values with the mid-point is exactly why detail is lost.
quiz.mistake: Thinks grouped data keep every detail

quiz.q: Raw data: 5, 12, 18, 23, 7, 15, 28, 21, 9, 14. Using classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30 (exclusive), what is the frequency of 10–20?
quiz.explain: Values from 10 up to but not including 20: 12, 18, 15, 14, so 4.
quiz.mistake: Includes values from another class or misses one

teach.ask: Gappu has 200 bird weights from 12 g to 96 g. 'How many classes should I make, and how wide?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Find the range, pick a width, divide to get the number of classes, then tally! Perfect table!
teach.nudge: Good! But how do you decide the number of classes? Which two numbers do you divide?

topics.title: Exclusive and inclusive classes

learn.hook: A student scores exactly 20. Does she go in 10–20 or 20–30? The method you use decides, and getting it wrong double-counts students.
points: Exclusive method: the upper limit of one class is the lower limit of the next (10–20, 20–30). A value equal to the upper limit is excluded from that class and goes into the next. So 20 goes into 20–30.
Inclusive method: both limits are included in the class (10–19, 20–29). There is a gap between the upper limit of one class and the lower limit of the next.
Inclusive classes suit discrete data (like marks in whole numbers).

Adjustment: to make inclusive classes continuous, find the gap between one class's upper limit and the next class's lower limit, then subtract half the gap from every lower limit and add half to every upper limit. E.g. 10–19, 20–29 → 9.5–19.5, 19.5–29.5.
The class mark is unchanged by the adjustment, but the class width becomes the true width (10 instead of 9).

example.q: Adjust the inclusive classes 30–39, 40–49, 50–59.

learn.reallife: Census age tables use inclusive groups like 0–4, 5–9, 10–14 years, because age there is recorded in completed whole years.

items.text: Inclusive classes 20–29, 30–39: half the gap is ___.
In exclusive classes 10–20 and 20–30, the value 20 is placed in ___.

quiz.q: In the exclusive method with classes 40–50 and 50–60, a value of exactly 50 goes into:
quiz.explain: The upper limit is excluded, so 50 goes into the class starting at 50.
quiz.mistake: Places the value in the class where it is the upper limit

quiz.q: In the inclusive method, classes are written as:
quiz.explain: Both limits are included, so classes do not share limits.
quiz.mistake: Confuses inclusive with exclusive form

quiz.q: Adjust the inclusive class 60–69 (next class 70–79). The adjusted class is:
quiz.mistake: Adds the full gap or adjusts only one limit

quiz.q: For inclusive classes 10–14, 15–19, 20–24, what is the correction (half the gap) to be applied?
quiz.explain: Gap = 15 − 14 = 1, half of it is 0.5.
steps: Gap = next lower limit − this upper limit = 15 − 14 = 1
quiz.mistake: Uses the full gap or the class width

quiz.q: After adjusting 10–14 to 9.5–14.5, what is the true class width?
quiz.explain: 14.5 − 9.5 = 5. The unadjusted '14 − 10 = 4' understates the width.
quiz.mistake: Uses the unadjusted limits

quiz.q: The class mark of the inclusive class 20–29 is:
quiz.mistake: Assumes the mid-point is a round number like 25

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Inclusive classes need adjustment before drawing a histogram.
Reason (R): Inclusive classes have gaps between the upper limit of one class and the lower limit of the next.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A histogram needs continuous classes, so the gaps must be removed by adjustment.
quiz.mistake: Does not see why gaps matter

quiz.q: Marks (whole numbers) are to be grouped by the inclusive method with class width 10, starting at 0. The third class is:
quiz.explain: Classes are 0–9, 10–19, 20–29, so the third is 20–29.
quiz.mistake: Writes exclusive-style limits or starts the count at the wrong class

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'A bird weighs exactly 30 g. Should it go in 20–30 or 30–40? And what are classes like 20–29?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Exclusive: 30 goes to 30–40. Inclusive classes include both limits, and we adjust them by half the gap!
teach.nudge: Good! But how do we turn 20–29 and 30–39 into continuous classes? What do we add or subtract?

topics.title: Frequency arrays and bivariate distributions

learn.hook: Survey 30 families on how many members they have and the answers are just 2, 3, 4, 5, 6… Grouping them into classes like 2–4 would be silly. A frequency array is the neat solution.
points: A frequency array is a frequency distribution for a discrete variable: each value is listed with its frequency, without class intervals (e.g. household size 1, 2, 3… with number of households).
A univariate distribution deals with one variable. A bivariate (two-way) frequency distribution shows the joint frequencies of two variables in a table.
In a bivariate table, the rows are classes of one variable and the columns classes of the other; each cell shows how many units fall into both classes.
Example: companies classified by advertisement spending (rows) and sales (columns). Row and column totals give each variable's own (marginal) distribution.

example.q: A bivariate table shows firms by ad spend (₹ lakh) and sales (₹ lakh). The cell 'ad spend 10–20, sales 200–300' shows 4. What does it mean?
steps: Locate the row (ad spend 10–20) and column (sales 200–300).
The cell value counts firms that satisfy both conditions.
example.answer: 4 firms spend ₹10–20 lakh on ads and have sales of ₹200–300 lakh.

learn.reallife: A frequency array of household size from survey data helps planners decide what sizes of homes to build under housing schemes.

games.title: Match each to its distribution type
pairs: Household size with number of households

Height and weight of students cross-classified

items.q: Same data. How many households in total?
Words: in, the, of, a. How many have 2 letters?

quiz.q: A frequency array is used for:
quiz.explain: A frequency array lists each value of a discrete variable with its frequency.
quiz.mistake: Confuses frequency arrays with grouped continuous distributions

quiz.q: Household sizes from a survey: 3, 4, 2, 4, 5, 3, 4, 6, 4, 3. What is the frequency of household size 4?
quiz.explain: Size 4 appears four times.
quiz.mistake: Miscounts when scanning the list

quiz.q: Using the same data (3, 4, 2, 4, 5, 3, 4, 6, 4, 3), how many households have more than 4 members?
quiz.explain: More than 4 means 5 or 6: one each, so 2 households.
quiz.mistake: Includes households of size 4

quiz.q: A distribution showing the joint frequencies of two variables is called:
quiz.explain: Bivariate means two variables classified together.
quiz.mistake: Confuses bivariate with a cumulative table

quiz.q: In a bivariate table of 20 firms, the cell for 'ad spend 5–10' and 'sales 100–200' is 3, and the row total for 'ad spend 5–10' is 8. How many firms with ad spend 5–10 have sales outside 100–200?
quiz.explain: 8 − 3 = 5 firms in that row lie in other sales classes.
quiz.mistake: Adds instead of subtracting from the row total

quiz.q: The row totals in a bivariate table give:
options: The distribution of the row variable alone
quiz.explain: Adding across a row gives that variable's own frequency for each class.
quiz.mistake: Thinks totals still show the joint distribution

quiz.q: Count the letters in each word of the phrase 'DATA IS THE NEW OIL'. What is the frequency of 3-letter words?
quiz.explain: Word lengths: DATA 4, IS 2, THE 3, NEW 3, OIL 3. Three words have 3 letters.
quiz.mistake: Miscounts letters or words

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A bivariate distribution can show whether two variables tend to move together.
Reason (R): It records how often each combination of classes of the two variables occurs.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Seeing which combinations are common hints at how the variables are related.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a two-way table shows only one variable at a time

teach.ask: Gappu has data on both wing span and weight of 50 birds. 'Can I put both in one table? And how do I tabulate egg counts?'
teach.praise: Tweet! A bivariate table for two variables, cells show joint frequencies, and a frequency array for discrete egg counts!
teach.nudge: Good! What do we call a table showing two variables together? And what about a discrete variable like egg count?

topics.title: Forms of presentation and textual presentation

learn.hook: A news anchor reading 'Of 120 crore Indians, about 69% live in villages' uses words. A table or a pie chart could say the same thing. Which works best depends on the data.
points: Data can be presented in three forms: textual (descriptive), tabular and diagrammatic.
Textual presentation describes data in sentences within the text, e.g. 'In a strike, 28 out of 140 workers stayed away'.
It suits small amounts of data and lets the writer emphasise certain points.
Its drawback: the reader must go through the whole passage to grasp the figures, and comparison is difficult when data are many.

example.q: Which form suits this best: 'In a class of 40, 22 are girls and 18 are boys'?
steps: The data have only two figures.
A sentence conveys them clearly without a table.
A table or diagram would add little.
example.answer: Textual presentation, because the data are small.

topics.title: Tabular presentation and classification in tables

learn.hook: A single table in the Census can show literacy for men and women, in villages and cities, for every state. That's the power of rows and columns.
points: A table arranges data in rows (horizontal) and columns (vertical). Each box where a row meets a column is a cell.
Qualitative classification in a table: by attributes, e.g. literacy rate by sex (male/female) and location (rural/urban).
Quantitative classification: by measurable classes, e.g. population by age group 0–14, 15–59, 60+.
Temporal classification: by time, e.g. India's exports for 2019, 2020, 2021.
Spatial classification: by place, e.g. share of India's exports going to different countries.

example.q: A table has 3 rows (Rural, Urban, Total) and 3 columns (Male, Female, Total). How many cells does the body have, and what kind of classification is it?

learn.reallife: RBI's Handbook of Statistics on the Indian Economy is mostly tables, organised by year (temporal) and by state (spatial).

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What exactly is a table? And can I classify bird data in a table in different ways?'
