topics.title: Parts of a table and rules of a good table

learn.hook: A table without a title or unit is like a cricket scorecard without team names. You see numbers but can't tell what they mean.
points: One-way table: data classified by one characteristic; two-way: by two characteristics; three-way: by three characteristics.
Table number (for reference) and title (what, where, when, in brief, placed at the top).
Captions are the column headings; stubs are the row headings. The body holds the actual data.
Unit of measurement (e.g. ₹ crore, '000 tonnes) is stated, usually with the title or headings. Source says where the data came from; a note explains anything special, placed below the table.
Large figures are rounded and the unit stated (e.g. 12,34,56,789 written as 12.35 crore).

example.q: Convert into a table: 'In 2011, literacy was 82% among males and 65% among females; in 2001 it was 75% among males and 54% among females.'
steps: Title: Literacy rate in India by sex, 2001 and 2011 (in %)
example.answer: A two-way table with years as stubs and sex as captions.

learn.reallife: Every table in the Economic Survey carries a title, unit, and a source line such as 'Source: NSO, MoSPI'.

quiz.explain: Captions head the columns.

topics.title: Bar diagrams: simple, multiple and component

learn.hook: In one glance at a bar chart, you can see which state grows the most rice. That speed is why diagrams exist, even though tables are more exact.
points: Diagrams give a quick, attractive picture of data and help memory, but they are less exact than tables.
Simple bar diagram: bars of equal width with equal gaps; only the height (length) shows the value. Used for discrete variables, attributes, time series and non-frequency data.
Multiple bar diagram: two or more bars drawn side by side for each category to compare data sets, e.g. literacy in 2001 and 2011 for each state.
Component (sub-divided) bar diagram: each bar is split into parts showing components of a total, e.g. enrolment split into boys and girls.
Percentage component bar: every bar has height 100 and the parts show percentage shares.

example.q: A school has 300 students: 120 in Science, 105 in Commerce, 75 in Arts. In a percentage component bar, what heights do the three parts have?

learn.reallife: News channels on results day use multiple bar diagrams to compare seats won by parties in two elections, side by side.

Only the height shows the value; widths are equal and arbitrary.
Bars in a bar diagram have equal gaps between them.
Equal spacing is a rule of bar diagrams.
In a percentage component bar, each bar's total height is 100.
Parts show percentage shares of the total.
Diagrams are more exact than tables.
Tables give exact values; diagrams are approximate.
Multiple bars place bars for different series side by side.
This allows direct comparison.

quiz.q: In a simple bar diagram, the value of each item is shown by the bar's:

quiz.mistake: Mixes up bar diagrams and histograms

options: Both A and R are true and R explains A

topics.title: Pie diagrams

learn.hook: Every rupee the Union Government spends can be shown as one pie: interest, defence, subsidies, states' share... Each slice's angle tells its share.
points: A pie diagram is a circle divided into sectors, each sector showing a component's share of the total.
Sector angle = (component value ÷ total) × 360°. If shares are already in percent, angle = percentage × 3.6°.
All the sector angles add up to 360° and all percentages to 100.

Pie diagrams suit data showing parts of a whole at one point of time (e.g. budget shares, religious or occupational composition). They do not suit time series like monthly rainfall, where a bar diagram or line graph is better.

example.q: A family spends: food ₹8,000, rent ₹6,000, education ₹4,000, others ₹2,000. Find the sector angles.

learn.reallife: The Budget at a Glance document shows 'Rupee comes from' and 'Rupee goes to' as pie charts every year.

games.title: Is a pie diagram suitable?

quiz.q: Out of ₹5,000 monthly expenses, a student spends ₹1,250 on books. The sector angle for books is:
quiz.mistake: Gives the percentage (25) instead of the angle

quiz.q: In a pie diagram, the sum of all sector angles is:
quiz.explain: A full circle measures 360°.
quiz.mistake: Confuses angles with percentages (which add to 100)

quiz.q:

Reason (R): The angles of all sectors together make up the full circle of 360°, representing the total.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because the circle stands for the total, its slices naturally show parts of the whole.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the full circle to the whole

topics.title: Histograms

learn.hook: A histogram looks like a bar diagram with its bars squeezed together. But the missing gaps carry real meaning.
points: A histogram is a set of adjacent rectangles drawn on class intervals of a continuous variable; the area of each rectangle is proportional to the class frequency.
It is used only for continuous data (classes in exclusive form, so inclusive classes must first be adjusted). There are no gaps between rectangles.
With equal classes, heights can be the frequencies. With unequal classes, heights are frequency densities = frequency ÷ class width.

Mode can be located from a histogram: join the top-right corner of the tallest rectangle to the top-right corner of the rectangle before it, and its top-left corner to the top-left corner of the rectangle after it; the x-value directly below the point where these two lines cross is the mode.
Histogram vs bar diagram: in a histogram both width and height matter (area shows frequency); in a bar diagram only height matters, bars have equal width and gaps.

example.q: Classes 0–10 (f = 5), 10–30 (f = 20), 30–35 (f = 10). Find the heights for a histogram.

learn.reallife: Hospitals plot histograms of patients' waiting times to see where most patients wait, and to spot the modal waiting time.

games.title: Histogram or bar?
items: A histogram has gaps between rectangles.
Rectangles are adjacent because the variable is continuous.
In a histogram the area of a rectangle is proportional to frequency.
That is the defining rule.
A histogram can be drawn for qualitative data like religion.
It needs a continuous variable.
With unequal classes, heights should be frequency densities.
Density = frequency ÷ width keeps areas proportional.
Mode can be estimated graphically from a histogram.
Using the tallest rectangle and its neighbours.
In a bar diagram, bar width matters.
Only height matters in a bar diagram.

quiz.q: A histogram can be drawn only for:
quiz.explain: Its rectangles stand on continuous class intervals.
quiz.mistake: Thinks histograms suit any data

quiz.q: In a histogram, the frequency of a class is proportional to the rectangle's:
quiz.explain: Area (width × height) represents frequency.
quiz.mistake: Applies the bar diagram rule

quiz.q: Class 20–40 has frequency 30. If classes are unequal, the height of its rectangle (frequency density) is:
quiz.mistake: Uses the frequency itself as height with unequal classes

quiz.q: Classes 0–5 (f = 10) and 5–15 (f = 10). Which rectangle is taller in the histogram?
quiz.explain: Densities: 10/5 = 2 and 10/10 = 1. Equal frequencies spread over a wider class give a shorter rectangle.
quiz.mistake: Uses raw frequency as height despite unequal widths

quiz.q: Inclusive classes 10–19, 20–29 must be converted before drawing a histogram because:
options: Histograms need continuous classes without gaps
quiz.explain: The gaps (19 to 20) must be removed: 9.5–19.5, 19.5–29.5.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the gap problem

quiz.q: Which can be located graphically using a histogram?
quiz.explain: The mode is found from the tallest rectangle and lines to its neighbours.
quiz.mistake: Confuses with the median, which is found from ogives

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): In a histogram, rectangles are drawn without gaps.
Reason (R): The class intervals of a continuous variable are continuous, with no breaks between them.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Continuous classes run into each other, so the rectangles touch.
quiz.mistake: Thinks gaps are just a style choice

quiz.q: A class 50–60 has frequency 12 and the next class 60–80 has frequency 12. What is the frequency density of 60–80?
quiz.explain: Width = 20, density = 12/20 = 0.6.
quiz.mistake: Divides by 10 out of habit instead of by the actual width

teach.ask: Gappu drew bars with gaps for bird weights 10–20 g, 20–30 g. 'Is that a histogram? What makes a histogram special?'
teach.praise: Tweet! No gaps for continuous classes, area shows frequency, use density for unequal classes, and it even shows the mode!

topics.title: Frequency polygon, frequency curve and ogives

learn.hook: Draw two ogives on the same graph and something magical happens: the point where they cross drops straight down to the median.
points: Frequency polygon: join the mid-points of the tops of histogram rectangles with straight lines, and close it by joining to the mid-points of zero-frequency classes at both ends. Or plot frequency against class marks directly.
Frequency curve: a smooth freehand curve drawn through the points of the frequency polygon.
Less-than ogive: cumulative frequencies ('less than' the upper limit) plotted against upper class limits; it rises from left to right.
More-than ogive: cumulative frequencies ('more than' the lower limit) plotted against lower class limits; it falls from left to right.
The two ogives intersect at a point whose x-coordinate is the median.

example.q: Classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40 have frequencies 4, 6, 8, 2. Find the less-than and more-than cumulative frequencies.

learn.reallife: Board result analysts use ogives to read off how many students scored below 33% or above 90% without listing every score.

games.title: Match the graph to its rule

quiz.q: A less-than ogive is drawn by plotting cumulative frequencies against:
quiz.explain: 'Less than' totals are measured up to the upper limit of each class.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the rules for the two ogives

quiz.q: A more-than ogive generally:
quiz.explain: 'More than' totals get smaller as the lower limit increases.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all cumulative curves rise

quiz.q: The median of a distribution can be found graphically from:
options: The intersection of less-than and more-than ogives
quiz.explain: The x-value of the meeting point of the two ogives is the median.
quiz.mistake: Confuses with the mode, which is found from a histogram

quiz.q: Frequencies 5, 8, 12, 5 for classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40. What is the 'less than 30' cumulative frequency?
quiz.mistake: Takes only the frequency of the 20–30 class

quiz.q: Same data (5, 8, 12, 5 for 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40). What is the 'more than 20' cumulative frequency?
quiz.mistake: Includes the 10–20 class or only one class

quiz.q: A frequency polygon is closed at both ends by:
options: Joining to the mid-points of imaginary zero-frequency classes
Joining the first and last points directly
quiz.explain: Extending to zero-frequency classes on each side closes the polygon on the x-axis.
quiz.mistake: Does not know how the polygon is closed

quiz.q: Less-than and more-than ogives meet at a point where x = 34 and y = 25. What is the median?
quiz.explain: The median is the x-coordinate of the intersection: 34. (The y-value 25 is N/2.)
quiz.mistake: Reads the y-coordinate instead of the x-coordinate

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A frequency curve is drawn as a smooth freehand curve.
Reason (R): It is drawn through the points of a frequency polygon to smooth out its sharp corners.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Smoothing the polygon's points gives the frequency curve.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the curve is drawn with straight lines

topics.title: Arithmetic line graphs and choosing a diagram

learn.hook: Plot India's exports and imports year by year on one graph and the widening gap between the two lines tells the trade deficit story without a single sentence.
points: An arithmetic line graph (time series graph) plots time on the x-axis and the value of the variable on the y-axis; points are joined by straight lines.
It shows trends, cycles and seasonal ups and downs, e.g. monthly vegetable prices or yearly GDP growth.
Multiple line graphs plot two or more series on the same axes for comparison, e.g. exports and imports, or growth rates of agriculture, industry and services.

Choosing a diagram: time series → line graph or bar diagram; parts of a whole → pie or component bar; continuous frequency distribution → histogram, polygon or ogive; categories → simple or multiple bar.

example.q: Which diagram suits each? (a) monthly rainfall in Chennai, (b) share of food, rent and travel in a budget, (c) heights of 200 students in classes, (d) sectoral growth rates over 10 years.
steps: (a) A time series: bar diagram or line graph.
(b) Parts of a whole: pie diagram.
(d) Several time series: multiple line graph.
example.answer: (a) bar/line graph, (b) pie, (c) histogram, (d) multiple line graph

learn.reallife: RBI and MoSPI release charts of monthly CPI inflation as line graphs, making it easy to see if inflation is rising or easing.

items: In a time series graph, time is plotted on the x-axis.
The horizontal axis shows years, months etc.
A line graph is suitable for showing trends over time.

quiz.explain: It is a time series graph, so time goes on the horizontal axis.

quiz.explain: Three time series on the same axes are best compared with a multiple line graph.
quiz.mistake: Picks a pie because there are three sectors

quiz.q: Exports were ₹400 crore and imports ₹550 crore in a year. If both are plotted on a multiple line graph, what is the vertical gap (trade deficit) that year, in ₹ crore?
quiz.explain: Deficit = imports − exports = 550 − 400 = ₹150 crore.
quiz.mistake: Adds the two series instead of finding the gap

quiz.q: A line graph mainly helps to show:
quiz.explain: It reveals upward or downward movement over time.
quiz.mistake: Confuses with a pie diagram

quiz.q: Which data are best shown by a histogram?
options: Number of students in each stream
Weights of 100 babies in classes 2–2.5 kg, 2.5–3 kg, etc.
quiz.explain: A continuous frequency distribution suits a histogram.
quiz.mistake: Uses a histogram for categories

quiz.q: Vegetable prices rise every summer and fall every winter, year after year. On a monthly line graph, this pattern is called:
quiz.explain: Regular movements within a year are seasonal.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a seasonal pattern with a long-term trend

quiz.q: A firm's sales were 100, 120, 150 and 180 units in four years. By how many units did sales rise from the first to the last year, as shown by the line graph?
quiz.mistake: Reads only the last value

items: Yr 1
Yr 2
Yr 3
Yr 4

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A multiple line graph is useful for comparing India's exports and imports over time.
Reason (R): Both series can be plotted on the same axes, showing their trends and the gap between them.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Plotting both on common axes makes their comparison direct.
quiz.mistake: Thinks each series needs a separate graph

teach.ask: Gappu recorded the forest temperature every month for two years. 'What graph shows how it changed? And what if I add rainfall too?'
teach.praise: Tweet! A line graph with time on the x-axis shows trends and seasons, and a multiple line graph compares two series!
teach.nudge: Good! Which axis holds time? And how would you show temperature and rainfall together?

topics.title: Averages and the arithmetic mean of ungrouped data

learn.hook: A batter scores 12, 98, 45, 0 and 70 in five innings. One number, the average, sums up the whole series. But which way of computing it is fastest?
points: An average (measure of central tendency) is a single value that represents the whole data set. We study three: arithmetic mean, median and mode. (Geometric and harmonic means exist but are not studied here.)
Arithmetic mean = sum of observations ÷ number of observations: X̄ = ΣX / N (direct method).
Assumed mean method: pick a convenient A, find deviations d = X − A, then X̄ = A + Σd / N.
Step deviation method: if deviations share a common factor c, use d′ = (X − A)/c, then X̄ = A + (Σd′ / N) × c.
All three methods give exactly the same answer; the short-cut methods only reduce arithmetic.

example.q: Find the mean of 40, 50, 55, 78 and 58 by the direct and assumed mean (A = 55) methods.

learn.reallife: Cricket's batting average and a city's average daily AQI reported by the CPCB are both arithmetic means.

items.q: Mean of the first 5 natural numbers

games.title: Match the method to its formula

quiz.q: Find the arithmetic mean of 12, 15, 18, 21 and 24.
quiz.mistake: Gives the total instead of dividing by N

quiz.q: Using an assumed mean A = 50, the sum of deviations of 10 observations is 20. What is the mean?
quiz.mistake: Adds Σd directly to A without dividing by N

quiz.q: By the step deviation method: A = 50, c = 10, Σd′ = −3, N = 6. Find the mean.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by c, or ignores the negative sign

quiz.q: Marks: 60, 70, 80, 90, 100. Using A = 80 and c = 10, Σd′ equals:
quiz.explain: d′ = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, which sum to 0, so X̄ = 80.
quiz.mistake: Adds only the positive deviations

quiz.q: Daily earnings of 4 auto drivers are ₹600, ₹750, ₹820 and ₹830. What is their mean earning?
quiz.mistake: Takes the middle values' average or forgets to divide

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the three averages studied in this chapter?
quiz.explain: Geometric and harmonic means exist but are outside this chapter.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every mean is part of the syllabus

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The assumed mean and direct methods give the same arithmetic mean.
Reason (R): The assumed mean method simply shifts the origin to A and then adds A back.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Subtracting A and adding it back cannot change the mean; it only makes the arithmetic easier.
quiz.mistake: Thinks short-cut methods give approximate answers

quiz.q: What is the mean of the first 10 natural numbers?
quiz.mistake: Picks the middle number 5 or the sum 55

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'I counted 3, 5, 6, 8 and 8 seeds in five nests. How do I find one number for all of them? Is there a shortcut?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Add them, divide by 5: 6 seeds. And the assumed mean shortcut gives the same answer!
teach.nudge: Good! After adding the values, what do you divide by? And is there a shortcut using deviations?

topics.title: Mean of discrete and continuous series

learn.hook: When 50 families report their sizes or 200 workers report wages in classes, you can't add values one by one. Frequencies and mid-points do the heavy lifting.
points: Discrete series: X̄ = ΣfX / Σf. Short cuts: X̄ = A + Σfd / Σf, or X̄ = A + (Σfd′ / Σf) × c.
Continuous series: replace each class by its mid-point m, then X̄ = Σfm / Σf (or the same short cuts with d = m − A).
Inclusive classes: mid-points are the same before and after adjustment, so the mean is unaffected. Unequal classes: just use each class's own mid-point.
Cumulative tables: first convert 'less than' or 'more than' cumulative frequencies back into simple class frequencies by subtraction, then find the mean.

example.q: Classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40 have f = 5, 10, 20, 15. Find the mean by direct and step deviation methods.

learn.reallife: Labour Bureau wage surveys group workers into wage classes; average wages are computed exactly this way using mid-points.

games.title: Mean of a continuous series
items: Find the mid-point m of each class
Multiply each mid-point by its frequency (fm)
Add to get Σfm and Σf
Divide Σfm by Σf

quiz.q: X: 10, 20, 30 with f: 2, 3, 5. Find the mean.
quiz.mistake: Takes the simple mean of the X values (20) ignoring frequencies

quiz.q: Classes 0–20, 20–40, 40–60 have frequencies 4, 6, 10. Find the mean.
quiz.mistake: Uses class limits instead of mid-points, or forgets to divide

quiz.q: Using step deviation: A = 45, c = 10, Σfd′ = 6 and Σf = 30. What is the mean?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by c (gets 45.2) or adds Σfd′ directly

quiz.q: Less-than cumulative frequencies: <10: 3, <20: 8, <30: 15, <40: 20. What is the frequency of the class 20–30?
quiz.mistake: Reads the cumulative figure as the class frequency

quiz.q: More-than cumulative frequencies: >0: 50, >10: 45, >20: 35, >30: 15, >40: 0. Find the mean (classes 0–10 to 30–40).
quiz.mistake: Uses the cumulative frequencies directly as frequencies

quiz.q: Unequal classes 0–10, 10–30, 30–60 have frequencies 5, 10, 5. Find the mean.
quiz.mistake: Assumes equal class widths and uses wrong mid-points

quiz.q: For inclusive classes 10–19, 20–29, 30–39, the mid-point used for the class 20–29 is:
quiz.explain: (20 + 29)/2 = 24.5, and adjustment to 19.5–29.5 gives the same 24.5.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the mid-point is a round number

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Adjusting inclusive classes does not change the arithmetic mean.
Reason (R): Adjustment changes all class mid-points by half the gap.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Adjustment lowers each lower limit and raises each upper limit by the same amount, so mid-points do not change; R is false.
quiz.mistake: Thinks adjustment shifts the mid-points

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'I grouped birds by weight into classes with frequencies. How do I find the mean weight now?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Mid-points times frequencies, add them up, and divide by the total frequency!
teach.nudge: Good! But what value represents each class? And what do you divide by at the end?

topics.title: Properties of the mean, weighted mean and missing frequencies

learn.hook: If a billionaire walks into a village tea stall, the average wealth of the people inside jumps to thousands of crores. Nobody got richer. That is the mean's biggest weakness.
points: Property 1: the sum of deviations of observations from their arithmetic mean is always zero: Σ(X − X̄) = 0.
Property 2: the mean is affected by extreme values; one very large or small item can pull it a long way.
Weighted mean X̄w = ΣwX / Σw, where weights w reflect the relative importance of items (e.g. budget shares, credits of subjects).
Missing frequency: write ΣfX and Σf in terms of the unknown, set ΣfX / Σf equal to the given mean, and solve.
Changes: adding k to every value raises the mean by k; multiplying every value by k multiplies the mean by k; replacing one value changes the sum and hence the mean.

example.q: X: 10, 20, 30, 40 with f: 5, f₁, 10, 5. The mean is 25. Find f₁.

learn.reallife: Your CGPA is a weighted mean: a 4-credit subject counts twice as much as a 2-credit one.

games.title: Properties of the mean
items: The sum of deviations from the mean is always zero.
Positive and negative deviations exactly cancel.
The mean is not affected by extreme values.
The mean uses every value, so extremes pull it.
If 5 is added to every observation, the mean rises by 5.
The total rises by 5N, so the mean rises by 5.
In a weighted mean, all items always get equal weight.
Weights reflect different importance.
Doubling every observation doubles the mean.
The sum doubles while N is unchanged.

items.q: Mean 20 of 5 values; one value 30 changed to 80. New mean?
Mean is 12. Add 3 to every value. New mean?
Mean is 7. Multiply every value by 4. New mean?
Deviations from mean: −3, −1, 4 and x. x?

quiz.q: For the data 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, what is the sum of deviations from the mean?
quiz.explain: Mean = 8; deviations −4, −2, 0, 2, 4 sum to 0. This always holds for the mean.
quiz.mistake: Adds absolute deviations or the values themselves

quiz.q: A student scores 80 in Economics (weight 3), 70 in English (weight 2) and 40 in Hindi (weight 1). Find the weighted mean.
quiz.explain: ΣwX = 240 + 140 + 40 = 420; Σw = 6; weighted mean = 70.
quiz.mistake: Takes the simple mean (190/3 = 63.33) ignoring weights

quiz.q: The mean of 10 observations is 15. Later it is found that one value 24 was wrongly recorded as 42. What is the correct mean?
quiz.explain: Wrong sum = 150; correct sum = 150 − 42 + 24 = 132; correct mean = 13.2.
quiz.mistake: Adds the difference instead of subtracting it

quiz.q: X: 1, 2, 3, 4 with f: 4, f₁, 6, 4. The mean is 2.5. Find f₁.
quiz.explain: ΣfX = 4 + 2f₁ + 18 + 16 = 38 + 2f₁ and Σf = 14 + f₁. Then 2.5(14 + f₁) = 38 + 2f₁, so 35 + 2.5f₁ = 38 + 2f₁, giving 0.5f₁ = 3 and f₁ = 6.
quiz.mistake: Sets up ΣfX or Σf incorrectly, e.g. forgets to multiply f₁ by its X value

quiz.q: Five workers earn ₹10,000 each. A sixth worker who earns ₹70,000 joins. What happens to the mean wage?
quiz.explain: New total = 50,000 + 70,000 = ₹1,20,000; mean = 1,20,000/6 = ₹20,000. One extreme value doubles the mean.
quiz.mistake: Thinks one person cannot change the average much

quiz.q: The mean of 6 observations is 40. If 5 is added to each observation, the new mean is:
quiz.explain: Adding a constant to every value raises the mean by that constant.
quiz.mistake: Adds 5 × 6 = 30 to the mean

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The arithmetic mean may not represent data with extreme values well.
Reason (R): The sum of deviations of items from the mean is zero.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, but the zero-sum property does not explain why extremes distort the mean; the reason is that every value enters the sum.
quiz.mistake: Links two true statements that are not cause and effect

quiz.q: A household index uses weights 50 for food, 30 for housing and 20 for others. Price relatives are 120, 110 and 130. Find the weighted mean relative.
quiz.mistake: Uses the simple mean 120 and ignores the weights

quiz.q: X: 10, 20, 30 with f: 3, f₁, 4. The mean is 21. Find f₁ and then the median.
quiz.explain: ΣfX = 30 + 20f₁ + 120 = 150 + 20f₁ and Σf = 7 + f₁. 21(7 + f₁) = 150 + 20f₁ gives f₁ = 3. Then N = 10, cf = 3, 6, 10, and the 5th and 6th items are both 20, so the median is 20.
quiz.mistake: Stops after finding f₁, or gives the mean (21) instead of the median

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'My flock's average weight shot up when one giant eagle joined. Why? And how do I give some birds more importance?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The mean is pulled by extreme values, a weighted mean gives importance, and deviations from the mean sum to zero!
teach.nudge: Good! Why did one eagle change the mean so much? And how would weights work?

topics.title: Median of ungrouped and discrete data

learn.hook: Line up five friends by height. The one in the middle is the median, and she stays the middle even if the tallest friend is swapped for a basketball star.
points: The median is the middle value of data arranged in ascending or descending order; it divides the data into two equal halves. It is a positional average.
It is not affected by extreme values, since only position matters.
Ungrouped data: median = size of the ((N + 1)/2)th item. If N is even, it is the mean of the two middle items (N/2 and N/2 + 1).
Discrete series: arrange X in order, find cumulative frequencies (cf), locate the ((N + 1)/2)th item; the X whose cf first equals or exceeds this position is the median.

example.q: X: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 with f: 2, 5, 8, 6, 4. Find the median.
steps: cf first reaches 13 or more at 15, where X = 3

learn.reallife: Household income reports often quote the median income, because a few billionaires would distort the mean.

games.title: Finding the median of raw data
items: Arrange the data in ascending order
Count the number of items N
Find the position (N + 1)/2
Read the value at that position (average the two middle values if N is even)

quiz.q: Find the median of 7, 3, 9, 5, 11.
quiz.explain: Ordered: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11. The 3rd item is 7.
quiz.mistake: Picks the middle value without arranging the data first

quiz.q: Find the median of 12, 5, 8, 20, 15, 10.
quiz.explain: Ordered: 5, 8, 10, 12, 15, 20. Middle items are 10 and 12, so median = 11.
steps: N = 6, so take the 3rd and 4th items
quiz.mistake: Takes only one of the two middle items

quiz.q: In ungrouped data with N = 15 items arranged in order, the median is the:
quiz.mistake: Uses N/2 instead of (N + 1)/2 for ungrouped data

quiz.q: X: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 with f: 2, 5, 8, 6, 4. What is the median?
quiz.explain: N = 25, cf = 2, 7, 15, 21, 25. The 13th item falls where cf = 15, at X = 3.
quiz.mistake: Picks the X with the highest frequency (that is the mode)

quiz.q: X: 10, 20, 30, 40 with f: 3, 4, 5, 4. Find the median.
quiz.explain: N = 16; (N + 1)/2 = 8.5th item. cf: 3, 7, 12, 16. Both the 8th and 9th items are 30, so median = 30.
steps: 8th and 9th items both lie in cf 8–12 → X = 30
quiz.mistake: Averages two X values without checking where the items fall

quiz.q: Data: 3, 5, 7, 9, 1000. The median is:
quiz.explain: The median is the middle item, 7; the extreme value 1000 does not affect it. (The mean would be 204.8.)
quiz.mistake: Computes the mean instead of the median

quiz.q: Why is the median called a positional average?
options: Because it uses all values in the calculation
Because it is the most frequent value
Because it is always the largest value
Because its value depends on the position of the middle item in ordered data
quiz.explain: It is located by position, not computed from all values.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the median with the mean or mode

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The median is not affected by extreme values.
Reason (R): The median depends only on the middle position of the ordered data.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Since only the middle position matters, changing an extreme value does not move it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the median is sensitive like the mean

teach.ask: Gappu lined up seven birds by weight. 'Which bird is the median? What if one bird is a giant eagle?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Arrange them, pick the middle one, and the giant eagle doesn't move the median at all!
teach.nudge: Good! But do you need to arrange the birds first? And what if one is huge?

topics.title: Median of a continuous series

learn.hook: With 10 lakh board candidates in mark classes, you can't line them up. One neat formula finds the median mark from the class table.
points: Find cumulative frequencies (cf) and N = Σf. The median class is the class containing the (N/2)th item (use N/2 for continuous series).
Median = L + ((N/2 − c.f.) / f) × h
L = lower limit of the median class; c.f. = cumulative frequency of the class just before the median class; f = frequency of the median class; h = width of the median class.
For less-than cumulative data, the given figures already are cf; find simple frequencies by subtraction. For inclusive classes, adjust first so L is the true lower limit (e.g. 19.5).
learn.reallife: NSS reports on household consumption give the median monthly per capita expenditure in addition to the mean, from class-wise tables.

games.title: Match each symbol in the median formula
pairs: Lower limit of the median class
Cumulative frequency before the median class

games.title: Median of a grouped distribution
items: Find cumulative frequencies
Compute N/2
Locate the median class
Note L, c.f., f and h
Apply Median = L + ((N/2 − c.f.)/f) × h

quiz.q: Classes 10–20, 20–30, 30–40, 40–50 have f = 5, 15, 20, 10. Find the median.
quiz.mistake: Uses the cf of the median class itself instead of the class before it

quiz.q: Given L = 40, N/2 = 50, c.f. = 38, f = 24 and h = 10, the median is:
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by h

quiz.q: Less than 10: 5, less than 20: 15, less than 30: 30, less than 40: 36, less than 50: 40. Find the median.
quiz.mistake: Uses the cumulative figure 30 as the class frequency

quiz.q: A distribution has N = 60. The median item for a continuous series is the:
quiz.explain: For a continuous series, the median position is N/2 = 30.
quiz.mistake: Uses (N + 1)/2 for a continuous series

quiz.q: cf of classes 0–10, 10–20, 20–30, 30–40 are 8, 18, 34, 40. Which is the median class?
quiz.explain: N = 40, N/2 = 20. The first cf that equals or exceeds 20 is 34, in the class 20–30.
quiz.mistake: Picks the class whose cf is closest to 20 from below (10–20)

quiz.q: In the median formula, c.f. stands for the cumulative frequency of:
options: The class just before the median class
quiz.explain: c.f. is the cumulative frequency of the class preceding the median class.
quiz.mistake: Uses the median class's own cf

quiz.q: The median class is the inclusive class 30–39 (next class 40–49). Which value of L should be used?
quiz.explain: Adjust first: 30 − 0.5 = 29.5.
quiz.mistake: Uses the unadjusted lower limit

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The median can be calculated even when the first and last classes are open-ended.
Reason (R): The median formula uses only the median class and the cumulative frequency before it.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The end classes' limits are not needed unless one of them is the median class.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every class limit is required

teach.ask: Gappu has bird weights in classes with frequencies. 'How do I find the median weight without lining up all the birds?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Cumulative frequencies, find N/2, locate the median class, and apply L + ((N/2 − cf)/f) × h!
teach.nudge: Good! Which class holds the middle item? How do you find it from the frequencies?

topics.title: Quartiles and percentiles

learn.hook: 'You scored in the 98th percentile' does not mean you got 98 marks. It means you did better than (or as well as) about 98% of test takers.
points: Note: quartiles and percentiles are in the NCERT book; check whether your school examines them this year.
Quartiles divide ordered data into four equal parts. There are three quartiles: Q1 (lower quartile), Q2 (the median) and Q3 (upper quartile).
For ungrouped data: Q1 = size of the ((N + 1)/4)th item; Q3 = size of the (3(N + 1)/4)th item.
Percentiles divide data into 100 equal parts (99 percentiles). P50 is the median, P25 = Q1, P75 = Q3.
Use: 25% of items lie below Q1 and 25% above Q3; e.g. if Q3 of incomes is ₹60,000, the top 25% earn more than ₹60,000.

example.q: Data: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. Find Q1, median and Q3.

learn.reallife: Entrance exams like JEE Main report scores as percentiles, so candidates from different shifts can be compared fairly.

games.title: Quartile facts
items: There are three quartiles.
Q1, Q2 and Q3 split data into four parts.
Q2 is the same as the median.
It divides data into two halves.
The 90th percentile means a score of 90%.
It means 90% of values lie at or below it.
Q3 is also called the upper quartile.
75% of items lie below Q3.
Percentiles divide data into 10 parts.
Deciles do that; percentiles divide into 100 parts.

quiz.q: How many quartiles divide a data set into four equal parts?
quiz.explain: Three cut points (Q1, Q2, Q3) make four parts.
quiz.mistake: Counts parts instead of cut points

quiz.q: For N = 15 ordered items, Q1 is the size of which item?
quiz.mistake: Uses N/4 = 3.75
Picks the 5th item or averages two values
Uses the 2nd item or N/4

quiz.q: P50 (the 50th percentile) is equal to:
quiz.explain: The 50th percentile splits data in half, like the median.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the median with the mean

quiz.q: A student is at the 85th percentile of a test. This means:
options: About 85% of candidates scored at or below her
quiz.explain: A percentile rank tells the share of values at or below that score.
quiz.mistake: Confuses percentile with percentage marks

quiz.q: The upper quartile (Q3) of monthly incomes in a town is ₹60,000. What can we say?
quiz.explain: 75% lie below Q3, so the top 25% earn above it.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the shares above and below Q3

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Like the median, quartiles are positional measures.
Reason (R): Quartiles are located by the positions of items in ordered data.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Quartiles, like the median, depend on position, not on adding all values.
quiz.mistake: Thinks quartiles are computed from the sum of values

teach.ask: Gappu heard that he is in the 90th percentile for singing. 'Did I get 90 marks? Teach me quartiles and percentiles!'
teach.praise: Tweet! The 90th percentile means 90% scored at or below me. Quartiles split data into four parts, and Q2 is the median!
teach.nudge: Hmm, is the 90th percentile the same as 90 marks? What does a percentile tell me?

topics.title: Mode

learn.hook: A shoe shop doesn't care about the average foot size. It wants the size most customers ask for. That's the mode.
points: Mode is the value that occurs most frequently. Data may be unimodal (one mode), bimodal (two), multimodal (more), or have no mode if all values occur equally.
Discrete series: the mode is the value with the highest frequency.
Continuous series: the modal class has the highest frequency. Mode = L + (D1 / (D1 + D2)) × h, where D1 = f1 − f0 and D2 = f1 − f2 (f1 = modal class frequency, f0 = previous class, f2 = next class).
The formula needs equal, exclusive class intervals; convert cumulative or inclusive data first.
Mode suits qualitative data and choices like the most popular shoe, garment or collar size. It can also be located graphically from a histogram.
learn.reallife: Clothing brands decide how many M, L and XL shirts to stock using the modal size in each city.

items.q: X with frequencies 3, 9, 6, 2 for X = 5, 10, 15, 20. Mode?

quiz.q: Find the mode of 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 3, 5.
quiz.explain: 3 occurs three times, more than any other value.
quiz.mistake: Picks the median or mean instead

quiz.q: The data 2, 2, 4, 4, 6 are:
quiz.explain: Both 2 and 4 occur twice, so there are two modes.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a data set can have only one mode
Uses the mid-point of the modal class (35)

quiz.q: Given L = 40, D1 = 8, D2 = 4 and h = 6, the mode is:
quiz.mistake: Uses D1/D2 instead of D1/(D1 + D2)

quiz.q: X: 5, 10, 15, 20 with f: 3, 9, 6, 2. What is the mode?
quiz.explain: The value with the highest frequency (9) is X = 10.
quiz.mistake: Reports the highest frequency instead of the value

quiz.q: A shoe company wants to decide which size to produce in the largest quantity. Which average should it use?
quiz.explain: The most frequently demanded size is the mode.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the mean size is what most customers wear

quiz.q: Why must class intervals be equal before applying the mode formula?
options: Because the mode is always a whole number
Because unequal classes have no frequencies
Because the formula compares frequencies of neighbouring classes, which is fair only when widths are equal
quiz.explain: Frequencies of classes of different widths are not comparable, so the modal class could be misjudged.
quiz.mistake: Does not see why equal widths matter

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Mode can be found for qualitative data such as the most popular colour.
Reason (R): Mode is based on frequency of occurrence, not on numerical values.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Counting which category occurs most needs no numbers, so mode works for attributes.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every average needs numeric data

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Most birds in my flock like mango seeds. Is that the mode? How do I find the mode of grouped weights?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Mode is the most frequent value, the modal class has the highest frequency, and the formula is L + D1/(D1 + D2) × h!
teach.nudge: Good! For grouped data, which class do you start from? And what are D1 and D2?

topics.title: Comparing mean, median and mode

learn.hook: A start-up says 'average salary ₹18 lakh'. The intern says 'most of us earn ₹4 lakh'. Both are telling the truth, using different averages.
points: In a symmetric distribution, mean = median = mode.
In an asymmetric (skewed) distribution, the median lies between the mean and the mode.
Mean: uses all values and suits further algebraic work, but is pulled by extremes and cannot be found with open-ended classes.
Median: unaffected by extremes, works with open-ended classes, suits qualitative ranking (e.g. intelligence) and income or wage data with a few very high values.
Mode: best for the most popular item or size (shoes, garments) and for qualitative data; may not be unique or may not exist.

example.q: Choose the best average: (a) typical wage in a firm where the owner earns ₹50 lakh and 40 workers earn ₹2–3 lakh; (b) the most popular collar size; (c) average marks of a class for computing total marks.
steps: (c) Need a value that relates to the total → mean

learn.reallife: Real-estate portals often quote median home prices, because a few luxury homes would push the mean up.

games.title: Which average fits best?
items: Average runs to compute total runs for a season
Typical income where a few earn crores
Most popular shirt size
Most common mode of travel among students
Middle value of data with open-ended classes
Average daily output for further calculations

games.title: Mean, median, mode
items: In a symmetric distribution, mean, median and mode are equal.
The data balance around the centre.
The median lies between the mean and the mode in a skewed distribution.
This is a standard relation.
The mean can be computed easily for open-ended classes.
Open-ended classes have no mid-points.
The upper quartile is the same as the median.
The upper quartile is Q3; the median is Q2.
The median is a positional average.
It depends on position in ordered data.

quiz.q: In a perfectly symmetric distribution, the mean is 50. The median is:
quiz.explain: In a symmetric distribution mean = median = mode.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the averages always differ

quiz.q: In a skewed distribution, the mean is 40 and the mode is 30. Which value could be the median?
quiz.explain: The median lies between the mean and the mode, so only 35 fits.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the median lies outside the mean–mode range

quiz.q: Which average is most suitable for the typical wage of workers when a few managers earn extremely high salaries?
quiz.explain: The median ignores the extreme salaries.
quiz.mistake: Uses the mean, which is distorted by extremes

quiz.q: Which average should a garment maker use to decide the size to produce most?
quiz.explain: Mode identifies the most demanded size.
quiz.mistake: Picks the mean size

quiz.q: For a distribution with open-ended classes like 'below 10' and '60 and above', the best average is generally the:
quiz.explain: The median can be found without knowing the open ends' limits.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that open-ended classes have no mid-points

quiz.q: Five values have mean 12. Their sum of deviations from the mean is:
quiz.explain: The sum of deviations from the arithmetic mean is always zero.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the mean by N

quiz.q: Which statement is correct?
options: The mean is a positional average
The median is affected by extreme values
The median cannot be found for qualitative data that can be ranked
The mode may not be unique
quiz.explain: Data can be bimodal or multimodal, so the mode may not be unique.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up properties of the three averages

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The arithmetic mean is preferred when further algebraic treatment is needed.
Reason (R): The mean is based on all observations and has useful mathematical properties.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because it uses every value and is algebraically defined, the mean is easy to use in further calculations.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the median is better for algebraic work

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Mean, median or mode: which one should I use to describe my flock? Does it depend?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Use the median when there are extremes, the mode for the most popular, and the mean when every value matters!
teach.nudge: Good! When would the median beat the mean? And when should I use the mode?

topics.title: What correlation studies: types of relationship

learn.hook: Ice-cream sales and drowning cases rise together every summer. Does ice-cream cause drowning? Of course not. Welcome to the trickiest idea in statistics.
points: Correlation studies whether two variables move together, in which direction, and how strongly.
Some relationships are cause and effect (a fall in price raises quantity demanded); others are coincidental.
Spurious correlation: two variables move together because both are driven by a third variable (ice-cream sales and drowning both rise with temperature).
Correlation measures covariation, not causation. The coefficient studied here measures linear (straight-line) relationships.
Positive correlation: both move in the same direction (income and consumption). Negative correlation: they move in opposite directions (price and quantity demanded).

example.q: Classify: (a) height and weight of children, (b) price of a good and quantity demanded, (c) hours of practice and errors made in typing.
steps: (a) Taller children tend to be heavier: same direction → positive.
(b) Higher price, lower quantity demanded: opposite → negative.
(c) More practice, fewer errors: opposite → negative.

learn.reallife: When onion prices rise sharply, families buy fewer onions: a negative correlation between price and quantity demanded that markets see every year.

games.title: Positive or negative correlation?
items: Family income and spending on consumption
Price of a good and quantity demanded
Rainfall and umbrella sales
Hours of study and marks (usually)
Speed of a car and time taken for a trip
Temperature and sales of woollens
Fertiliser use and crop yield (within limits)

games.title: Correlation vs causation
items: A high correlation always means one variable causes the other.
Correlation shows covariation, not causation.
Two variables may be correlated because a third variable affects both.
This is spurious correlation.
Correlation can tell us the direction of a relationship.
It can be positive or negative.
Price and quantity demanded usually show negative correlation.
They move in opposite directions.
Ice-cream sales cause drowning.
Both are driven by hot weather.

quiz.q: Correlation analysis studies:
options: Whether, in which direction and how strongly two variables move together
Only the average of two variables
quiz.explain: Correlation measures the existence, direction and strength of covariation.
quiz.mistake: Thinks correlation establishes causation

quiz.q: Income and consumption expenditure usually show:
quiz.explain: As income rises, consumption tends to rise.
quiz.mistake: Confuses direction of movement

quiz.q: The price of a good and its quantity demanded usually show:
quiz.explain: A higher price usually reduces quantity demanded.
quiz.mistake: Thinks higher price leads to higher demand

quiz.q: Sales of ice-cream and the number of drowning cases are found to be positively correlated. The best explanation is:
options: Both rise because of a third factor, hot weather
Drowning causes people to buy ice-cream
quiz.explain: Hot weather increases both, giving a spurious correlation.
quiz.mistake: Assumes correlation means direct cause

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A strong correlation between two variables proves that one causes the other.
Reason (R): Correlation measures how two variables vary together.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Correlation measures covariation (R is true) but does not prove causation (A is false).
quiz.mistake: Equates covariation with cause and effect

quiz.q: Which pair is most likely to show a cause-and-effect relationship?
options: Shoe size and reading ability of children of different ages
Number of storks and number of births in towns
Height of a tree and a student's marks
Price of a good and its quantity demanded
quiz.explain: A fall in price causes buyers to buy more; the others are coincidental or driven by a third factor (age, town size).
quiz.mistake: Treats every observed association as causal

quiz.q: The correlation coefficient studied in this chapter measures relationships that are:
quiz.explain: It measures the degree of linear (straight-line) relationship.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it measures any kind of relationship

quiz.q: If one variable rises while the other falls, the correlation is:
quiz.explain: Opposite movements mean negative correlation.
quiz.mistake: Confuses negative with zero correlation

teach.ask: Gappu notices: 'When more birds sing, more flowers bloom! Does my singing make flowers bloom? Teach me correlation!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Correlation shows variables moving together, positively or negatively, but it is not causation. Spring causes both!
teach.nudge: Good! But does moving together prove that one causes the other? Could a third factor explain it?

topics.title: Scatter diagrams

learn.hook: Plot each student's study hours against marks as a dot. Before any formula, the cloud of dots already tells the story.
points: A scatter diagram plots each pair of values (X, Y) as a point on a graph, showing the relationship visually.
Points rising from lower left to upper right show positive correlation; falling from upper left to lower right show negative correlation.
Points scattered with no pattern show no (zero) correlation. Points lying exactly on a straight line show perfect correlation (+1 if rising, −1 if falling).
The closer the points lie to a straight line, the stronger the correlation.
A scatter diagram can reveal non-linear relationships (curves), but it does not give a numerical measure of correlation.

example.q: Pairs (study hours, marks): (1, 40), (2, 50), (3, 60), (4, 70), (5, 80). What will the scatter diagram show?
steps: Each extra hour adds exactly 10 marks.
All points lie on one rising straight line.

learn.reallife: Economists plot inflation against interest rates for several years as a scatter to see if the two move together.

games.title: Match the scatter pattern to its correlation
pairs: Points rise on a straight line
Points fall on a straight line
Points rise in a loose band
Points fall in a loose band

games.title: Scatter facts
items: A scatter diagram gives the exact value of the correlation coefficient.
It shows the relationship visually, not numerically.
Points clustered close to a rising line show strong positive correlation.
Closer to a line means stronger.
A scatter diagram can show a curved relationship.
Non-linear patterns are visible.
Points falling from left to right show positive correlation.
That pattern is negative correlation.
Each point represents one pair of observations.
One point per (X, Y) pair.

quiz.q: In a scatter diagram, each point represents:
options: A pair of values of X and Y
quiz.explain: Every observation pair (X, Y) is plotted as one point.
quiz.mistake: Thinks points represent single values

quiz.q: Points in a scatter diagram fall from the upper left to the lower right in a narrow band. The correlation is:
quiz.explain: A falling, tight pattern means a strong negative relationship.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the direction

quiz.q: All points lie exactly on a straight line rising to the right. The correlation coefficient is:
quiz.explain: Points on a rising straight line indicate perfect positive correlation.
quiz.mistake: Confuses perfect positive and perfect negative

quiz.q: Points are scattered all over the graph with no visible pattern. This suggests:
quiz.explain: No trend means no (linear) correlation.
quiz.mistake: Reads a pattern into random scatter

quiz.q: Pairs: (1, 10), (2, 8), (3, 6), (4, 4), (5, 2). What does the scatter diagram show?
quiz.explain: Y falls by exactly 2 for each unit rise in X: all points on a falling straight line, r = −1.
quiz.mistake: Looks only at the first pair

quiz.q: A main limitation of a scatter diagram is that it:
options: Cannot be drawn for economic data
Does not give a numerical measure of correlation
quiz.explain: It gives a visual idea only, not an exact figure.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it cannot show direction

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A scatter diagram can reveal a non-linear relationship that the correlation coefficient may miss.
Reason (R): The correlation coefficient measures only linear relationships.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A curve may give r close to 0, but the scatter clearly shows a pattern.
quiz.mistake: Thinks r captures every kind of relationship

quiz.q: Points form a U-shaped curve on a scatter diagram. The correct conclusion is:
quiz.explain: A U-shape is a clear curved relationship, even though linear correlation may be low.
quiz.mistake: Equates low linear correlation with no relationship

teach.ask: Gappu plotted dots for how high birds fly and how cold they feel. 'The dots go up to the right. What does that mean?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Rising dots mean positive correlation, falling dots negative, no pattern means none, and a straight line is perfect!
teach.nudge: Good! What would falling dots mean? And what if the dots form a perfect line?

topics.title: Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation

learn.hook: One number between −1 and +1 sums up how tightly two variables move together. Karl Pearson gave us the formula that does it.
points: Karl Pearson's coefficient (product moment or simple correlation coefficient) r measures the degree of linear relationship between two variables.
Covariance: cov(X, Y) = Σ(X − X̄)(Y − Ȳ)/N = Σxy/N, where x = X − X̄ and y = Y − Ȳ. Standard deviations: σx = √(Σx²/N), σy = √(Σy²/N).
r = Σxy / (N σx σy), which simplifies to r = Σxy / (√Σx² × √Σy²).
Direct (actual values) formula: r = [NΣXY − ΣXΣY] / [√(NΣX² − (ΣX)²) × √(NΣY² − (ΣY)²)].
Typical uses: years of schooling of farmers vs farm yield; price index vs money supply.
learn.reallife: Studies of Indian farmers have used Pearson's r to check whether more years of schooling go along with higher crop yields.

games.title: Match the symbol to its meaning
Computing r from deviations
items: Find the means X̄ and Ȳ
Find deviations x = X − X̄ and y = Y − Ȳ
Compute xy, x² and y² for each pair
Add to get Σxy, Σx² and Σy²
Apply r = Σxy / (√Σx² × √Σy²)

quiz.q: Given Σxy = 16, Σx² = 10 and Σy² = 40, find r.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the square roots in the denominator

quiz.q: Σxy = 30, N = 10, σx = 2, σy = 3. Find r.
quiz.mistake: Leaves out N from the denominator

quiz.q: For 5 pairs, Σxy = 16. What is the covariance of X and Y?
quiz.mistake: Gives Σxy without dividing by N

quiz.q: Covariance is 3.2, σx = √2 and σy = √8. Find r.
quiz.mistake: Divides by only one standard deviation

quiz.q: N = 5, ΣX = 15, ΣY = 50, ΣXY = 166, ΣX² = 55, ΣY² = 540. Find r by the direct method.
quiz.mistake: Squares ΣX wrongly or forgets to multiply by N

quiz.q: Karl Pearson's coefficient is also known as the:
quiz.explain: It is also called the product moment or simple correlation coefficient.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with Spearman's rank correlation

quiz.q: Σxy = −24, Σx² = 16 and Σy² = 64. Find r.
quiz.mistake: Drops the negative sign

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Pearson's r is a better measure of the degree of relationship than covariance.
Reason (R): Covariance depends on the units of X and Y, while r is a pure number.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Dividing covariance by both standard deviations removes units, so r can be compared across data sets.
quiz.mistake: Thinks covariance and r are equally comparable

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do I turn my scatter of dots into one number? Teach me Karl Pearson's formula!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Find deviations from the means, multiply and add them, divide by the square roots of the squared sums. That's r!
teach.nudge: Good! After finding deviations, what do you multiply? And what goes in the denominator?

topics.title: Properties and interpretation of r

learn.hook: A student computes r = 1.4 and proudly calls it 'super strong correlation'. A strict examiner circles it in red, because it is impossible.
points: r is a pure number with no units, so relationships measured in different units can be compared. This is why it is preferred to covariance.
−1 ≤ r ≤ +1. Any value outside this range means a calculation error.
r is unaffected by a change of origin (adding or subtracting a constant) and of scale (multiplying or dividing by a positive constant).
r = +1: perfect positive; r = −1: perfect negative; r close to ±1: strong; r close to 0: weak; r = 0: no LINEAR relationship (a non-linear one may still exist, so it does not prove independence).
Use common sense: areas with more doctors may show more deaths during an epidemic (doctors are sent where the disease is), but doctors do not cause deaths.

example.q: Heights in cm give r = 0.6 between brothers and sisters. If heights are converted to inches (÷ 2.54), what is r?
steps: Converting units is a change of scale.
r is unaffected by change of scale.

learn.reallife: Market analysts report r between rainfall and kharif output; a value of 0.7 means a fairly strong positive linear link, not that rain is the only cause.

games.title: Properties of r
items: r can be 1.2 if the relationship is very strong.
r cannot exceed +1; 1.2 means an error.
r has no units.
It is a pure number.
Adding 10 to every X value changes r.
Change of origin does not affect r.
r = 0 means the variables are definitely independent.
It only means no linear relation; a curved relation is possible.
r = −1 means perfect negative correlation.
All points lie on a falling straight line.
Multiplying every Y by 5 leaves r unchanged.
Change of scale by a positive constant does not affect r.

quiz.q: The unit of the correlation coefficient is:
options: Product of the units of X and Y
quiz.explain: r is a pure number.
quiz.mistake: Confuses r with covariance, which has units

quiz.q: Which of the following values of r is impossible?
quiz.explain: r must lie between −1 and +1; 1.05 indicates a calculation error.
quiz.mistake: Thinks stronger relationships can exceed 1

quiz.q: r between X and Y is 0.6. If every X is increased by 50 and every Y is divided by 10, the new r is:
quiz.explain: r is unaffected by change of origin and (positive) scale.
quiz.mistake: Applies the transformations to r itself

quiz.q: r = 0 between two variables means:
options: They are independent in every sense
There is no linear relationship between them
quiz.explain: There could still be a non-linear relationship.
quiz.mistake: Equates zero correlation with independence

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Correlation coefficient r is preferred to covariance for measuring the degree of relationship.
Reason (R): r can lie outside the range −1 to +1.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: r is preferred because it is unit-free, but it always lies between −1 and +1; R is false.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the range of r

quiz.q: During an epidemic, districts with more doctors record more deaths. The correct interpretation is:
options: Doctors and deaths are negatively correlated
More doctors were sent to districts where the disease was worse
quiz.explain: The epidemic's severity drives both; common sense rejects a causal reading.
quiz.mistake: Interprets correlation as causation

quiz.q: Which value of r shows the strongest relationship?
quiz.explain: Strength depends on the absolute value; |−0.90| is the largest.
quiz.mistake: Thinks negative values are always weaker

quiz.q: A positive value of r indicates that:
options: X and Y tend to move in the same direction
X and Y move in opposite directions
quiz.explain: Positive r means both tend to rise or fall together.
quiz.mistake: Reads positive r as causation

teach.ask: Gappu got r = 1.3 for wing size and flight speed. 'Wow, super strong! Is that right?' Teach Gappu the properties of r.
teach.praise: Tweet! r lies between −1 and +1, has no units, ignores changes of origin and scale, and r = 0 means no linear relation!
teach.nudge: Hmm, can r ever be more than 1? What range must it stay within?

topics.title: Step deviation method and computing r

learn.hook: Big numbers like 1,20,000 and 3,40,000 make Pearson's formula painful. Shift and shrink them first: r won't even notice.
points: Because r is unaffected by change of origin and scale, define U = (X − A)/B and V = (Y − C)/D for convenient A, B, C, D (B, D > 0).
Compute r using U and V exactly as with X and Y: r_UV = r_XY.
Perfectly linear data (e.g. Y = 2X + 3) give r = +1; Y = −3X + 10 gives r = −1.
Symmetric data such as X: −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 with Y = X² (4, 1, 0, 1, 4) give r = 0, although Y depends exactly on X (non-linear).
learn.reallife: Analysts studying the price index and money supply (in lakh crore) shift and scale the figures first to make hand calculations manageable.

games.title: Step deviation and special cases
items: r calculated from U and V equals r calculated from X and Y.
r is unaffected by change of origin and scale.
Y = 2X + 3 for all observations gives r = +1.
Exactly linear and rising.
Y = X² for X = −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 gives r = +1.
It gives r = 0 because the relation is non-linear and symmetric.
Y = 10 − 3X for all observations gives r = −1.
Exactly linear and falling.
Step deviation changes the strength of correlation.
It only simplifies arithmetic.

quiz.q: U = (X − 30)/10 and V = (Y − 100)/20. If r between U and V is 0.8, then r between X and Y is:
quiz.explain: Change of origin and scale (positive factors) does not alter r.
quiz.mistake: Adjusts r by the scale factors

quiz.q: U: −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 and V: −1, −2, 1, 0, 2 (both means zero). Find r.
quiz.mistake: Miscomputes ΣUV by ignoring signs

quiz.explain: Y = 2X + 3 exactly, a rising straight line, so r = +1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks r must be computed only from the full formula and expects a fraction

quiz.explain: Y = 16 − 3X exactly, a falling straight line, so r = −1.
quiz.mistake: Drops the negative sign

quiz.explain: x = X (mean 0), y = Y − 2 = 2, −1, −2, −1, 2. Σxy = −4 + 1 + 0 − 1 + 4 = 0, so r = 0, even though Y depends on X.
quiz.mistake: Assumes an exact relationship always gives r = ±1

quiz.q: Why is the step deviation method used for computing r?
options: To change the value of r
To convert r into a percentage
To simplify calculations with large numbers, without changing r
quiz.explain: Shifting and scaling makes numbers small; r stays the same.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it changes the result

quiz.q: Σuv = 12, Σu² = 16 and Σv² = 25, where u and v are deviations from their means. Find r.
quiz.mistake: Divides by Σu² × Σv² without square roots

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The Y = X² data with X symmetric around zero give r = 0.
Reason (R): r measures only the linear relationship between variables.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The relation is perfect but curved, and r captures only linear relationships.
quiz.mistake: Thinks r = 0 means no relationship at all

teach.ask: Gappu has huge numbers like 12,000 and 34,000 for nest heights and egg weights. 'Must I square these monsters? Is there a shortcut?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Subtract a constant and divide by another: r stays the same and the numbers become tiny!
teach.nudge: Good idea! But will shifting and dividing the numbers change r? Why or why not?

topics.title: Spearman's rank correlation

learn.hook: Three judges at a college dance contest rank ten performers. Which two judges think most alike? You can't measure 'grace' in centimetres, but you can rank it.
points: Use rank correlation when attributes cannot be measured (beauty, honesty, intelligence), when only ranks are available, when data have extreme values, or when the relationship is monotonic but not linear.
Spearman's formula: r_s = 1 − 6ΣD² / (n³ − n), where D = difference between the two ranks of each item and n = number of pairs.
Case 1, ranks given: find D for each item, square, add, apply the formula.
Case 2, ranks not given: first rank each series (e.g. highest marks = rank 1), then proceed as in Case 1.
Comparing judges: compute r_s for each pair of judges; the pair with the highest r_s agree most.

example.q: Two judges rank 5 dancers: Judge A: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5; Judge B: 2, 1, 4, 3, 5. Find r_s.

learn.reallife: Rankings such as NIRF college rankings can be compared year to year with rank correlation to see how stable the list is.

games.title: Rank correlation or Pearson's r?
items: Judges ranking beauty contestants
Heights and weights of 50 students
Honesty and intelligence ratings
Income and consumption of households
Only the merit-list positions of students are known
Price and quantity data from a market survey

quiz.q: Two judges rank 5 items; ΣD² = 10. Find Spearman's rank correlation.
quiz.mistake: Uses n² − 1 or forgets to multiply ΣD² by 6

quiz.q: For 10 pairs of ranks, ΣD² = 33. Find r_s.
quiz.mistake: Uses n³ instead of n³ − n

quiz.q: Ranks by two judges for 4 contestants: A: 1, 2, 3, 4 and B: 4, 3, 2, 1. Find r_s.
quiz.explain: D = −3, −1, 1, 3; ΣD² = 20; n³ − n = 60; r_s = 1 − 120/60 = −1. Complete disagreement.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square D, giving ΣD = 0

quiz.q: Marks of 5 students in Economics: 85, 70, 92, 60, 78. If the highest marks get rank 1, what is the rank of the student who scored 78?
quiz.mistake: Ranks in ascending order by mistake

quiz.q: Spearman's rank correlation is most appropriate when:
options: Variables are qualitative attributes like honesty that can only be ranked
Both variables are measured precisely in units
Data are only on one variable
quiz.explain: Attributes that cannot be measured can still be ranked.
quiz.mistake: Uses rank correlation only for numerical data

quiz.q: Judges P and Q have r_s = 0.62, Q and R have 0.35, P and R have 0.81. Which pair of judges agree most?
quiz.explain: The highest rank correlation (0.81) shows the closest agreement.
quiz.mistake: Picks the first pair listed

quiz.q: Ranks of 5 items by two judges are identical (D = 0 for all). Find r_s.
quiz.explain: ΣD² = 0, so r_s = 1 − 0 = 1: perfect agreement.
quiz.mistake: Thinks D = 0 means no correlation

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Rank correlation can be used when data contain extreme values.
Reason (R): Ranks are not affected by how extreme a value is, only by its order.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: An extreme value just becomes rank 1 or rank n, so it does not distort the measure.
quiz.mistake: Thinks ranks magnify extremes

teach.ask: Gappu and his friend ranked 5 songs differently. 'How can we tell how much we agree? We can't measure niceness!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Rank the songs, find the rank differences, square and add them, and use 1 − 6ΣD²/(n³ − n)!
teach.nudge: Good! We can rank the songs. What do we do with the differences in our ranks?

topics.title: Tied ranks and comparing the two measures

learn.hook: Two students both score 60 and tie for 2nd place. Who gets rank 2 and who gets rank 3? Neither: both get 2.5.
points: Tied (repeated) ranks: give each tied item the average of the ranks they would have occupied. Two items tied for 2nd and 3rd place each get 2.5; three tied for 4th, 5th, 6th each get 5.
Correction: for each group of m tied items, add (m³ − m)/12 to ΣD².
Formula with ties: r_s = 1 − 6[ΣD² + Σ(m³ − m)/12] / (n³ − n).
Like r, the rank correlation coefficient lies between −1 and +1.
Rank correlation is generally less precise than Pearson's r because it uses ranks rather than actual values, and so uses less information.

example.q: X marks: 50, 60, 60, 70, 80 (ranked ascending: 1, 2.5, 2.5, 4, 5); Y ranks: 2, 1, 3, 5, 4. Find r_s.

learn.reallife: You can try it: rank the prices of 6 vegetables in two different markets of your city and compute rank correlation, handling equal prices as ties.

topics.title: What an index number measures

learn.hook: Your nani says, 'In my day a cinema ticket cost one rupee!' An index number turns that kind of nostalgia into a precise measure of how much prices have really changed.
points: An index number is a statistical device for measuring the average change in a group of related variables over two different situations, such as two periods of time or two places.
The base period is the period of comparison; its index is set at 100. The current period is the one being compared.
Reading an index: 250 means the level is 2.5 times the base, i.e. a 150% rise over the base. An index of 80 means a 20% fall.

A price index measures changes in prices (e.g. CPI, WPI). A quantity index measures changes in physical volume, e.g. of production, employment or construction (e.g. the Index of Industrial Production).

example.q: The price index of a basket is 180 with base 2012 = 100. Interpret it.
steps: So prices on average are 1.8 times the base, 80% higher.
example.answer: Prices have risen on average by 80% since 2012.

learn.reallife: When MoSPI reports that the CPI (base 2012 = 100) is around 190 or more, it means the consumer basket costs roughly double what it did in 2012.

topics.title: Aggregative price indices: simple, Laspeyres and Paasche

learn.hook: If rice goes up ₹2 a kg and saffron goes up ₹2 a gram, an unweighted index treats them alike. Households certainly don't. Weights fix that.
points: Simple aggregative price index: P01 = (Σp1 / Σp0) × 100, where p0 and p1 are base and current prices.
Drawbacks of the simple index: prices in different units (kg, litre, dozen) are simply added, and every item gets equal importance.
Weighted aggregative index uses quantities as weights. Laspeyres: P01 = (Σp1q0 / Σp0q0) × 100, using base-year quantities q0.
Paasche: P01 = (Σp1q1 / Σp0q1) × 100, using current-year quantities q1.
The two differ only in the weights. Laspeyres asks how much more the base-year basket costs now; Paasche asks how much more the current basket costs compared with the base.

example.q: Rice: p0 10, q0 10, p1 12, q1 10. Wheat: p0 5, q0 10, p1 7, q1 10. Dal: p0 25, q0 2, p1 30, q1 4. Find the simple aggregative, Laspeyres and Paasche indices.

learn.reallife: Most official price indices in India, such as CPI and WPI, use fixed base-period weights, which is the Laspeyres idea in practice.

topics.title: Price relatives and the weighted relatives method

learn.hook: Tomatoes up 50%, salt up 5%. Average them simply and you get 27.5%, which is fair only if a family spends equally on both. It doesn't.
points: Price relative of an item: R = (p1 / p0) × 100.
Simple average of price relatives: P01 = (1/n) Σ(p1/p0 × 100). It is unit-free, but gives every item equal weight.
Weighted average of price relatives: P01 = ΣWR / ΣW, where W is usually the base-year expenditure on each item (W = p0q0) or its share in the budget.
With W = p0q0, the weighted average of relatives gives the same answer as the Laspeyres index.

example.q: Rice (p0 10, p1 12), wheat (p0 5, p1 7), dal (p0 25, p1 30), with base expenditures 100, 50, 50. Find the simple and weighted average of relatives.

learn.reallife: The CPI is built as a weighted average of price relatives, with weights taken from household consumption expenditure surveys of NSO.

topics.title: Consumer Price Index

learn.hook: Your monthly expenses on dal, rent, bus fare and mobile data all change at different rates. The CPI combines them into one number that even decides how much DA government employees get.
points: The Consumer Price Index (CPI), or cost of living index, measures the average change in retail prices of a fixed basket of goods and services consumed by a target group.

CPI = ΣWR / ΣW, where W are weights (expenditure shares) and R are price relatives. If CPI is 140, a wage of ₹100 in the base must rise to ₹140; the 'excess over 100' (40%) is the compensation needed.

Different CPIs exist because baskets differ: CPI for industrial workers (CPI-IW), agricultural labourers (CPI-AL), rural labourers (CPI-RL), and CSO's CPI-Rural, CPI-Urban and CPI-Combined (base 2012 = 100 in the NCERT book).
In CPI-Combined (base 2012), the major groups are food and beverages (weight 45.86), pan, tobacco and intoxicants, clothing and footwear, housing, fuel and light, and miscellaneous.
The Consumer Food Price Index (CFPI) tracks retail food prices separately.

example.q: Weights: food 50, clothing 10, housing 20, fuel 10, misc 10. Price relatives: 150, 120, 130, 140, 110. Find the CPI.
example.answer: CPI = 138: the cost of living has risen 38%

learn.reallife: Dearness allowance for central government employees is revised using the All-India CPI for industrial workers compiled by the Labour Bureau.

topics.title: Wholesale Price Index and inflation measures

learn.hook: Headlines often say 'WPI inflation turns negative' while 'CPI inflation is 5%' in the same month. How can both be true? They measure different baskets.
points: The Wholesale Price Index (WPI) measures the general level of prices of goods traded in bulk (at the wholesale stage). It does not cover services.
WPI series used in the NCERT book: base 2011–12 = 100. Its three major groups and weights: primary articles 22.62, fuel and power 13.15, manufactured products 64.23.
WPI is used to track price movements in the goods economy and to deflate aggregates like national income.
Headline inflation is measured on the full index (all items). Core inflation excludes volatile items such as food and fuel, to show the underlying trend.
The RBI targets CPI (Combined) headline inflation under its inflation-targeting framework.

example.q: WPI weights are 22.62 (primary), 13.15 (fuel and power) and 64.23 (manufactured). Check that they add up, and say which group dominates.
steps: Manufactured products have the largest weight.

learn.reallife: When global crude oil prices crash, WPI inflation can dip sharply because fuel and power and many manufactured products depend on oil.

topics.title: Index of Industrial Production, Sensex and other indices

learn.hook: When the Sensex jumps 1,000 points, TV anchors cheer. When the IIP dips, economists worry. Both are index numbers telling different stories.
points: Index of Industrial Production (IIP): a quantity index of the volume of industrial output. The series used in the NCERT book has base 2011–12; it uses the Laspeyres formula with weights based on value added.

Sectoral weights in IIP: mining 14.37, manufacturing 77.63, electricity 7.99. Use-based groups include primary, capital, intermediate, infrastructure/construction goods, consumer durables and non-durables.
Eight core industries (coal, crude oil, natural gas, refinery products, fertilisers, steel, cement, electricity) carry about 40% of the weight in IIP.
Human Development Index (HDI, by UNDP): a composite index of health (life expectancy), education and income.
BSE Sensex: index of 30 large, actively traded shares on the Bombay Stock Exchange, base 1978–79 = 100; a benchmark of stock market movement. An index of agricultural production tracks farm output.

example.q: IIP sector weights are mining 14.37, manufacturing 77.63 and electricity 7.99. Which sector dominates, and what does the index measure?
steps: The weights add to 100 (99.99 after rounding).
Manufacturing has by far the largest weight, so factory output drives the IIP.
IIP measures changes in the volume (quantity) of industrial production, not prices.
example.answer: Manufacturing dominates (77.63); IIP is a quantity index.

learn.reallife: A Sensex level of about 60,000 means its 30 shares, taken together, are worth roughly 600 times their 1978–79 level, because the base was set at 100.

topics.title: Issues in constructing an index number

learn.hook: Choose 2020 as your base year and every index after it looks wild, because the pandemic made 2020 anything but normal.
points: Purpose: be clear what the index is for (e.g. cost of living of factory workers), since this decides the items and the formula.
Selection of items: choose items representative of the target group's consumption or production; the basket must not be too small or too large.

Base year: should be a normal year, free of extreme events like droughts, wars or pandemics, and not too distant. Bases are revised periodically as consumption patterns change (e.g. WPI moved to 2011–12).
Choice of formula: Laspeyres, Paasche or weighted relatives, depending on the question asked.
Data: prices must be collected from reliable, representative markets; poor data give a misleading index.

example.q: A researcher considers 2009 (a severe drought year), 2016 (a normal year) and 1985 as base years for a food price index in 2025. Which is best?
steps: 1985: too distant; consumption patterns have changed.

learn.reallife: MoSPI periodically revises the CPI and WPI base years so that the baskets reflect what Indians actually buy today, such as mobile data and packaged foods.
