options: A normal year that is not too distant
quiz.explain: A normal, recent year allows meaningful comparison.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any year can serve as the base

quiz.q: Why should the items in a CPI be representative of the target group?
options: To reduce the number of calculations
So that the index reflects the group's actual cost of living
quiz.explain: If the basket differs from what the group buys, the index misrepresents its cost of living.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any basket of goods will do

quiz.q: Why are base years of index numbers revised from time to time?
options: Consumption patterns and products change over time
The base must always be the current year
quiz.explain: New products and changing spending shares make old weights outdated.
quiz.mistake: Thinks base revision is just routine

quiz.q: The first step in constructing an index number is to:
quiz.explain: The purpose decides the items, base and formula.
quiz.mistake: Jumps straight to computation

quiz.q: Why do we need index numbers at all?
options: To find the price of one item
To calculate a single household's income
To measure average changes in groups of related variables such as prices or production
quiz.explain: Index numbers summarise changes in many related items at once.
quiz.mistake: Thinks an index tracks a single item

quiz.q: A price index and a quantity index differ in that:
options: A quantity index has no base year
A price index tracks prices; a quantity index tracks physical volumes
A price index never uses weights
quiz.explain: One measures changes in prices, the other in quantities produced or consumed.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the two types

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): An index number based on unreliable price data may mislead policy makers.
Reason (R): The accuracy of an index depends on the quality of data used.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Poor data feed directly into a misleading index.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the formula alone guarantees accuracy

quiz.q: Which is NOT an issue to consider while constructing an index number?
options: The favourite colour of the statistician
quiz.explain: Purpose, items, base, formula and data quality matter; personal preferences do not.
quiz.mistake: Fails to separate relevant from irrelevant factors

teach.ask: Gappu wants to make a 'nest-building cost index'. 'Which year should be my base? What else must I decide?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Decide the purpose, choose representative items, a normal and recent base year, a formula and reliable data!
teach.nudge: Good! But what kind of year makes a good base? Should it be a drought year or a normal one?

topics.title: Using index numbers: inflation, real wages and purchasing power

learn.hook: Your salary doubled in ten years. Celebrate? Only if prices didn't also double. Index numbers tell you what your rupees are really worth.
points: Uses of CPI: wage and DA negotiations, income and price policy, rent control, taxation. Uses of WPI: measuring inflation in goods, deflating aggregates such as national income.
Inflation rate = (X_t − X_{t−1}) / X_{t−1} × 100, where X is the price index in the current (t) and previous (t − 1) period.
Purchasing power of money = 1 / cost of living index (with the index expressed as a ratio, e.g. 125 → 1.25). If CPI = 125, ₹1 buys what ₹0.80 bought in the base.
Real wage = (money wage / CPI) × 100. Salary needed to keep the same standard of living = base salary × CPI / 100.
Indices with different base years cannot be compared directly; they must first be shifted to a common base.

example.q: CPI rose from 160 to 168 in a year. Ravi's money wage is ₹33,600 and the CPI is 168. Find the inflation rate and his real wage.

learn.reallife: When the government revises dearness allowance twice a year, it is using the CPI to protect the real wages of its employees.

games.title: Match the use to the index

quiz.mistake: Divides by the new index or takes the point change as the percentage

quiz.q: Money wage ₹45,000 and CPI 150. What is the real wage?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by the CPI instead of dividing

Assertion (A): An IIP with base 2004–05 and one with base 2011–12 cannot be compared directly.

quiz.explain: Each series is 100 in a different year with different weights, so values must be linked or shifted first.

teach.praise: Tweet! Real pocket money = 150/200 × 100 = ₹75. Prices doubled, so I'm actually poorer!
teach.nudge: Hmm! You saw the money rise. But what happened to prices? How do we find what the money can really buy?

topics.title: Starting a project: problem, objectives and target group

learn.hook: Why do auto-rickshaws in your town overcharge at night? A good statistics project turns a question like this into data, findings and practical suggestions.
points: A project applies statistical tools to a real economic issue, studies it systematically and suggests improvements.
Step 1: identify the problem or area of study and set clear, specific objectives (what exactly do we want to find out?).
Step 2: choose the target group, i.e. the population whose members will be surveyed (e.g. auto drivers and commuters of a city, or households of a colony).
A precise objective decides what data are needed; a well-defined target group decides whom to ask and how to sample.

example.q: A student wants to study 'saving habits'. Turn this into a clear objective and target group.
steps: Specific objective: 'To find what share of monthly income households in Ward 12 save, and where they keep their savings.'
Target group: all households in Ward 12.
example.answer: Objective: share of income saved and savings instruments used; target group: households of Ward 12.

learn.reallife: Before launching a new metro line, planners first define the objective (reduce travel time) and target group (daily commuters on the corridor) before collecting any data.

options: Both A and R are true and R explains A

quiz.explain: Knowing exactly what we want to find tells us which data are needed.
quiz.mistake: Does not link objectives with data needs

teach.ask: Gappu wants to do a project on 'why some birds have tiny nests'. 'Where do I even start?'
teach.praise: Tweet! First define the problem, then set clear objectives, then pick the target group. Project launched!
teach.nudge: Good start! But who exactly will you collect data from? And what precisely do you want to find out?

topics.title: Collecting data for a project

learn.hook: You have two weeks and no budget. Do you knock on 500 doors or use the NSS report in the library? Smart projects choose their data sources deliberately.
points: Step 3: collect data. Primary data come from a questionnaire or interview schedule, through personal interviews, post, phone or email. Secondary data come from published sources such as the Census, NSS reports or RBI publications.
Decide census or sample; if sampling, choose a sampling method (random sampling is preferred to avoid bias).
A mailed questionnaire should carry a covering letter explaining the purpose of the survey, assuring confidentiality, and requesting a reply by a date.
When time or money is short, suitable secondary data are a sensible choice, but check that they match your purpose and are reliable.

example.q: A student studying women's employment in her district has 10 days and no funds. How should she collect data?
steps: A full primary survey of the district is too costly and slow.
Use secondary data (e.g. Census and PLFS reports) for the district picture.
Add a small random sample of households in her locality for primary insight, using a short questionnaire.
example.answer: Mainly secondary data, supplemented by a small random sample survey.

learn.reallife: NGOs studying sanitation often combine Census data on toilets per household with a small sample survey of their own villages.

teach.ask: Gappu must collect data for his nest project but has only a week. 'Should I survey every bird or use old forest records?'
teach.praise: Tweet! With little time and money, I'll use reliable records and a small random sample survey with a covering letter!
teach.nudge: Good! Think about time and cost. What are the two kinds of data you could use?

topics.title: Organising, analysing, concluding and the bibliography

learn.hook: A pile of 200 filled questionnaires is not a project. It becomes one only after it is tabulated, graphed, analysed and turned into clear conclusions.
points: Step 4: organise and present the data in tables and suitable diagrams (bar diagrams, pie diagrams, histograms).
Step 5: analyse and interpret using averages (mean, median, mode) and correlation. (The NCERT book also mentions measures of dispersion, which are not part of the current syllabus.)
Step 6: draw conclusions from the analysis, forecast future prospects if relevant, and suggest policies or improvements.
Step 7: prepare a bibliography listing every secondary source used (books, reports, websites) so that readers can check them.

example.q: A project finds that average monthly saving of 50 households is ₹4,500 and correlation between income and saving is 0.85. What conclusion and suggestion fit?
steps: Average saving of ₹4,500 summarises saving levels.
r = 0.85 means higher-income households tend to save more (strong positive correlation).
Suggestion: savings schemes could target lower-income families with small, regular deposit options.
example.answer: Saving rises strongly with income; suggest small-saving schemes for lower-income households.

learn.reallife: The Economic Survey ends many chapters with policy suggestions and lists its data sources, just like a well-written project report.

topics.title: Project ideas: playing an economic role

learn.hook: Imagine you are the transport advisor to your district collector, or a bank officer judging a loan for a pickle-making unit. Projects are most fun when you play a role.
points: Transport advisor: study bus routes, waiting times and fares to suggest better services. Bank loan proposal: assess costs, sales and profits of a cottage unit. Advertising: study whether ad spending raises a firm's sales.

Literacy and dropouts: find why children leave school in a locality. Overcharging: check whether shops charge above MRP. Drinking water: survey availability and quality. Women's employment: study participation and wages.
Health and sanitation, food adulteration, immunisation coverage, household saving habits, and problems of farmers are other good areas.
Each role-based project still follows the same steps: problem, objectives, target group, data, presentation, analysis, conclusions, bibliography.

example.q: As a bank officer, what data would you need to judge a loan proposal for a cottage unit making papads?
steps: Costs: raw materials, labour, rent, machines.
Expected profit = revenue − cost, and ability to repay.
example.answer: Cost, sales, profit and repayment-capacity data.

learn.reallife: Many schools encourage CBSE projects on local issues, such as checking whether packaged water is sold above MRP at railway stations.

topics.title: A consumer survey: questionnaire and presentation

learn.hook: Which toothpaste do families in your colony use, and why? A consumer survey answers this the way real marketing teams do.
points: A consumer survey questionnaire covers: demographic details (age, sex, family size), income and occupation, brand used, satisfaction, preferences (taste, ingredients, price) and media that influenced the choice.

Present the age distribution of respondents with a table and a bar diagram. Family size and spending can be grouped into classes and shown with suitable diagrams: a bar diagram for counts of a discrete variable, a histogram for continuous classes.
Make a frequency distribution of income or monthly spending and find the mean, using the assumed mean or step deviation method to simplify arithmetic.
Show occupational status of respondents with a pie diagram; tabulate brand preferences and the reasons for choice as counts or percentages.

example.q: In a survey of 120 respondents, 48 are salaried, 36 self-employed, 24 students and 12 retired. Find the pie angles.

learn.reallife: FMCG companies like those selling toothpaste and soaps run such consumer surveys across Indian towns before launching new variants.

teach.nudge: Good! What personal details and brand details would you ask? How will you present the answers?

topics.title: Interpreting results and writing the conclusion

learn.hook: Your survey shows 60% of users like Brand A, but only 30% are 'very satisfied'. What does that mean for the company? Interpretation turns numbers into insight.
points: Interpret satisfaction by brand: compare the share of 'satisfied' users across brands, not just the number of users.
Interpret preferences: e.g. if most respondents prefer herbal ingredients, products with such ingredients may gain share.
Interpret media influence: identify which medium (TV, social media, newspapers, word of mouth) influenced most buyers.
The concluding note summarises the main findings, states their limits (sample size, area covered) and gives practical suggestions.

example.q: Brand A has 80 users, of whom 40 are very satisfied; Brand B has 40 users, of whom 30 are very satisfied. Which brand satisfies its users better?
steps: Brand B has fewer users but a higher satisfaction rate.

learn.reallife: Market research firms tell clients both 'reach' (how many use the product) and 'satisfaction rate' (how happy users are), because the two can differ.

teach.ask: Gappu's survey shows 70 birds use Brand A seeds but only 20 love them, while 30 use Brand B and 25 love them. 'Which brand is better?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Brand A: 20/70 ≈ 29%, Brand B: 25/30 ≈ 83%. Brand B wins on satisfaction, so compare rates, not counts!
teach.nudge: Hmm, is it fair to compare 20 and 25 directly when the brands have different numbers of users? What should we compare?

topics.title: The economy and its central problems

learn.hook: Every economy, from a village to India, must answer the same three questions every single day: what to make, how to make it, and who gets it.
points: In any society people produce goods and services, exchange them and consume them to meet their needs. But the resources available (land, labour, capital, raw materials) are limited.
Scarcity of resources relative to wants forces every society to choose how to allocate its resources among competing uses.
What to produce and in what quantities: more food or more clothes, more consumer goods or more capital goods, more public services like schools and hospitals?
How to produce: which technique to use. Labour-intensive techniques use more labour; capital-intensive techniques use more machines.
For whom to produce: how the output is distributed among people, i.e. who gets how much.

example.q: A government must decide whether to build a dam using thousands of workers or a few huge machines, and whether its electricity will go to farms or factories. Identify the central problems.
steps: Choosing workers versus machines is 'how to produce' (technique).
Choosing farms versus factories as users is 'for whom to produce'.
Deciding to build a dam rather than something else is 'what to produce'.
example.answer: All three: what, how and for whom to produce.

learn.reallife: India's MGNREGA rural works often use labour-intensive techniques to create jobs, while metro rail projects use tunnel-boring machines: two different answers to 'how to produce'.

games.title: Which central problem?
items: More wheat or more cotton?
Tractors or bullocks for ploughing?
Should the poor get subsidised rice?
More defence goods or more hospitals?
Handloom or power-loom technique?
How is national output shared among families?

games.title: Central problems
items: Central problems arise because resources are scarce.
With unlimited resources there would be no need to choose.
'How to produce' deals with the choice of technique.
Labour-intensive versus capital-intensive methods.
Rich countries do not face central problems.
Every economy faces scarcity and must choose.
'For whom to produce' is about distribution of output.
It decides who gets how much.
A capital-intensive technique uses relatively more labour.
It uses relatively more machines (capital).

quiz.q: The central problems of an economy arise mainly because of:
options: Scarcity of resources with alternative uses
quiz.explain: Limited resources that can be used in many ways force choices.
quiz.mistake: Thinks central problems arise only from lack of money

quiz.q: Deciding between labour-intensive and capital-intensive techniques is the problem of:
quiz.explain: Choice of technique is 'how to produce'.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up what and how

quiz.q: Deciding how national output is distributed among households is the problem of:
quiz.explain: Distribution of output is 'for whom'.
quiz.mistake: Confuses distribution with technique

quiz.q: A country deciding whether to produce more consumer goods or more capital goods faces the problem of:
quiz.explain: Choosing the mix of goods is 'what to produce'.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it is about technique

quiz.q: A road can be built by 200 workers in 50 days, or by 40 workers with machines in 25 days. How many worker-days does the labour-intensive method use?
quiz.explain: 200 workers × 50 days = 10,000 worker-days (the machine method uses 40 × 25 = 1,000).
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the wrong pair of numbers

quiz.q: Which is an example of a capital-intensive technique?
options: Harvesting wheat with a combine harvester
Building a wall by hand with many masons
quiz.explain: A combine harvester replaces a lot of labour with machinery.
quiz.mistake: Picks a method that relies mainly on workers

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Every economy must decide what, how and for whom to produce.
Reason (R): Resources are limited relative to wants in every economy.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Universal scarcity is why every economy faces these problems.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only poor economies face central problems

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the central problems of an economy?
quiz.explain: The three central problems concern production and distribution of goods.
quiz.mistake: Treats any social decision as a central problem

teach.ask: Gappu's forest council must decide: build nests or gather food, use beaks or tools, and give food to which birds? 'What are these problems called?'
teach.praise: Tweet! What, how and for whom to produce: the three central problems, all because resources are scarce!
teach.nudge: Good! You named one problem. What about choosing the method, and deciding who gets the output?

topics.title: Production possibility set and frontier

learn.hook: With a fixed farm, a farmer can grow lots of corn, lots of cotton, or some of both. Draw all the best-possible combinations and you get a curve that sums up scarcity.
points: Production possibility set: all combinations of two goods that can be produced with the given resources and technology.
Production possibility frontier (PPF): the combinations obtained when resources are fully and efficiently used. Producing more of one good then means producing less of the other.
A point inside the PPF means resources are under-utilised or wasted (e.g. unemployment, idle factories).
A point outside the PPF is unattainable with the current resources and technology.
The PPF is drawn with one good on each axis and is usually concave (bowed out) to the origin.

example.q: A PPF passes through (corn 2, cotton 7). Classify the points (2, 5) and (2, 9).
steps: At corn = 2, the maximum cotton possible is 7.
(2, 5): less cotton than possible → inside the PPF → under-used resources.
(2, 9): more than possible → outside the PPF → unattainable.

learn.reallife: During the 2020 lockdown, many factories and workers were idle, so India's output moved to a point well inside its PPF.

games.title: Inside, on or outside the PPF?
items: Factories idle due to a strike
All resources fully and efficiently used
A combination needing more resources than exist
Widespread unemployment
Maximum cotton for a given amount of corn
Output beyond current technology

games.title: PPF basics
items: Points on the PPF show full and efficient use of resources.
That is how the frontier is defined.
A point inside the PPF is unattainable.
Inside points are attainable but wasteful.
Points outside the PPF cannot be reached with current resources.
They need more resources or better technology.
The production possibility set includes points inside and on the PPF.
It contains every attainable combination.
Unemployment pushes an economy outside its PPF.
It puts the economy inside the PPF.

quiz.q: The production possibility frontier shows combinations of two goods when:
options: Resources are fully and efficiently used
quiz.explain: Each point on the PPF uses all resources efficiently.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the PPF includes wasteful points

quiz.q: A point inside the PPF indicates:
quiz.explain: More of one or both goods could be produced with the same resources.
quiz.mistake: Confuses inside points with outside points

quiz.q: A point lying outside the PPF is:
options: Unattainable with current resources and technology
quiz.explain: It needs more resources or better technology.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any point can be reached with effort

quiz.q: A PPF passes through (4, 0), (3, 4), (2, 7), (1, 9) and (0, 10), where the first number is corn and the second is cotton. Is (2, 6) inside, on or outside the frontier?
quiz.explain: With corn = 2, up to 7 cotton is possible; producing only 6 means resources are under-used.
quiz.mistake: Compares the wrong coordinates

quiz.q: Using the same PPF, how much cotton is lost if production moves from (2, 7) to (2, 6)?
quiz.explain: Cotton falls from 7 to 6 while corn stays at 2: 1 unit of cotton is wasted.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the inside point loses nothing

quiz.q: Which situation would place an economy inside its PPF?
options: A long strike that shuts many factories
quiz.explain: Idle resources mean actual output is below potential.
quiz.mistake: Confuses idle resources with growth

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): An economy cannot produce at a point outside its PPF.
Reason (R): The PPF shows the maximum output possible with given resources and technology.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Since the PPF is the maximum, anything beyond it cannot be produced right now.
quiz.mistake: Thinks effort alone can exceed the PPF

quiz.q: The production possibility set consists of:
options: Only the points on the PPF
All points on and inside the PPF
quiz.explain: Every combination that can be produced, efficiently or not.
quiz.mistake: Equates the set with the frontier alone

teach.ask: Gappu's forest can make nests or gather berries. 'What does the PPF show? And what if some birds are lazy?'
teach.praise: Tweet! On the PPF all birds work efficiently, inside means lazy birds and waste, outside is impossible for now!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens if some birds stay idle? Where would the forest be compared with the PPF?

topics.title: Opportunity cost and the shape of the PPF

learn.hook: Moving land from cotton to corn is easy at first, using land that is better for corn. Push further and you must give up ever more cotton for each extra unit of corn.
points: Opportunity cost of a good: the amount of the other good that must be given up to produce one more unit of it.
Marginal opportunity cost along a PPF is also called the marginal rate of transformation (MRT): MRT = units of good Y given up ÷ extra units of good X gained.
MRT usually increases as more of one good is produced, because resources are not equally suited to both goods.
Increasing opportunity cost (increasing MRT) makes the PPF concave (bowed out) to the origin. Constant opportunity cost would give a straight-line PPF.
The slope of the PPF (in absolute value) equals the MRT.

example.q: Corn: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4; Cotton: 10, 9, 7, 4, 0. Find the opportunity cost of each extra unit of corn.
example.answer: 1, 2, 3, 4 units of cotton: rising opportunity cost, so the PPF is concave

learn.reallife: If India shifts land from rice to sugarcane in Maharashtra, the first hectares moved may be well suited to sugarcane, but later ones are better rice land, so each extra tonne of sugarcane costs more rice.

items.q: Cotton falls 9 → 7 for 1 more corn. MRT?
Cotton falls 20 → 14 for 2 more corn. MRT?
Guns 0 → 1 lowers butter 50 → 45. Cost of 1 gun?
Y falls 30 → 20 as X rises 5 → 7. MRT?
Cotton falls 4 → 0 for 1 more corn. MRT?
Wheat falls 100 → 85 for 3 more cloth. MRT?

games.title: Match the PPF idea
pairs: Units of the other good given up
Resources not equally efficient in both goods

quiz.q: Opportunity cost of producing one more unit of corn is:
options: The amount of cotton given up to produce it
quiz.explain: It is measured by the alternative output forgone.
quiz.mistake: Equates opportunity cost with the money price

quiz.q: Corn: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4; Cotton: 10, 9, 7, 4, 0. What is the opportunity cost of the 3rd unit of corn?
quiz.explain: Moving from 2 to 3 corn reduces cotton from 7 to 4: 3 units of cotton.
quiz.mistake: Reads the cotton level instead of the change

quiz.q: In the same table (Corn 0–4, Cotton 10, 9, 7, 4, 0), what is the MRT when corn rises from 3 to 4 units?
quiz.explain: Cotton falls from 4 to 0, so MRT = 4.
quiz.mistake: Uses the previous step's MRT

quiz.q: Increasing marginal opportunity cost makes the PPF:
quiz.explain: A rising MRT means the curve bows outward.
quiz.mistake: Confuses concave and convex

quiz.q: If the opportunity cost of one good in terms of the other were constant, the PPF would be:
quiz.explain: A constant slope gives a straight line.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every PPF must be curved

quiz.q: When good X rises from 5 to 7 units, good Y falls from 30 to 20 units. Find the MRT.
quiz.explain: MRT = ΔY/ΔX = 10/2 = 5.
quiz.mistake: Uses only the fall in Y without dividing by the rise in X

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A PPF is usually concave to the origin.
Reason (R): As more of one good is produced, resources less suited to it must be used, so MRT rises.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Rising MRT due to imperfectly adaptable resources gives the bowed-out shape.
quiz.mistake: Knows the shape but not the reason

quiz.q: The slope of the PPF at any point measures:
quiz.explain: Its (absolute) slope is the MRT, the rate at which one good is converted into the other.
quiz.mistake: Confuses MRT with MRS from consumer theory

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'If my forest makes one more nest, how many berries do we lose? And why does it get worse each time?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Each extra nest costs more berries because resources aren't equally good at both, so MRT rises and the PPF is concave!
teach.nudge: Good! But why does the cost keep rising? Think about whether all birds are equally good at both jobs.

topics.title: Shifts and rotations of the PPF

learn.hook: The Green Revolution let Indian farmland grow far more wheat and rice than before. In PPF language, it pushed the frontier outward.
points: The PPF is drawn for given resources and technology. If these change, the PPF moves.
Growth of resources (more labour, more capital, new mineral finds) or general improvement in technology shifts the whole PPF outward (to the right).
Loss of resources (war, earthquake, epidemic deaths) shifts the PPF inward (to the left).
If technology improves for only one good, the PPF rotates: its intercept on that good's axis moves out, while the intercept on the other axis stays the same.
An economy moving from inside the PPF to a point on it (e.g. reducing unemployment) is NOT a shift; the PPF itself is unchanged.

example.q: A PPF between cloth and wheat. A new high-yield wheat seed is invented. What happens?
steps: The maximum wheat (if all resources go to wheat) increases.
The maximum cloth stays the same.
example.answer: The PPF rotates outward along the wheat axis, pivoting on the cloth intercept.

learn.reallife: ISRO's satellite-based weather forecasting helps farmers reduce crop losses; better technology like this can push the economy's PPF outward over time.

games.title: Shift, rotation or movement?
items: Increase in the labour force
A major earthquake destroys factories
New technology only in cloth production
Discovery of new mineral deposits
War destroys capital stock
High-yield seed improves only rice output

games.title: PPF movements
items: Better technology for both goods shifts the PPF outward.
More of both can now be produced.
Reducing unemployment shifts the PPF outward.
It moves the economy from inside to onto the existing PPF.
An improvement in technology for one good rotates the PPF.
Only that good's intercept changes.
Loss of resources due to a natural disaster shifts the PPF inward.
Fewer resources mean less potential output.
The PPF stays fixed even if resources grow.
Growth in resources shifts it outward.

quiz.q: An increase in the stock of capital and labour in an economy will:
options: Move the economy inside the PPF
quiz.explain: More resources raise the maximum possible output of both goods.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only technology shifts the PPF

quiz.q: A severe earthquake destroys many factories. The PPF will:
quiz.explain: Loss of resources reduces productive capacity.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it only moves the economy inside the PPF

quiz.q: New technology improves only the production of wheat (on the x-axis). The PPF will:
options: Rotate outward on the wheat axis, keeping the other intercept fixed
quiz.explain: Only the maximum wheat output increases.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any technology change shifts the whole PPF

quiz.q: Government schemes put unemployed workers back to work. On a PPF diagram, this is shown as:
options: An outward shift of the PPF
A movement from a point inside the PPF towards the PPF
quiz.explain: The resources already existed; they are now being used.
quiz.mistake: Confuses using idle resources with gaining new resources

quiz.q: A PPF has maximum outputs of 100 cloth or 50 wheat. A wheat-only technology raises maximum wheat by 20%. What is the new maximum wheat output?
quiz.explain: 50 × 1.2 = 60; maximum cloth stays at 100.
quiz.mistake: Applies the increase to cloth or adds 20 directly

quiz.q: Which event shifts the PPF outward?
quiz.explain: New resources raise potential output.
quiz.mistake: Picks an event that wastes or destroys resources

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Economic growth is shown by an outward shift of the PPF.
Reason (R): Growth increases the economy's capacity to produce goods and services.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Higher productive capacity means a bigger set of attainable combinations.
quiz.mistake: Thinks growth only moves the economy along the PPF

quiz.q: Which of these does NOT shift the PPF?
options: Moving resources from wheat to cloth production
quiz.explain: Re-allocating existing resources only moves the economy along the same PPF.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any change in output mix shifts the PPF

teach.ask: Gappu's forest learnt a faster way to weave nests, but berry-picking is unchanged. 'What happens to our PPF?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Technology for nests only rotates the PPF outward on the nest axis. More resources would shift it outward!
teach.nudge: Good! Does the berry maximum change too? What happens to the nest maximum?

topics.title: Organisation of economic activities: planned, market and mixed

learn.hook: In a market economy, no minister decides how many samosas a city needs, yet there are always enough. Prices do the coordinating.
points: Centrally planned economy: the government (central authority) makes the major decisions about what, how and for whom to produce, aiming at the society's overall welfare.
Market economy: economic activities are organised through the market. A market is any arrangement where people can freely buy and sell goods; it need not be a physical place (online platforms count).
In a market economy, prices act as signals: if demand for a good rises, its price tends to rise, which encourages producers to supply more of it.
Mixed economy: both the market and the government play important roles; the government steps in where markets fail (e.g. defence, public health, help for the poor). India is a mixed economy.

example.q: Demand for electric scooters rises sharply in Bengaluru. How does a market economy respond, with no central order?
steps: Higher demand pushes up the price and profits of e-scooters.
Firms are attracted to produce more and new firms enter.
Output rises to meet demand: prices have coordinated the decision.
example.answer: Price signals lead producers to supply more e-scooters.

learn.reallife: In India, prices of most goods are set in markets, but the government runs the Public Distribution System, Indian Railways and public hospitals: a mixed economy at work.

games.title: Which type of economy?
items: Government decides all output targets
Prices alone coordinate production
Private firms plus government-run railways and hospitals
Central authority allocates goods to households
Buyers and sellers freely exchange at market prices
India's economic system

games.title: Organising an economy
items: A market must be a physical place like a mandi.
Any arrangement for free buying and selling, including online, is a market.
In a market economy, a rise in demand tends to raise price and supply.
Prices act as signals.
In a centrally planned economy, the government makes the key decisions.
A central authority plans production and distribution.
India is a purely planned economy.
India is a mixed economy.
In a mixed economy, both markets and the government have important roles.
That is its defining feature.

quiz.q: In a centrally planned economy, the central problems are solved by:
quiz.explain: The central authority decides what, how and for whom.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with a market economy

quiz.q: In a market economy, the main coordinating mechanism is:
quiz.explain: Prices signal what buyers want and guide producers.
quiz.mistake: Thinks government directs a market economy

quiz.q: A market, in economics, means:
options: Any arrangement where buyers and sellers can freely exchange goods
quiz.explain: It need not be a place; online platforms are markets too.
quiz.mistake: Takes the everyday meaning of 'market'

quiz.q: If demand for a good increases in a market economy, its price tends to:
quiz.explain: Rising price raises profitability and induces producers to supply more.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the price signal

quiz.q: India's economy is best described as a:
quiz.explain: Both the market and the government have significant roles.
quiz.mistake: Ignores either the market or the state

quiz.q: Which is a role of the government in a mixed economy?
options: Fixing the price of every single good
quiz.explain: The state supplies public goods and corrects market failures, while markets handle most goods.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a mixed economy is fully planned

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Prices act as signals in a market economy.
Reason (R): A rise in the price of a good indicates greater scarcity or demand, guiding producers to supply more.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Price changes carry information that steers production decisions.
quiz.mistake: Does not see how prices carry information

quiz.q: Online shopping platforms where buyers and sellers never meet face to face are:
options: Not markets because there is no physical place
Markets, because buyers and sellers can freely exchange
quiz.explain: The economic meaning of a market does not require a physical place.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a market must be a building or street

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Who decides how many nests to build in a forest? Is it the eagle chief, the market, or both?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The chief decides in a planned economy, prices decide in a market economy, and both share the job in a mixed economy like India!
teach.nudge: Good! What guides decisions when there is no chief? And what do we call a system where both work together?

topics.title: Positive vs normative economics, micro vs macro

learn.hook: 'Petrol prices rose 5% last year' can be checked with data. 'Petrol should be cheaper' is a judgement. Economists keep the two apart.
points: Positive economics describes how economic mechanisms actually work: what is, was or will be. Its statements can be tested with facts.
Normative economics evaluates whether outcomes are desirable: what ought to be. Its statements involve value judgements (often using 'should', 'ought to').
Microeconomics studies individual economic agents (consumers, firms) and how prices and quantities are determined in individual markets.
Macroeconomics studies the economy as a whole: aggregate output, employment, the general price level, growth and inflation.

example.q: Classify: (a) 'A rise in onion prices reduces quantity demanded.' (b) 'The government should give free electricity to farmers.' (c) 'India's GDP growth rate rose last year.'
steps: (a) Testable cause and effect in one market: positive, micro.
(c) A testable fact about the whole economy: positive, macro.

learn.reallife: The RBI's study of how a repo-rate change affects inflation is macroeconomics; a study of how a tomato price rise affects tomato demand is microeconomics.

games.title: Positive or normative?
items: Unemployment in India rose last year
The government should reduce unemployment
Higher prices reduce quantity demanded
Rich people ought to pay more tax
Inflation was 5% in a year
Minimum wages should be raised
A rise in income raises demand for normal goods

games.title: Micro or macro? Match each study to its branch
pairs: Price of wheat in one market

quiz.q: Positive economics deals with:
options: What is, was or will be
quiz.explain: It describes actual economic mechanisms and can be tested.
quiz.mistake: Confuses positive with normative

quiz.q: Which statement is normative?

quiz.explain: 'Should' signals a value judgement.

quiz.explain: It focuses on individual agents and individual markets.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): 'A rise in income increases demand for normal goods' is a positive statement.
Reason (R): It can be tested against facts.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A

A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Testability with data makes it positive.
quiz.mistake: Thinks economic theories are normative

quiz.mistake: Counts the normative ones instead

quiz.q: The study of how the price of rice is determined in a market is part of:

teach.ask: Gappu argues: 'Berries got costlier last month, and the forest should make them free!' Are both statements the same type? Teach me!

teach.nudge: Good! Which statement can be checked with data? Which one is an opinion about what ought to be?

topics.title: Utility, total utility and marginal utility

learn.hook: The first golgappa after a long day is heaven. The tenth? Not so much. Economists measure that feeling with utility.
points: Two-good model: a consumer chooses between two goods; a consumption bundle is written (x1, x2), e.g. (3, 2) means 3 units of good 1 and 2 of good 2.
Utility is the want-satisfying power of a commodity. It is subjective and varies from person to person, place to place and time to time.
Cardinal utility approach: utility can be measured in numbers called utils (e.g. 10 utils).
Total utility (TU) is the total satisfaction from consuming a given quantity. Marginal utility (MU) is the change in TU from one more unit: MU_n = TU_n − TU_(n−1).
TU is the sum of marginal utilities: TU_n = MU_1 + MU_2 + … + MU_n.

example.q: TU from 1, 2, 3, 4 chocolates is 12, 22, 28, 30 utils. Find MU of each.

learn.reallife: A glass of water is worth very little to you at home but a lot to a runner at the end of the Mumbai Marathon: utility depends on person, place and time.

games.title: Utility basics
items: Utility is the same for every person.
It is subjective and differs between people.
MU of the nth unit = TU_n − TU_(n−1).
That is the definition of marginal utility.
TU equals the sum of marginal utilities.
Adding each unit's extra utility gives total utility.
The cardinal approach measures utility in utils.
It assumes utility can be expressed in numbers.
A bundle (2, 5) means 5 units of good 1 and 2 of good 2.
(x1, x2) = (2, 5) means 2 of good 1 and 5 of good 2.

quiz.q: Utility of a commodity means its:
quiz.explain: Utility is the capacity to satisfy a want, whether or not the good is 'useful'.
quiz.mistake: Confuses utility with usefulness or price

quiz.q: TU from 2 units is 22 utils and from 3 units is 28 utils. What is the MU of the 3rd unit?
quiz.mistake: Reports TU instead of the change

quiz.q: MUs of the first four units are 20, 15, 10 and 5. What is the TU of 4 units?
quiz.mistake: Takes the last MU as TU

quiz.q: TU from 4 units is 30 and the MU of the 5th unit is −4. What is the TU from 5 units?
quiz.mistake: Ignores the negative sign of MU

quiz.q: In the cardinal approach, utility is:
quiz.explain: The cardinal approach assumes utility can be expressed numerically.
quiz.mistake: Confuses cardinal with ordinal

quiz.q: The bundle (4, 1) in the two-good model means:
options: 4 units of good 2 and 1 unit of good 1
4 units of good 1 and 1 unit of good 2
quiz.explain: The first number is x1 (good 1), the second x2 (good 2).
quiz.mistake: Swaps the order of goods

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Utility of a woollen sweater is higher in Shimla in winter than in Chennai in summer.
Reason (R): Utility depends on place and time.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The same good satisfies wants differently in different places and seasons.
quiz.mistake: Thinks utility is fixed for a good

quiz.q: TU from 1, 2, 3 units of tea is 10, 18 and 24 utils. What is the MU of the 2nd cup?
quiz.mistake: Uses the wrong pair of TU values

teach.ask: Gappu ate 3 mangoes: total joy 10, 16 and 19 utils. 'How much joy did each extra mango add?'
teach.praise: Tweet! MU = 10, 6 and 3 utils: subtract the previous total from the new total!
teach.nudge: Good! How do we find the extra joy from the 2nd mango using the totals?

topics.title: Diminishing marginal utility and the consumer's equilibrium

learn.hook: Why will you pay ₹20 for your first vada pav but not for your fifth? The answer explains why demand curves slope down.
points: Law of diminishing marginal utility: as consumption of a good increases (other things unchanged), the MU from each additional unit falls.
TU–MU relationship: TU rises while MU is positive; TU is maximum when MU = 0; TU falls when MU is negative.
One-good equilibrium: with utility measured in money terms, the consumer buys until MU of the good = its price.
Two-good equilibrium (law of equi-marginal utility): MU_x / P_x = MU_y / P_y, i.e. the last rupee spent on each good gives equal utility.
Deriving demand: if the price falls, MU > price at the old quantity, so the consumer buys more until MU falls to the new price. Diminishing MU thus gives a downward-sloping demand curve.

example.q: MU (in ₹) of successive ice-creams: 50, 40, 30, 20, 10. The price is ₹30. How many does the consumer buy? What if price falls to ₹20?
steps: At ₹30: buy while MU ≥ price → units 1, 2, 3 (MU 50, 40, 30).
Lower price → more quantity: law of demand.

learn.reallife: Unlimited thali restaurants rely on diminishing MU: each extra roti gives less satisfaction, so diners stop after a few.

games.title: TU and MU over units
games.prompt: Arrange the stages as consumption increases
items: MU positive and falling, TU rising
MU becomes zero, TU at its maximum
MU negative, TU falling

games.title: DMU and equilibrium
items: TU is maximum when MU is zero.
Adding a unit with zero MU adds nothing more.
When MU is negative, TU rises.
Negative MU makes TU fall.
A consumer of one good is in equilibrium when MU = price.
With utility in money terms.
In two-good equilibrium, MU_x/P_x = MU_y/P_y.
The equi-marginal rule.
Diminishing MU explains why demand curves slope upward.
It explains a downward-sloping demand curve.

quiz.q: The law of diminishing marginal utility states that, as more units of a good are consumed:
options: MU from each additional unit falls
TU falls from the first unit
quiz.explain: Each extra unit adds less satisfaction than the previous one.
quiz.mistake: Confuses falling MU with falling TU

quiz.q: When MU is zero, TU is:
quiz.explain: TU stops rising exactly when MU = 0.
quiz.mistake: Thinks zero MU means zero TU

quiz.q: When MU becomes negative, TU:
quiz.explain: Each extra unit now reduces total satisfaction.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the sign of MU

quiz.q: MU (in ₹) of successive units of a good: 50, 40, 30, 20, 10. At a price of ₹20, how many units will the consumer buy?
quiz.explain: She buys while MU ≥ price: units 1–4 (MU 50, 40, 30, 20).
quiz.mistake: Stops before the unit where MU equals price

quiz.q: MU_x = 40, P_x = ₹10, MU_y = 30, P_y = ₹5. What should the consumer do?
options: Buy more Y and less X
Buy more X and less Y
quiz.explain: MU_x/P_x = 4 and MU_y/P_y = 6. A rupee on Y gives more utility, so shift spending to Y.
quiz.mistake: Compares MU alone without dividing by price

quiz.q: A consumer is in equilibrium with MU_x = 24 and P_x = ₹8. If P_y = ₹5, what must MU_y be?
quiz.mistake: Sets MU_y equal to MU_x

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Diminishing marginal utility leads to a downward-sloping demand curve.
Reason (R): A consumer buys more only when the price falls to match the lower MU of extra units.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Extra units are worth less, so they are bought only at lower prices.
quiz.mistake: Does not link DMU to the law of demand

quiz.q: TU from 1 to 5 units: 10, 18, 24, 24, 20. At which unit is MU zero?
quiz.mistake: Picks the unit where TU first reaches 24

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'My third berry gave less joy than my first. Why? And how do I decide how many berries to buy at ₹5 each?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Each extra berry gives less joy (diminishing MU), so I buy until MU equals the price!
teach.nudge: Good! Why did the third berry give less joy? And when should I stop buying?

topics.title: Ordinal utility: indifference curves and MRS

learn.hook: You can't say a samosa gives exactly 7 utils, but you can say 'I like this combo more than that one'. Ranking is all the ordinal approach needs.
points: Ordinal approach: the consumer cannot measure utility in numbers but can rank bundles (prefer, or be indifferent between them).
Indifference curve (IC): a curve joining all bundles that give the consumer the same level of satisfaction. An indifference schedule lists such bundles in a table.
Marginal rate of substitution (MRS): the rate at which the consumer is willing to give up good 2 for one more unit of good 1 while staying on the same IC. MRS = |Δx2 / Δx1|.
Diminishing MRS: as the consumer has more of good 1, she is willing to give up less and less of good 2 for each extra unit of good 1.

example.q: Indifference schedule: (1, 15), (2, 11), (3, 8), (4, 6), (5, 5) for (x1, x2). Find MRS at each step.

learn.reallife: A cricket fan indifferent between (2 match tickets, 5 pizzas) and (3 tickets, 3 pizzas) gives up 2 pizzas for the 3rd ticket: an MRS of 2.

items.q: x2 falls 15 → 11 as x1 rises 1 → 2. MRS?
x2 falls 8 → 6 as x1 rises 3 → 4. MRS?
x2 falls 20 → 14 as x1 rises 2 → 4. MRS?
x2 falls 10 → 9 as x1 rises 5 → 6. MRS?
x2 falls 12 → 7 as x1 rises 1 → 2. MRS?

games.title: Match the ordinal idea
pairs: Good 2 given up for one more good 1
Willing to give up less and less of good 2

quiz.q: The ordinal approach assumes that the consumer can:
options: Rank bundles in order of preference
Know the MU of money exactly
quiz.explain: Only rankings (more, less or equal satisfaction) are needed.
quiz.mistake: Confuses ordinal with cardinal

quiz.q: An indifference curve shows combinations of two goods that:
options: Are produced with the same resources
Give the same level of satisfaction
quiz.explain: All points on an IC are equally preferred.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the IC with the budget line or PPF

quiz.q: On an IC, a consumer moves from (2, 11) to (3, 8). What is the MRS?
quiz.explain: She gives up 3 units of good 2 for 1 more unit of good 1: MRS = 3.
quiz.mistake: Reads a quantity level instead of the change

quiz.q: On an IC, a consumer moves from (2, 20) to (4, 14). What is the MRS?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by the change in x1

quiz.q: Diminishing MRS means that as the consumer gets more of good 1, she is willing to give up:
quiz.explain: Each extra unit of good 1 is worth less in terms of good 2.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the direction

quiz.q: MRS is defined as:
quiz.explain: It is the absolute slope of the indifference curve.
quiz.mistake: Confuses MRS with the price ratio

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): MRS usually diminishes along an indifference curve.
Reason (R): As a consumer has more of good 1 and less of good 2, good 2 becomes relatively more valuable to her.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Scarcer good 2 is valued more, so she gives up less of it for each extra unit of good 1.
quiz.mistake: Knows MRS diminishes but not why

quiz.q: Indifference schedule: (1, 12), (2, 7), (3, 4), (4, 2). What is the MRS when moving from the 3rd to the 4th bundle?
quiz.explain: x2 falls from 4 to 2 as x1 rises by 1: MRS = 2.
quiz.mistake: Uses an earlier step

teach.ask: Gappu is equally happy with (2 berries, 6 worms) or (3 berries, 4 worms). 'What's the curve called, and what is my MRS?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Both bundles lie on one indifference curve, and I give up 2 worms for 1 berry, so MRS = 2!
teach.nudge: Good! How many worms did I give up for one more berry? What do we call that rate?

topics.title: Properties of indifference curves and preferences

learn.hook: Two indifference curves can never cross. Try to draw them crossing and you'll prove the consumer contradicts herself.
points: Indifference curves are usually convex to the origin because of diminishing MRS. For perfect substitutes (e.g. two brands of identical salt) the IC is a straight line with constant MRS.
Monotonic preferences: between two bundles, the consumer prefers the one with more of at least one good and no less of the other.
Indifference map: a family of ICs. With monotonic preferences, a higher IC (further from the origin) gives higher satisfaction.
Properties: (1) ICs slope downward from left to right; (2) a higher IC gives higher utility; (3) two ICs never intersect.

Proof that ICs cannot intersect: if IC1 and IC2 met at A, with B on IC1 and C on IC2 and C having more of both goods than B, then A ~ B and A ~ C imply B ~ C. But monotonicity says C is preferred to B: a contradiction.

example.q: Bundles (5, 6) and (5, 8). Which does a consumer with monotonic preferences prefer, and why can they not lie on the same IC?
steps: (5, 8) has more of good 2 and no less of good 1.
By monotonicity (5, 8) is preferred, so they cannot give equal satisfaction.
example.answer: (5, 8) is preferred; they lie on different ICs.

learn.reallife: For a person who sees two brands of iodised salt as identical, the indifference curve between them is a straight line: perfect substitutes.

ICs slope downward from left to right.

With monotonic preferences, it has more of at least one good.
For perfect substitutes the IC is a straight line.
MRS is constant.

They are convex because MRS diminishes.
Monotonic preferences mean more is preferred to less.
More of at least one good, no less of the other, is preferred.

games.prompt: Arrange the steps of the proof
items: Assume IC1 and IC2 intersect at A
Take B on IC1 and C on IC2, where C has more of both goods than B
A ~ B and A ~ C, so B ~ C

Contradiction, so ICs cannot intersect

quiz.q: Indifference curves are convex to the origin because of:
quiz.explain: As MRS falls, the curve flattens, giving a convex shape.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the reason for the IC's shape with the PPF's

quiz.q: For two perfect substitutes, the indifference curve is:
quiz.explain: The consumer swaps them at a constant rate, so MRS is constant.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all ICs are curved

quiz.q: With monotonic preferences, which bundle is preferred: (4, 6) or (4, 9)?
quiz.explain: (4, 9) has more of good 2 and the same good 1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal x1 means indifference

quiz.q: Why do indifference curves slope downward?
options: To keep satisfaction constant, more of one good must be balanced by less of the other
quiz.explain: With monotonic preferences, getting more of both would raise satisfaction, so one must fall.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the slope reflects prices

quiz.q: An indifference map is:
options: A family of ICs, with higher ones giving higher satisfaction
quiz.explain: It shows the consumer's whole preference pattern.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the map with one curve

quiz.q: Which of these bundles lies on a higher IC than (3, 3) for a consumer with monotonic preferences?
quiz.explain: (4, 3) has more of good 1 and the same good 2.
quiz.mistake: Picks a bundle with less of one good

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Two indifference curves cannot intersect.
Reason (R): If they did, one bundle with more of both goods would give the same satisfaction as another, violating monotonic preferences.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: That contradiction is exactly the proof.
quiz.mistake: Accepts the property without the logic

quiz.q: A consumer is indifferent between (1, 10) and (2, 8), and between (2, 8) and (3, 6). Is the MRS diminishing along this curve?
quiz.explain: Both steps give up 2 units of good 2 for 1 of good 1: MRS is constant at 2, so this part is a straight line.
quiz.mistake: Assumes MRS always diminishes

teach.ask: Gappu drew two indifference curves that cross. 'Is that allowed? Teach me the properties of ICs!'
teach.praise: Tweet! ICs slope down, are convex, higher ones mean more satisfaction, and they can never cross!
teach.nudge: Good! But can two ICs ever cross? What would that say about bundles with more of both goods?

topics.title: The budget set and the budget line

learn.hook: ₹100 of pocket money, pens at ₹5, notebooks at ₹10. Every combination you can afford forms your budget set, and its edge is the budget line.
points: Budget set: all bundles the consumer can buy with income M at prices p1 and p2: p1x1 + p2x2 ≤ M.
Budget line: bundles that cost exactly M: p1x1 + p2x2 = M.
Intercepts: if all income goes on good 1, x1 = M/p1; on good 2, x2 = M/p2. Slope of the budget line (good 1 on the horizontal axis) = −p1/p2.
The budget line slopes downward because, with fixed income, buying more of one good means buying less of the other.
The price ratio p1/p2 is the market rate of exchange: the amount of good 2 that must be given up to buy one more unit of good 1.

example.q: M = ₹100, p1 = ₹5, p2 = ₹10. Write the budget equation, intercepts and slope. Is (6, 7) affordable?
steps: (6, 7) costs 30 + 70 = 100 = M → on the budget line, affordable
example.answer: 5x1 + 10x2 = 100; intercepts 20 and 10; slope −0.5; (6, 7) is on the line.

learn.reallife: A student with ₹300 for the week choosing between metro rides (₹30) and canteen meals (₹50) faces the budget line 30x1 + 50x2 = 300.

games.title: Inside, on or outside the budget line? (M = 100, p1 = 5, p2 = 10)

quiz.q: A consumer has ₹120. p1 = ₹6, p2 = ₹10. The budget equation is:
quiz.explain: Spending on each good = price × quantity, and the total equals income.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the prices of the goods

quiz.q: M = ₹120, p1 = ₹6, p2 = ₹10. What is the maximum quantity of good 1 she can buy?
quiz.mistake: Divides by p2 instead of p1

quiz.q: p1 = ₹6, p2 = ₹10 (good 1 on the x-axis). The slope of the budget line is:
quiz.mistake: Inverts the price ratio

quiz.q: A bundle (4, 6) lies on the budget line with p1 = ₹5 and p2 = ₹10. What is the consumer's income?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies the wrong price with the wrong quantity

quiz.q: M = ₹10, p1 = p2 = ₹5, and goods come in whole units only. How many bundles (including (0, 0)) are in the budget set?
quiz.mistake: Counts only bundles on the budget line (3)

quiz.q: The budget line slopes downward because:
options: With fixed income, buying more of one good requires buying less of the other
quiz.explain: Spending on one good can rise only if spending on the other falls.
quiz.mistake: Uses the IC's reasoning for the budget line

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The absolute slope of the budget line equals the price ratio p1/p2.
Reason (R): To buy one more unit of good 1, the consumer must give up p1/p2 units of good 2.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: The price ratio is the market rate of exchange between the goods.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the slope as a rate of exchange

quiz.q: M = ₹100, p1 = ₹5, p2 = ₹10. Which bundle is NOT affordable?
quiz.mistake: Does not compute the cost of each bundle

teach.ask: Gappu has ₹60. Berries cost ₹3 and worms ₹6. 'What can I afford? Teach me the budget line!'
teach.praise: Tweet! 3x1 + 6x2 = 60: up to 20 berries or 10 worms, slope −0.5. Everything on or below the line is affordable!
teach.nudge: Good! How many berries could I buy if I spent everything on berries? And what is the slope?

topics.title: Changes in the budget line

learn.hook: Diwali bonus arrives: your budget line jumps outward. Petrol price rises: one end of it swings inward. Learn to predict each move.
points: Change in income (prices constant): the budget line shifts parallel. A rise in income shifts it outward; a fall shifts it inward. The slope −p1/p2 is unchanged.
Change in the price of good 1 only: the line rotates around the x2-intercept (M/p2 stays fixed). A fall in p1 rotates it outward (x1-intercept rises); a rise in p1 rotates it inward.
Change in the price of good 2 only: the line rotates around the x1-intercept.
If income and both prices change in the same proportion (e.g. all double), the budget line does not change at all.

example.q: M = ₹100, p1 = ₹5, p2 = ₹10. What happens if (a) M rises to ₹150; (b) p1 falls to ₹4?
steps: (a) New intercepts: 150/5 = 30 and 150/10 = 15; slope still −0.5 → parallel outward shift.
(b) x1-intercept becomes 100/4 = 25; x2-intercept stays 10; slope becomes −0.4 → rotates outward about the x2-intercept.
example.answer: (a) parallel outward shift; (b) outward rotation with the x2-intercept fixed

learn.reallife: When cooking-gas prices rise while incomes stay the same, a household's budget line between LPG and other goods rotates inward along the LPG axis.

games.title: Match the change to the budget line's movement

items.q: M = 100, p1 falls to 4. New x1-intercept?
M = 100, p2 rises to 20. New x2-intercept?

quiz.q: A rise in the consumer's income, with prices unchanged, causes the budget line to:
quiz.explain: Both intercepts rise in proportion and the slope stays −p1/p2.
quiz.mistake: Thinks income changes the slope

quiz.q: A fall in the price of good 1 (on the x-axis), with income and p2 unchanged, makes the budget line:
options: Rotate outward, keeping the x2-intercept fixed
quiz.explain: Only the x1-intercept M/p1 increases.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any price change shifts the line parallel

quiz.q: M = ₹100, p1 = ₹5. If p1 falls to ₹4, the new maximum quantity of good 1 is:
quiz.mistake: Uses the old price

quiz.q: M = ₹100, p1 = ₹5, p2 = ₹10. Income rises to ₹150. What is the new x2-intercept?
quiz.mistake: Divides by p1

quiz.q: Income doubles and both prices also double. The budget line will:
quiz.explain: M/p1 and M/p2 are unchanged, and so is p1/p2.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a higher income always helps

quiz.q: p1 rises from ₹5 to ₹10, p2 = ₹10, M = ₹100. The slope of the new budget line is:
quiz.explain: Slope = −p1/p2 = −10/10 = −1, steeper than before.
quiz.mistake: Uses the old p1

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A change in income does not change the slope of the budget line.
Reason (R): The slope depends only on the price ratio p1/p2.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Income affects the intercepts, not the price ratio.
quiz.mistake: Thinks income tilts the budget line

quiz.q: The price of good 2 rises while M and p1 stay the same. Which intercept stays fixed?
quiz.explain: Only M/p2 falls; M/p1 is unchanged, so the line rotates around the x1-intercept.
quiz.mistake: Picks the intercept of the good whose price changed

teach.ask: Gappu's pocket money rose from ₹60 to ₹90, and later berries became cheaper. 'How does my budget line move each time?'
teach.praise: Tweet! More income shifts it out parallel; cheaper berries rotate it out along the berry axis!
teach.nudge: Good! Does a change in income change the slope? What happens when only one price changes?

topics.title: Consumer's equilibrium: indifference curve approach

learn.hook: Your preferences say what you'd like; your budget says what you can afford. The best choice is where the two just touch.
points: The consumer chooses the bundle on the highest indifference curve she can reach with her budget.
At the optimum, the budget line is tangent to an IC: MRS = p1/p2 (the slope of the IC equals the slope of the budget line).
The optimum lies on the budget line (she spends all income, given monotonic preferences).
If MRS > p1/p2, she values good 1 more than the market does, so she buys more of good 1 (and less of good 2), moving down the budget line until MRS falls to p1/p2.
If MRS < p1/p2, she buys less of good 1 and more of good 2 until MRS rises to p1/p2.

example.q: At a bundle on her budget line, a consumer's MRS = 3 while p1 = ₹4 and p2 = ₹2. Is she at the optimum? What should she do?
steps: MRS = 3 > 2: she is willing to give up 3 units of good 2 for one unit of good 1, but the market asks only 2.
So buying more of good 1 makes her better off.
example.answer: Not optimal; she should buy more of good 1 and less of good 2 until MRS = 2.

learn.reallife: An online shopper comparing earbuds and a speaker within a fixed budget is, without knowing it, trying to equate MRS with the price ratio.

The IC is tangent to the budget line.

Bundles outside are unaffordable.
If MRS > p1/p2, the consumer should buy more of good 1.
She values good 1 more than its market price ratio.
If MRS < p1/p2, the consumer should buy more of good 1.
She should buy less of good 1.
The consumer chooses the highest IC that touches the budget line.
That is the best affordable bundle.

options: The budget line is tangent to the highest attainable IC
The budget line cuts an IC at two points
The IC is highest regardless of budget
quiz.explain: Tangency gives the highest satisfaction possible within the budget.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a crossing point is optimal

quiz.q: The condition for consumer's equilibrium in the IC approach is:
quiz.explain: The slope of the IC (MRS) equals the slope of the budget line (p1/p2).
quiz.mistake: Inverts the price ratio

quiz.q: p1 = ₹6 and p2 = ₹3. At the optimum, the MRS must be:
quiz.mistake: Computes p2/p1

quiz.q: MRS = 4 and p1/p2 = 2 at the current bundle. The consumer should:
quiz.explain: She values good 1 more than the market rate, so more good 1 raises her satisfaction.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the direction of adjustment

quiz.q: MRS = 1 and p1 = ₹3, p2 = ₹1 at the current bundle. The consumer should:
options: Buy less of good 1 and more of good 2
quiz.explain: MRS (1) < p1/p2 (3): good 1 is worth less to her than its market cost in terms of good 2.
quiz.mistake: Compares MRS with p1 alone

quiz.q: Why does the optimal bundle lie on (not inside) the budget line?
options: Because with monotonic preferences, spending leftover income on more goods raises satisfaction
quiz.explain: Any bundle inside leaves money unspent that could buy more and raise utility.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the optimum could leave money unused

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): At the consumer's optimum, the rate at which she is willing to substitute equals the rate at which the market allows her to substitute.
Reason (R): At the optimum, MRS = p1/p2.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: MRS is her willingness; p1/p2 is the market rate; equality is the tangency condition.
quiz.mistake: Does not interpret the two slopes

quiz.q: A consumer's MRS = 2.5 at her chosen bundle, and p2 = ₹4. If she is at the optimum, what is p1?
quiz.mistake: Divides instead of multiplying

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'With my ₹60, which berry–worm bundle makes me happiest? How do I know I've found it?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Pick the point where my budget line just touches the highest IC, where MRS equals the price ratio!
teach.nudge: Good! But which IC should I aim for, and what must be equal at the best point?

topics.title: Demand: the demand curve and the law of demand

learn.hook: Cut the price of off-peak metro tickets and more people ride. Lower price, more bought: the most famous law in economics.
points: Demand: the quantity of a good a consumer is willing and able to buy at a given price, during a period. Demand function: q = d(p), with other factors (prices of related goods, income, tastes) held constant.
A demand schedule is a table of prices and quantities demanded; plotting it gives the demand curve, e.g. a linear demand curve q = a − bp.
Law of demand: other things remaining the same, quantity demanded rises when the price falls and falls when the price rises.

Deriving the demand curve: as p1 falls, the budget line rotates outward and the new optimum (tangency with a higher IC) usually has more of good 1. Plotting price against quantity gives the demand curve.
A price change has two effects: the substitution effect (the good is now relatively cheaper, so buy more of it) and the income effect (purchasing power rises, so demand rises for a normal good).

example.q: Demand function q = 20 − 2p. Make a schedule for p = 2, 4, 6, 8 and state the law shown.
example.answer: q falls from 16 to 4 as p rises from 2 to 8: the law of demand.

learn.reallife: Falling smartphone prices in India during the 2010s helped push sales up sharply: a lower price, a larger quantity demanded.

games.title: Match the demand idea
pairs: Relation between price and quantity demanded
Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions
Good becomes relatively cheaper, so buy more
Change in purchasing power from a price change
Table of prices and quantities demanded

quiz.q: Demand for a good means the quantity a consumer is:
options: Willing and able to buy at a given price
quiz.explain: Desire must be backed by ability to pay at that price.
quiz.mistake: Confuses desire with effective demand

quiz.q: The law of demand states that, other things remaining the same:
options: Price and quantity demanded move in the same direction
Price and quantity demanded move in opposite directions
quiz.explain: A fall in price raises quantity demanded, and vice versa.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the law of demand with the law of supply

quiz.mistake: Adds instead of subtracting, or forgets to multiply by 5

options: Buy more of it, since it is now relatively cheaper
quiz.explain: The good becomes cheaper relative to others, so she substitutes towards it.
quiz.mistake: Confuses substitution and income effects

quiz.q: For a normal good, when its price falls, the income effect:
quiz.explain: Higher purchasing power raises demand for a normal good, reinforcing the substitution effect.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a price fall reduces real income

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The demand curve can be derived from indifference curves and budget lines.
Reason (R): As price falls, the budget line rotates outward and the new optimum usually contains more of the good.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false

quiz.explain: Tracing optimum quantities at different prices gives the demand curve.

quiz.explain: q = 0 when p = 10, so at any price above ₹10 nothing is demanded.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Berry prices fell and I bought more. Is there a law about that? And why does it happen?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The law of demand: lower price, more demand, other things constant, thanks to substitution and income effects!
teach.nudge: Good! But why do I buy more when it's cheaper? Think about relative prices and my real income.

topics.title: Normal, inferior and related goods

learn.hook: Get your first job and you might buy fewer bus rides and more cab rides. Same rise in income, opposite effects: that's normal versus inferior goods.
points: Normal good: demand rises when income rises (and falls when income falls), e.g. branded clothes, fruits.
Inferior good: demand falls when income rises, e.g. coarse cereals for some households. A good can be normal at low income levels and inferior at higher levels.
Giffen good: a special inferior good whose demand rises when its price rises, because the negative income effect outweighs the substitution effect. It violates the law of demand.
Substitutes (tea and coffee): a rise in the price of one raises the demand for the other.
Complements (tea and sugar, cars and petrol): a rise in the price of one reduces the demand for the other.

example.q: Income rises from ₹20,000 to ₹30,000. Demand for coarse grain falls from 30 kg to 20 kg; demand for fruit rises from 5 kg to 9 kg. Classify the goods.
example.answer: Coarse grain is inferior; fruit is normal for this household.

learn.reallife: When petrol prices rise, demand for petrol cars tends to fall (complements), while demand for CNG and electric vehicles tends to rise (substitutes).

games.title: Substitutes or complements?

Printer and cartridge

games.title: Types of goods

That is the definition.
For an inferior good, demand rises when income rises.
Demand falls as income rises.
A rise in the price of coffee raises the demand for tea.
They are substitutes.
A rise in the price of petrol raises the demand for petrol cars.
They are complements, so demand falls.
A Giffen good's demand rises when its price rises.
The income effect outweighs the substitution effect.

quiz.q: Pen and ink are an example of:
quiz.explain: They are used together.

Both A and R are true but R does not explain A

options: Quantity of tea demanded rises along the curve

quiz.mistake: Treats complements as substitutes

teach.ask: Gappu got a raise and stopped eating old dry seeds, buying fresh berries instead. 'What kind of goods are these?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Berries are normal goods, dry seeds are inferior goods for me, and seeds and berries are substitutes!
teach.nudge: Good! What happens to demand for each when income rises? What do we call goods with falling demand?

topics.title: Shifts vs movements, and market demand

learn.hook: 'Demand for mangoes rose' and 'quantity demanded of mangoes rose' sound alike but mean different things on a graph. Examiners love this distinction.
points: Movement along the demand curve (change in quantity demanded): caused only by a change in the good's own price. Extension = more bought at a lower price; contraction = less at a higher price.
Shift of the demand curve (change in demand): caused by other factors: income, prices of related goods, tastes and preferences. Rightward shift = increase in demand; leftward = decrease.
Rightward shift examples: rise in income (normal good), rise in price of a substitute, fall in price of a complement, favourable change in tastes.
Market demand is the horizontal summation of individual demands: at each price, add the quantities demanded by all consumers.
Example: d1 = 10 − p and d2 = 15 − p. For p ≤ 10, market demand = 25 − 2p; for 10 < p ≤ 15, only consumer 2 buys: 15 − p; for p > 15, zero.

example.q: d1 = 10 − p and d2 = 15 − p. Find market demand at p = 4 and p = 12.

learn.reallife: A viral health video about millets can shift the demand curve for millets to the right, even with no change in their price.

games.title: Movement or shift?

Consumer's income rises
Price of a substitute rises
Price of the good rises
Tastes change in favour of the good
Price of a complement falls

games.title: Market demand sprint (d1 = 10 − p, d2 = 15 − p)

quiz.mistake: Adds only one consumer's demand or forgets to subtract the price twice

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A fall in the price of a good leads to an increase in demand.
Reason (R): A fall in own price causes an extension (movement down) along the demand curve.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false

quiz.q: Three identical consumers each have demand q = 20 − 2p. What is the market demand at p = ₹5?

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Berry demand went up because I got richer, and also because berries got cheaper. Are these the same kind of change?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Richer = shift of the demand curve; cheaper berries = movement along it. Different changes!
teach.nudge: Good! Which change moves me along the same curve, and which shifts the whole curve?

topics.title: Price elasticity of demand: meaning and the percentage method

learn.hook: Raise the price of salt by 10% and people still buy almost the same amount. Raise the price of a particular brand of chips by 10% and sales crash. Elasticity measures this sensitivity.
points: Price elasticity of demand (e_D) = percentage change in quantity demanded ÷ percentage change in price. Because price and quantity move oppositely, e_D is negative; we usually state its absolute value.
Percentage (proportionate) method: e_D = (ΔQ / Q) × (P / ΔP), using the original P and Q.
Elastic demand: |e_D| > 1. Inelastic: |e_D| < 1. Unitary elastic: |e_D| = 1.
Perfectly elastic (e_D = ∞): horizontal demand curve. Perfectly inelastic (e_D = 0): vertical demand curve.
Using a known elasticity: %ΔQ = e_D × %ΔP. With e_D = 2, a 10% price rise cuts quantity demanded by 20%.

example.q: Price rises from ₹10 to ₹12 and quantity demanded falls from 50 to 45. Find e_D.

learn.reallife: Demand for life-saving medicines like insulin is highly inelastic, which is one reason the government caps prices of essential drugs.

items.q: e_D = 2, price rises 10%. % fall in quantity?
e_D = 0.5, price falls 20%. % rise in quantity?

quiz.q: Price falls from ₹5 to ₹4 and quantity demanded rises from 100 to 130 units. Find the price elasticity of demand (absolute value).
quiz.mistake: Uses the new price or quantity as the base

quiz.q: Price rises from ₹20 to ₹25 and quantity demanded falls from 80 to 70. Find |e_D|.
quiz.mistake: Inverts the ratio

quiz.q: e_D = 2 and the price of a good rises by 10%. Quantity demanded was 500 units. What is the new quantity demanded?
quiz.explain: Quantity falls by 2 × 10% = 20%, i.e. by 100 units: 500 − 100 = 400.
quiz.mistake: Applies only a 10% fall

quiz.q: Demand for a good is called elastic when:
quiz.explain: Quantity changes by a larger percentage than price.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up elastic and inelastic

quiz.q: A perfectly inelastic demand curve is:
quiz.explain: Quantity demanded does not change at all with price (e_D = 0).
quiz.mistake: Confuses perfectly inelastic with perfectly elastic

quiz.q: Price falls by 10% and quantity demanded rises by 10%. The demand is:
quiz.mistake: Thinks equal changes mean perfectly elastic

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The price elasticity of demand is usually negative.
Reason (R): Price and quantity demanded generally move in opposite directions.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Opposite signs of ΔQ and ΔP make the ratio negative; we often drop the sign.
quiz.mistake: Thinks elasticity is always positive by definition

quiz.q: Quantity demanded falls by 12% when price rises. If e_D = 0.8, by what percentage did price rise?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies instead of dividing

teach.ask: Gappu's berry price rose 10% and he bought 30% fewer. 'What's my elasticity? Is my demand elastic?'
teach.praise: Tweet! e_D = 30%/10% = 3, more than 1, so my berry demand is elastic!
teach.nudge: Good! Which percentage do you divide by which? Is the answer more or less than 1?

topics.title: Elasticity along a demand curve, its determinants and total expenditure

learn.hook: On a single straight-line demand curve, elasticity changes at every point: zero at one end, infinity at the other, exactly 1 in the middle.
points: Linear demand q = a − bp: e_D = b × p / q (absolute value). It is 0 where the line meets the quantity axis, 1 at the mid-point, and ∞ where it meets the price axis.
Geometric (point) method: e_D at a point = lower segment ÷ upper segment of the demand line (lower = from the point to the quantity axis; upper = from the point to the price axis).
A demand curve shaped like a rectangular hyperbola (p × q = constant) has unitary elasticity at every point, because total expenditure never changes.
Determinants: nature of the good (necessities inelastic, luxuries elastic), availability of close substitutes (more substitutes → more elastic), share in the budget, habits, and time period.
Total expenditure (p × q) method: if price rises, expenditure rises when demand is inelastic, falls when elastic, and stays constant when unitary elastic.

example.q: q = 20 − 2p. Find e_D at p = 5 and at p = 4.

learn.reallife: Salt has few substitutes and takes a tiny share of the budget, so its demand is very inelastic; one brand of biscuits among dozens has elastic demand.

games.title: Total expenditure test
items: If price rises and total expenditure rises, demand is inelastic.
Quantity fell by a smaller percentage than price rose.
If price falls and total expenditure falls, demand is elastic.
That shows inelastic demand.
Unitary elastic demand keeps total expenditure unchanged when price changes.
Percentage changes offset exactly.
At the mid-point of a straight-line demand curve, e_D = 1.
Lower and upper segments are equal.
A rectangular hyperbola demand curve has e_D = 1 at every point.
p × q is constant.
Goods with many close substitutes have inelastic demand.
Many substitutes make demand elastic.

quiz.explain: Lower and upper segments are equal, so e_D = 1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a straight line has constant elasticity

quiz.q: q = 100 − 5p. Find |e_D| at p = 12.
