quiz.explain: e_D = lower/upper = 6/3 = 2.
quiz.mistake: Divides upper by lower

quiz.q: Where a straight-line demand curve meets the quantity axis, e_D is:
quiz.explain: At that point price is zero, so the upper segment is the whole line and the lower segment is zero.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the two ends

quiz.q: Price of a good rises from ₹10 to ₹12, and quantity demanded falls from 100 to 90. What happens to total expenditure, and what does it show?
quiz.explain: Expenditure = 10 × 100 = 1,000 before and 12 × 90 = 1,080 after. A price rise that raises expenditure means inelastic demand.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the expenditure rule

quiz.q: A demand curve is a rectangular hyperbola, with p × q = 600 throughout. If price is ₹20, how much is demanded, and what is e_D?
quiz.explain: q = 600/20 = 30. Expenditure is constant along the curve, so e_D = 1 everywhere.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies instead of dividing

quiz.q: Demand for a good is more elastic when:
options: It takes a tiny share of income
quiz.explain: Buyers can easily switch, so they respond strongly to price changes.
quiz.mistake: Confuses determinants of elastic and inelastic demand

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Demand for salt is inelastic.
Reason (R): Salt is a necessity with few close substitutes and takes a very small share of the budget.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Each factor in R makes demand less responsive to price.
quiz.mistake: Knows salt is inelastic but cannot explain why

teach.ask: Gappu's berry price rose from ₹5 to ₹6, and his total spending on berries went up. 'Is my demand elastic or inelastic?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Price up and spending up means inelastic demand: I barely cut my berry quantity!
teach.nudge: Good! When price rose, what happened to my total spending? What does that tell you about elasticity?

topics.title: The production function

learn.hook: A dosa stall with 1 tawa and 2 cooks makes 60 dosas an hour; add a third cook and maybe 80. The production function is the recipe linking inputs to the maximum output.
points: A production function shows the maximum output a firm can produce from given quantities of inputs, with a given technology: q = f(L, K), where L is labour and K is capital.
It is a technical relationship; improved technology changes the function itself.
An output table shows the output for different combinations of L and K; read across a row (K fixed) to see the effect of more labour.
Isoquant (in the NCERT book; check your syllabus): a curve showing all combinations of L and K that give the same output. Isoquants slope downward, and a higher isoquant means a higher output.

example.q: An output table: with K = 2, output is 10, 24, 36 for L = 1, 2, 3; with K = 3, output is 14, 30, 45 for L = 1, 2, 3. What is the output with L = 2, K = 3? What happens if K rises from 2 to 3 with L = 2?
steps: Read row K = 3, column L = 2: output = 30.
With L = 2, output rises from 24 (K = 2) to 30 (K = 3).
example.answer: Output = 30; it rises by 6 units when K rises from 2 to 3.

learn.reallife: A textile mill in Surat can make the same 1,000 metres of cloth with many workers and old looms or with fewer workers and modern looms: two points on the same isoquant.

games.title: Production function facts
items: A production function shows the maximum output from given inputs.
It assumes inputs are used efficiently.
A production function depends on the given technology.
Better technology changes the relationship.
An isoquant shows combinations of goods giving the same satisfaction.
That is an indifference curve; an isoquant shows input combinations giving the same output.
A higher isoquant represents a higher level of output.
More inputs give more output.
Isoquants usually slope upward.
To keep output constant, more of one input means less of the other.

games.title: Match the term

quiz.mistake: Confuses production with demand or cost functions

quiz.explain: L is labour and K is capital.

quiz.mistake: Confuses isoquant with indifference curve

quiz.q: A production function assumes that technology is:

Both A and R are true but R does not explain A

teach.ask: Gappu's nest workshop uses 3 birds and 2 twig-cutters to build 12 nests a day. 'What's the rule linking inputs and nests called?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The production function gives the maximum output from inputs like labour and capital, for a given technology!

topics.title: Short run, long run, and TP, AP and MP

learn.hook: A café can hire an extra waiter tomorrow, but building a bigger kitchen takes a year. That difference is the short run versus the long run.
points: Short run: at least one factor (e.g. capital, the building) is fixed; output changes only by varying the variable factor (e.g. labour). Long run: all factors can be varied.
These periods are defined by the flexibility of inputs, not by calendar time; the long run of a tea stall may be weeks, of a steel plant years.
Total product (TP): total output as one variable input (L) changes, other inputs fixed. Average product AP = TP / L.
Marginal product MP = ΔTP / ΔL, or with unit changes MP_L = TP_L − TP_(L−1).
TP is the sum of the MPs; AP at L units is the average of the MPs up to L.

example.q: TP for L = 1, 2, 3, 4: 10, 24, 36, 44. Find AP and MP.

learn.reallife: During festive rush, a sweet shop adds helpers (variable factor) in the same kitchen (fixed factor): a short-run decision.

items.q: TP rises 40 → 52 as L rises 4 → 6. MP?

topics.title: Numericals on TP, AP and MP

learn.hook: Board papers love this: give any one of TP, AP or MP, and ask for the other two. Master the three links and these become free marks.
points: From TP: AP = TP/L; MP = TP_L − TP_(L−1).
From AP: TP = AP × L; then MP = TP_L − TP_(L−1).
From MP: TP = running sum of MPs; then AP = TP/L.
Always build the TP column first if it is missing; everything else follows.

example.q: AP for L = 1, 2, 3, 4 is 20, 18, 16, 14. Find TP and MP.

learn.reallife: A garment unit manager uses these calculations to decide whether one more tailor on the shop floor adds enough shirts to justify the wage.

teach.ask: Gappu knows his team's AP: 10 nests with 1 bird, 9 with 2, 8 with 3. 'Can I find TP and MP from this?'
teach.praise: Tweet! TP = 10, 18, 24 by multiplying AP by birds; MP = 10, 8, 6 by subtracting!
teach.nudge: Good! How do we get TP from AP first? Then how do we find MP?

topics.title: Law of variable proportions (returns to a factor)

learn.hook: Add workers to one small farm: first they help each other, then they get in each other's way, and finally they trample the crop. Output tells this whole story.
points: Law of variable proportions: when more units of a variable factor are added to a fixed factor, the MP of the variable factor first rises, then falls, and may eventually become negative.
Phase I, increasing returns to a factor: MP rises, because the fixed factor is better utilised and workers can specialise.
Phase II, diminishing returns to a factor: MP falls but stays positive, because the fixed factor becomes relatively scarce (factor proportions worsen).
Phase III, negative returns: MP becomes negative and TP falls, because too many variable units crowd the fixed factor.
A rational producer operates in Phase II.

example.q: MP of labour on a farm for L = 1 to 7: 10, 14, 12, 8, 4, 0, −3. Identify the phases.
steps: MP falls from 12 down to 0 (L = 3 to 6) without becoming negative: diminishing returns (TP is at its maximum when MP = 0)
example.answer: Phase I: L 1–2; Phase II: L 3–6; Phase III: L 7

learn.reallife: In parts of rural India, many family members work on one small plot; the extra worker adds little or nothing to output, a sign of diminishing or even zero marginal product.

teach.praise: Tweet! MP rises, then diminishes as the tree gets crowded, then turns negative. That's the law of variable proportions!

topics.title: Shapes of TP, MP and AP curves

learn.hook: Three curves, one story. When you draw TP, AP and MP together, their key points line up exactly. Examiners check those alignments.
points: TP first rises at an increasing rate (MP rising), then at a diminishing rate (MP falling but positive), reaches its maximum when MP = 0, and falls when MP is negative.
MP and AP curves are both inverse-U shaped: they rise, reach a maximum and then fall.
MP cuts AP at the maximum point of AP.
When MP > AP, AP rises; when MP = AP, AP is at its maximum; when MP < AP, AP falls.
AP stays positive as long as TP is positive, but MP can become negative.

example.q: TP for L = 1 to 6: 10, 24, 36, 44, 48, 48. Where is AP maximum, and where is TP maximum?
steps: TP maximum (48) where MP = 0, at L = 6
example.answer: AP max = 12 (where MP = AP); TP max = 48 (where MP = 0)

learn.reallife: Factory managers who track output per worker (AP) and extra output of the last worker hired (MP) can see that hiring beyond the point where MP falls below AP lowers average productivity.

topics.title: Returns to scale and long-run costs

learn.hook: Double every input of a pizza chain, ovens, chefs, outlets, and does output exactly double? That's the long-run question of returns to scale.
points: Note: returns to scale and long-run costs are in the NCERT book; check whether your school examines them this year.

Returns to scale describe what happens to output when ALL inputs increase in the same proportion: constant (output rises in the same proportion), increasing (more than proportionately) or decreasing (less than proportionately).
Cobb–Douglas production function: q = x1^a × x2^b. Returns to scale are constant if a + b = 1, increasing if a + b > 1, decreasing if a + b < 1.

In the long run all inputs are variable, so there are no fixed costs. The long-run average cost (LRAC) curve is U-shaped: it falls under increasing returns to scale, is flat under constant returns, and rises under decreasing returns.
The long-run marginal cost (LRMC) curve cuts LRAC at LRAC's minimum point.

example.q: q = x1^0.5 × x2^0.5. Find output when x1 = 4, x2 = 9, and identify the returns to scale.
steps: a + b = 0.5 + 0.5 = 1 → constant returns to scale
Check: doubling inputs to (8, 18) gives √8 × √18 = √144 = 12, exactly double.

learn.reallife: Large Indian car plants enjoy increasing returns to scale up to a point, which is why carmakers prefer big plants over many small ones.

topics.title: Cost concepts: fixed, variable, average and marginal

learn.hook: A food truck pays ₹500 a day for parking whether it sells 0 or 300 rolls. The cost of ingredients rises with every roll. Two very different kinds of cost.
points: The cost function shows the least cost of producing each level of output, given input prices.

Total fixed cost (TFC): costs that do not change with output (rent, salaries of permanent staff, interest). Total variable cost (TVC): costs that vary with output (raw materials, wages of casual workers). TC = TFC + TVC.
AFC = TFC / q; AVC = TVC / q; AC (SAC) = TC / q = AFC + AVC.
Marginal cost (SMC) = ΔTC / Δq = ΔTVC / Δq (fixed cost does not change). With unit steps, MC_q = TC_q − TC_(q−1).
TVC = sum of MCs up to that output (TFC is not included).

example.q: TFC = ₹100. TVC at q = 1, 2, 3: ₹40, ₹70, ₹90. Find TC, AFC, AVC, AC and MC at q = 3.

learn.reallife: For Indian Railways, track maintenance is largely a fixed cost, while fuel for each additional train is a variable cost.

topics.title: Shapes of short-run cost curves

learn.hook: Picture cost curves on a graph: one flat line, two rising ones running parallel, a curve that keeps falling, and three U-shapes. Each shape has a reason.
points: TFC is a horizontal straight line. TVC starts from the origin and rises; TC starts from the level of TFC and rises parallel to TVC (the vertical gap is always TFC).
AFC is a rectangular hyperbola: it falls continuously as output rises (AFC × q = TFC is constant) but never touches the x-axis.
SMC, AVC and SAC are U-shaped, because of the law of variable proportions: returns to the variable factor first increase (costs fall), then diminish (costs rise).
SMC cuts AVC and SAC from below at their minimum points. The minimum of SAC lies to the right of the minimum of AVC.
The vertical gap between SAC and AVC equals AFC; it narrows as output rises because AFC keeps falling.

example.q: TFC = 100. At q = 4, AVC = 30 and at q = 5, AVC = 34. Find AFC and SAC at both outputs and the gap between SAC and AVC.
steps: The gap (AFC) narrows as output rises.
example.answer: Gap = AFC: 25 at q = 4, 20 at q = 5

learn.reallife: A newspaper's printing press is a big fixed cost; as circulation grows, the fixed cost per copy (AFC) keeps shrinking, which is why bigger print runs make each copy cheaper.

topics.title: Completing cost schedules

learn.hook: Given a few numbers, an examiner expects you to fill an entire cost table. One golden rule: always find TC (or TVC) first.
points: From TC: TFC = TC at zero output; TVC = TC − TFC; MC = TC_q − TC_(q−1); AFC, AVC and AC by dividing by q.
From MC and TFC: TVC = running sum of MCs; TC = TFC + TVC; then the averages.
From AC: TC = AC × q; then the rest.
Check your table: MC should cut AVC and AC near their minimum values, and AC − AVC should equal AFC.

example.q: TC at q = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4: 100, 140, 170, 190, 220. Find TFC, TVC, MC and AVC.

learn.reallife: Small business owners in Indian MSME clusters use such tables to find the output where cost per unit is lowest.

topics.title: Revenue: TR, AR and MR

learn.hook: A street vendor sells pens at a fixed ₹10 each. Every extra pen brings exactly ₹10 more. That simple fact gives three straight-line revenue curves.
points: Total revenue TR = price × quantity = p × q.
Average revenue AR = TR / q = p. AR is always equal to price.
Marginal revenue MR = ΔTR / Δq = change in TR from selling one more unit.
When price is constant (as for a price-taking firm), AR = MR = price at every output, and the AR/MR line is horizontal.
With a constant price, TR is a straight line from the origin with slope equal to the price.

example.q: Price = ₹10. Complete TR, AR and MR for q = 1 to 4.
example.answer: AR = MR = ₹10 throughout; TR rises by ₹10 per unit.

learn.reallife: A farmer selling wheat at the government's fixed procurement price earns the same price on every quintal: AR = MR = price.

TR = p × q with constant slope p.
MR is total revenue divided by quantity.
That is AR; MR is the change in TR.

chapters.title: Microeconomics: The Theory of the Firm under Perfect Competition

topics.title: Features of perfect competition

learn.hook: Thousands of farmers sell the same variety of wheat at a mandi. If one farmer asks ₹50 more per quintal, buyers simply walk to the next heap. That is perfect competition.
points: Large number of buyers and sellers: each is too small to influence the market price.
Homogeneous product: every firm's output is identical, so buyers have no reason to prefer one seller.
Free entry and exit: firms can enter or leave the industry without restrictions.
Perfect information: all buyers and sellers know the market price and product details.
Result: each firm is a price taker. It can sell any quantity at the market price, so it faces a horizontal (perfectly elastic) demand curve.

example.q: A wheat farmer finds the market price is ₹2,300 per quintal. What happens if she charges (a) ₹2,350, (b) ₹2,250?
steps: (a) Buyers know the price and the wheat is identical, so they buy elsewhere: she sells nothing.
(b) She could sell all she wants at ₹2,300 anyway, so cutting price only lowers her revenue.
example.answer: She charges the market price of ₹2,300: she is a price taker.

learn.reallife: Agricultural produce like wheat or potatoes sold through mandis comes close to perfect competition; most other markets fall short of the ideal.

There is free entry and exit.
Each buyer and seller has perfect information about prices.
That is one of the features.

quiz.mistake: Confuses perfectly elastic with perfectly inelastic

options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

quiz.mistake: Adds price and quantity

teach.praise: Tweet! With many sellers of identical berries and perfect information, each seller must take the market price!
teach.nudge: Good! But why can't one seller charge more? Think about the products and how many sellers there are.

topics.title: Revenue of a price-taking firm

learn.hook: A candle maker sells boxes at the market price of ₹10. Every box adds exactly ₹10 to revenue, so her revenue curves are as simple as they get.
points: TR = p × q. With a constant market price, TR is a straight line through the origin whose slope equals the price.
AR = TR/q = p and MR = ΔTR/Δq = p for a price taker.
So the firm's price line = AR = MR = its demand curve: one horizontal line at the market price.
If the market price rises, the TR line becomes steeper and the AR = MR line shifts up.

example.q: Candle boxes sell at ₹10. Find TR and MR for 1 to 5 boxes.
example.answer: TR rises by ₹10 per box; AR = MR = ₹10.

learn.reallife: A farmer selling tomatoes at a mandi where the day's price is ₹20 per kg earns ₹20 on every extra kg: her MR equals the price.

items.q: Slope of TR line when p = 15?

quiz.mistake: Adds price and quantity

quiz.explain: TR rises from 500 to 600, an increase of ₹100.

teach.ask: Gappu sells berry boxes at ₹5 each in a huge market. 'What do my TR, AR and MR look like on a graph?'
teach.praise: Tweet! TR is a straight line from the origin, and AR = MR = ₹5 is a horizontal price line!
teach.nudge: Good! Is TR curved or straight? And how do AR and MR compare with the price?

topics.title: Conditions for profit maximisation

learn.hook: Should a firm stop producing when price equals marginal cost? Only if three conditions hold, and the third tells it when to shut down altogether.
points: Profit (π) = TR − TC. A firm chooses output to make profit as large as possible.
Condition 1: price = marginal cost (p = MC, i.e. MR = MC). If p > MC, one more unit adds to profit; if p < MC, cutting output raises profit.
Condition 2: MC must be non-decreasing (rising) at that output. Where MC is falling and equals p, producing more would still raise profit.
Condition 3 (short run): price must be at least minimum AVC. If p < min AVC, the firm should shut down; its loss is then only the TFC.
Condition 3 (long run): price must be at least minimum LRAC; otherwise the firm exits the industry.

example.q: A firm's MC equals the price of ₹20 at two outputs: 10 units (MC falling) and 40 units (MC rising). At 40 units AVC = ₹16. What output should it choose?
steps: At 10 units MC is falling: Condition 2 fails.
At 40 units MC is rising: Condition 2 holds.

learn.reallife: Sugar mills crush cane only when the sugar price covers their variable costs (cane, power, wages); otherwise they stay shut for the season.

games.title: Checking the profit-maximising output
items: Find the outputs where p = MC
Keep only the output where MC is rising
Check that p ≥ minimum AVC (short run)
If yes, produce that output; if not, shut down

p = ₹18, min AVC = ₹20
p = ₹40, min AVC = ₹40
p = ₹12, min AVC = ₹15

quiz.q: The first condition for profit maximisation of a price-taking firm is:
quiz.explain: Output is set where the price equals marginal cost.
quiz.mistake: Confuses profit maximisation with break-even

quiz.q: Why must MC be rising at the profit-maximising output?
options: If MC is falling where p = MC, producing a little more would add to profit
quiz.explain: Beyond that point p > MC, so profit is not yet maximised.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any point where p = MC is optimal

quiz.q: In the short run, a firm should shut down if the price is less than:
quiz.explain: Below minimum AVC, it cannot even cover variable costs.
quiz.mistake: Uses the long-run condition (minimum AC)

quiz.q: A firm with TFC = ₹500 shuts down in the short run. What is its loss?
quiz.explain: With zero output, TR = 0 and TC = TFC, so the loss equals TFC.
quiz.mistake: Thinks shutting down removes all losses

quiz.q: In the long run, a perfectly competitive firm stays in the industry only if price is at least:
quiz.explain: In the long run all costs must be covered.
quiz.mistake: Uses the short-run shut-down rule

quiz.mistake: Reverses the MR–MC rule

Assertion (A): A firm may continue producing in the short run even when it makes a loss.
Reason (R): If the price covers AVC, producing keeps the loss smaller than TFC.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Covering variable cost and part of fixed cost beats losing all of TFC.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a loss-making firm must close at once

quiz.q: p = ₹30, and at the output where p = MC (MC rising), AVC = ₹28 and AC = ₹33. In the short run the firm should:
options: Produce, since p ≥ AVC, accepting a small loss
quiz.explain: Price covers AVC (₹30 > ₹28), so producing minimises the loss.
quiz.mistake: Applies the long-run rule in the short run

teach.ask: Gappu's nest business: price ₹20, MC equals ₹20 at 8 nests (rising), AVC = ₹15. 'Should I make 8 nests?'
teach.praise: Tweet! p = MC at 8 nests, MC is rising and the price covers AVC, so 8 nests maximise profit!
teach.nudge: Good! Is MC rising there? And does the price at least cover my average variable cost?

topics.title: Profit and loss: graphs and numericals

learn.hook: On a graph, profit is literally a rectangle: its height is price minus average cost, and its width is output. Draw it right and you can read profit at a glance.
points: Graph: the firm produces q0 where the horizontal price line meets the rising SMC. Profit (or loss) = (p − SAC at q0) × q0.
If p > SAC at q0: super-normal profit, shown by the rectangle between price and SAC. If p < SAC but p ≥ AVC: a loss rectangle, but the firm still produces in the short run.
From a table: profit = TR − TC at each output; choose the output with the highest profit. Equivalently, keep producing while MC ≤ p.
Check: at the chosen output, MC of the next unit should exceed the price.

example.q: Price ₹10. TC at q = 0 to 6: 10, 15, 18, 22, 28, 36, 47. Find the profit-maximising output.
example.answer: q = 5, profit ₹14 (MC of the 6th unit, ₹11, exceeds the price).

learn.reallife: A hand-pump manufacturer in Ludhiana that checks profit at each output level is doing exactly this table analysis.

games.title: Reading profit from a graph
items: Draw the horizontal price line

Read SAC at q0
Profit = (price − SAC) × q0

quiz.q: Price = ₹20, output = 100 units, SAC at that output = ₹15. What is the profit?
quiz.mistake: Uses TR or TC instead of the difference

quiz.q: Price = ₹12, output = 80, SAC = ₹15, AVC = ₹10. What is the loss, and should the firm produce in the short run?
options: Loss ₹240; no, it must shut down
Loss ₹240; yes, since price covers AVC
quiz.explain: Loss = (15 − 12) × 80 = ₹240. Price (₹12) > AVC (₹10), so producing is better than shutting down.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to compare price with AVC

quiz.q: Price ₹10. TC for q = 0 to 6: 10, 15, 18, 22, 28, 36, 47. What is the profit-maximising output?
quiz.mistake: Picks the largest output

quiz.q: Using the same table (p = ₹10; TC 10, 15, 18, 22, 28, 36, 47 for q = 0–6), what is the maximum profit?
quiz.explain: At q = 5: TR = 50, TC = 36, profit = ₹14.
quiz.mistake: Reads TR instead of profit

quiz.q: Price ₹10; TC for q = 0 to 6 is 10, 15, 18, 22, 28, 36, 47. What is MC of the 6th unit, and why does the firm not produce it?
quiz.explain: MC6 = 47 − 36 = 11 > 10, so the 6th unit reduces profit.
quiz.mistake: Uses TC instead of MC

quiz.q: On a cost–revenue diagram, the profit of a firm is shown by a rectangle whose height is:
options: Price minus SAC at the chosen output
quiz.explain: Profit per unit (p − SAC) times output gives the rectangle's area.
quiz.mistake: Uses MC instead of AC for per-unit profit

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): When price equals SAC at the chosen output, the firm earns zero economic profit.
Reason (R): TR then exactly equals TC, which already includes normal profit.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: p = SAC means TR = TC, so only normal profit is earned.
quiz.mistake: Thinks zero economic profit means the owner earns nothing

quiz.q: A firm sells 60 units at ₹25. TC is ₹1,350. What is its profit?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts in the wrong order

teach.ask: Gappu's price is ₹8 per nest, he makes 50 nests, and his average cost is ₹6. 'How much profit? Can I show it on a graph?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Profit = (8 − 6) × 50 = ₹100, the rectangle between the price line and the AC curve!
teach.nudge: Good! What is the profit on each nest? Then multiply by what?

topics.title: The firm's supply curve, shut-down point and normal profit

learn.hook: Plot how much a firm produces at every price and you've drawn its supply curve. Surprise: it's just a piece of its marginal cost curve.
points: Short-run supply curve of a firm: the rising part of the SMC curve from minimum AVC upward. At prices below minimum AVC, output is zero.
Long-run supply curve: the rising part of the LRMC curve from minimum LRAC upward; below minimum LRAC, output is zero.
Shut-down point: in the short run, the point of minimum AVC (where SMC cuts AVC); in the long run, minimum LRAC.
Normal profit: the minimum profit needed to keep the firm in business. It is the opportunity cost of the entrepreneur (the return from the next best alternative) and is counted as part of cost.
Super-normal profit: profit above normal profit. Break-even point: where price = minimum AC, so the firm earns only normal profit (zero economic profit).

example.q: A firm's minimum AVC is ₹20 and minimum AC is ₹30. What does it do at prices of ₹15, ₹25 and ₹40?
steps: ₹25: between min AVC and min AC: produces where p = SMC, with a loss smaller than TFC.
₹40 > min AC: produces where p = SMC and earns super-normal profit.
example.answer: Shut down at ₹15; produce at a loss at ₹25; produce with super-normal profit at ₹40.

learn.reallife: A software engineer who leaves a ₹15 lakh job to start a firm counts that ₹15 lakh as normal profit: her opportunity cost.

teach.ask: Gappu's minimum AVC is ₹6 and minimum AC is ₹9. 'At what prices do I supply nests? What is my supply curve?'
teach.praise: Tweet! My supply curve is the rising MC above minimum AVC (₹6); below ₹6 I shut down, and at ₹9 I break even!
teach.nudge: Good! Below which price will I make nothing? Which part of the MC curve is my supply curve?

topics.title: Determinants of a firm's supply

learn.hook: A new drip-irrigation technique cuts a farmer's cost per kg; a hike in diesel prices raises it. Each pushes the supply curve in a different direction.
points: Supply schedule: quantities a firm is willing to sell at different prices. Law of supply: other things equal, quantity supplied rises with price.
Movement along the supply curve: caused by a change in the good's own price (extension or contraction of supply). Shift: caused by other factors.
Technological progress lowers MC, shifting the supply curve to the right.
A rise in input prices (wages, raw materials, fuel) raises MC, shifting supply to the left.
A unit (per-unit) tax raises the firm's MC by the amount of the tax, shifting supply to the left (upward by the tax).

example.q: A firm supplies 100 units at ₹20. The government imposes a tax of ₹4 per unit. At what price will it now supply 100 units?
steps: The tax raises MC by ₹4 at every output.
To supply 100 units it now needs ₹20 + ₹4.
example.answer: ₹24; the supply curve shifts up (left) by ₹4.

learn.reallife: When CNG prices rise, auto-rickshaw operators' costs rise; at any given fare fewer rides are supplied: a leftward shift of supply.

Unit tax imposed

Fall in the good's own price

It causes a movement along the curve.

teach.ask: Gappu's twig price rose and a new nest-weaving trick was invented in the same week. 'What happens to my supply curve?'

teach.nudge: Good! How does each change affect my marginal cost? Which way does each one shift supply?

topics.title: Market supply

learn.hook: Two dairy farms: one starts selling milk at ₹10 a litre, the other only at ₹15. Add their supplies and the market supply curve gets a kink at ₹15.
points: Market supply is the horizontal summation of the supply curves of all firms: at each price, add the quantities supplied.
If firms have different shut-down prices, the market supply curve has kinks where each new firm starts producing.
Example: s1 = p − 10 for p ≥ 10 (0 below); s2 = p − 15 for p ≥ 15 (0 below). Market: 0 for p < 10; p − 10 for 10 ≤ p < 15; 2p − 25 for p ≥ 15.
With n identical firms each supplying s(p), market supply = n × s(p).
An increase in the number of firms shifts the market supply curve to the right; a decrease shifts it to the left.

example.q: s1 = p − 10 (p ≥ 10) and s2 = p − 15 (p ≥ 15). Find market supply at p = 12 and p = 20.

learn.reallife: When many new solar-panel makers entered India's market, the market supply of panels shifted right at every price.

games.title: Market supply sprint (s1 = p − 10 for p ≥ 10; s2 = p − 15 for p ≥ 15)

items.q: 100 identical firms, each s = p − 5. Market at p = 8?

Horizontal summation.

A firm joins the market only above its shut-down price.

It shifts it to the right.
Market supply of 50 identical firms is 50 times one firm's supply.

Market supply is found by adding prices vertically.
Quantities are added horizontally at each price.

options: Vertical summation of firms' supply curves

quiz.mistake: Uses only one firm

Reason (R): At each price, market quantity is the sum of all firms' quantities, so it responds more in quantity to a price change.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false

teach.ask: Gappu and his cousin both sell nests. 'If I start selling at ₹5 and my cousin at ₹8, what does the market supply look like?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Add our quantities at each price. Below ₹8 only I sell, so the curve kinks at ₹8!
teach.nudge: Good! How do we combine our supply curves? What happens at the price where my cousin starts selling?

topics.title: Price elasticity of supply

learn.hook: When the price of cricket balls doubles before the IPL season, how quickly can Meerut's workshops raise output? Elasticity of supply measures that response.
points: Price elasticity of supply e_S = percentage change in quantity supplied ÷ percentage change in price. It is positive because price and quantity supplied move together.
Percentage method: e_S = (ΔQ/Q) × (P/ΔP). Use it both to compute e_S and to predict new quantities: %ΔQ = e_S × %ΔP.
Geometric method for a straight-line supply curve: if it meets the price axis (positive price intercept), e_S > 1; if it passes through the origin, e_S = 1; if it meets the quantity axis, e_S < 1.
Perfectly elastic supply (e_S = ∞): horizontal supply curve. Perfectly inelastic supply (e_S = 0): vertical supply curve (e.g. fixed stock of tickets for a match).

example.q: Price of cricket balls rises from ₹100 to ₹120 and quantity supplied rises from 500 to 650. Find e_S.

learn.reallife: The number of seats in a stadium for a World Cup final is fixed: supply of tickets is perfectly inelastic, whatever the price.

options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A

teach.ask: Gappu's nest price rose from ₹10 to ₹12 and he raised output from 50 to 55 nests. 'How elastic is my supply?'
teach.praise: Tweet! %ΔQ = 10%, %ΔP = 20%, so e_S = 0.5: my supply is inelastic!
teach.nudge: Good! What are the percentage changes in quantity and price? Which do you divide by which?

topics.title: Equilibrium, excess demand and excess supply

learn.hook: At 6 a.m. the fish market is chaos; by 8 a.m. a price has settled at which almost every fish finds a buyer. Nobody announced it. The market found its equilibrium.
points: Market equilibrium: the situation where the plans of all buyers and sellers match, i.e. market demand = market supply.
Equilibrium price (p*) and equilibrium quantity (q*) are the price and quantity at which this happens.
Excess demand: at a price below p*, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied (a shortage).
Excess supply: at a price above p*, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded (a surplus).
Invisible hand (Adam Smith): under excess demand, competing buyers bid the price up; under excess supply, sellers cut the price; this continues until equilibrium is reached.

example.q: At ₹30, qD = 80 and qS = 50. At ₹40, qD = 60 and qS = 60. At ₹50, qD = 40 and qS = 70. Find p*, q* and the situation at ₹30 and ₹50.
example.answer: p* = ₹40, q* = 60; excess demand of 30 at ₹30; excess supply of 30 at ₹50.

learn.reallife: When a new phone launches at a low introductory price, it sells out within minutes: excess demand, which often pushes resale prices up.

quiz.q: Market equilibrium occurs where:
quiz.explain: Plans of buyers and sellers match at that price.
quiz.mistake: Thinks equilibrium means maximum sales

quiz.q: At a price below the equilibrium price, there is:
quiz.explain: Lower price raises quantity demanded and lowers quantity supplied.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the cases

quiz.mistake: Adds the quantities

quiz.explain: Sellers with unsold stock cut prices.

quiz.mistake: Adds instead of subtracting

quiz.explain: Self-interested buyers and sellers push prices towards equilibrium without central direction.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it means government intervention

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): At equilibrium there is neither excess demand nor excess supply.
Reason (R): At the equilibrium price, the quantity buyers wish to buy equals the quantity sellers wish to sell.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Equality of planned purchases and sales leaves no gap.

quiz.q: At which price below is the market in equilibrium? (₹30: qD 80, qS 50; ₹40: qD 60, qS 60; ₹50: qD 40, qS 70)
quiz.explain: At ₹40, qD = qS = 60.
quiz.mistake: Chooses the price with the highest demand

teach.ask: Gappu sees berries selling out fast at ₹5 while sellers have empty baskets. 'What's happening, and what will happen to the price?'
teach.praise: Tweet! At ₹5 there's excess demand, so the price rises until demand equals supply at equilibrium!
teach.nudge: Good! Is there too much demand or too much supply at ₹5? Which way will the price move?

topics.title: Finding equilibrium with demand and supply functions

learn.hook: Two straight lines, one equation: set qD = qS and the market's price falls out like a magic trick.
points: Graphically, equilibrium is where the market demand and supply curves intersect: their intersection gives p* and q*.
Algebraically, set qD = qS and solve for p*, then substitute to find q*.
Excess demand function: ED(p) = qD − qS; excess supply function: ES(p) = qS − qD. At p*, both are zero.
For the example: ED(p) = 80 − 4p, so ED(15) = 20 and ED(25) = −20 (i.e. excess supply of 20).

example.q: qD = 200 − p and qS = 120 + p. Find p*, q* and the excess demand at p = 30.

learn.reallife: Economists estimate demand and supply equations for crops like onions to predict how prices will settle after a good or bad harvest.

quiz.mistake: Makes a sign error while moving terms

quiz.mistake: Gives qD instead of the gap

teach.praise: Tweet! 60 − 2p = 3p − 15 gives p* = 15 and q* = 30. Algebra solves markets!
teach.nudge: Good! What should you set equal to what? Then solve for p.

topics.title: Wage determination in a competitive labour market

learn.hook: Why does a delivery app pay its riders what it does? In a competitive labour market, the wage settles where the value of the last worker's output equals the wage.
points: Note: wage determination is in the NCERT book; check whether your school examines it this year.

In a perfectly competitive labour market, firms are wage takers and hire labour up to the point where the wage equals the value of the marginal product of labour: w = VMP_L = p × MP_L (here also equal to MRP_L, the marginal revenue product).
Because MP_L diminishes, the demand curve for labour slopes downward: more workers are hired only at lower wages.
The supply curve of labour slopes upward: higher wages attract more hours of work or more workers.
The equilibrium wage is where market demand for labour equals market supply of labour.

example.q: Output sells at ₹10 per unit. MP of the 4th worker is 30 units and of the 5th is 20 units. Wage is ₹250. How many workers will the firm hire?

learn.reallife: During the festive season, demand for e-commerce delivery staff rises; the labour demand curve shifts right and wages for delivery jobs tend to rise.

games.title: Labour market
items: A competitive firm hires labour until wage = VMP_L.
Hiring beyond that adds less value than its cost.
VMP_L = price × MP_L.
Value of the extra output from one more worker.
The labour demand curve slopes upward.
It slopes downward because MP_L diminishes.
The supply curve of labour usually slopes upward.
Higher wages attract more labour.
Equilibrium wage is where labour demand equals labour supply.
As in any competitive market.

options: Wage = value of marginal product of labour

Assertion (A): If the price of the good produced rises, a competitive firm demands more labour at each wage.
Reason (R): VMP_L = p × MP_L rises when p rises.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A

quiz.explain: Higher wages draw out more labour.

teach.ask: Gappu runs a nest workshop. Nests sell at ₹5, the 6th helper adds 8 nests, and wages are ₹45. 'Should I hire the 6th helper?'
teach.praise: Tweet! VMP = 5 × 8 = ₹40, less than the ₹45 wage, so I shouldn't hire the 6th helper!
teach.nudge: Good! What is the value of the extra nests the 6th helper makes? Compare it with the wage.

topics.title: Shifts in demand or supply

learn.hook: A good monsoon floods mandis with onions; a festival boosts demand for sweets. One shifts supply, the other shifts demand, and prices move in predictable ways.
points: Rightward shift of demand (supply unchanged): equilibrium price and quantity both rise. Leftward shift of demand: both fall.
Rightward shift of supply (demand unchanged): price falls and quantity rises. Leftward shift of supply: price rises and quantity falls.
Demand shifts due to: income, prices of related goods, tastes and preferences, number of consumers.
Supply shifts due to: input prices, technology, number of firms, unit taxes.

Numerical: with qD = 100 − 2p, if supply rises from qS = 20 + 2p to qS = 40 + 2p, new p* = 15 and q* = 70 (from 20 and 60). A unit tax of ₹4 changes supply to qS = 20 + 2(p − 4) = 12 + 2p, giving p* = 22, q* = 56.

example.q: qD = 100 − 2p, qS = 20 + 2p (p* = 20, q* = 60). A bumper harvest changes supply to qS = 40 + 2p. Find the new equilibrium.
steps: Price fell from 20 to 15, quantity rose from 60 to 70.

learn.reallife: Tomato prices often crash after a bumper crop (supply shifts right) and spike after unseasonal rains damage crops (supply shifts left).

games.title: Match the shift to its effect

quiz.q: If demand increases (shifts right) and supply is unchanged, equilibrium price and quantity:
quiz.explain: Higher demand at every price pushes up both.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up demand and supply shift effects

quiz.q: If supply increases (shifts right) and demand is unchanged:
quiz.explain: More is offered at each price, so price falls and more is bought.
quiz.mistake: Thinks more supply raises price

Higher equilibrium price and lower quantity
quiz.explain: Supply shifts left: price rises, quantity falls.

quiz.mistake: Uses the old supply function

quiz.mistake: Reports the old quantity

quiz.q: qD = 100 − 2p, qS = 20 + 2p. A unit tax of ₹4 is imposed on sellers, so supply becomes qS = 20 + 2(p − 4). What is the new equilibrium price paid by buyers?
quiz.explain: 100 − 2p = 12 + 2p → 4p = 88 → p = 22. Buyers pay ₹2 more; sellers keep 22 − 4 = ₹18.
quiz.mistake: Adds the full tax to the old price

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A fall in consumers' incomes lowers both the equilibrium price and quantity of a normal good.
Reason (R): Demand for a normal good falls when income falls, shifting the demand curve left.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A leftward demand shift with unchanged supply lowers both p and q.
quiz.mistake: Thinks income affects supply

options: A new tax on car makers
quiz.explain: Cheaper petrol (a complement) raises demand for cars; the others affect supply or cause movements.
quiz.mistake: Confuses own-price changes and supply factors with demand shifters

teach.ask: Gappu's forest had a bumper berry harvest. 'What happens to the price and quantity of berries?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Supply shifts right, so berries get cheaper and more are bought!
teach.nudge: Good! Which curve does a bumper harvest affect? Then what happens to price and quantity?

topics.title: Simultaneous shifts in demand and supply

learn.hook: Diwali raises demand for sweets, while costlier milk cuts their supply. Will sweet prices rise? Certainly. Will more sweets be sold? That depends on which shift is bigger.
points: Both curves shift right: quantity definitely rises; price may rise, fall or stay the same (depends on the relative size of the shifts).
Both curves shift left: quantity definitely falls; price is ambiguous.
Demand shifts right and supply shifts left: price definitely rises; quantity is ambiguous.
Demand shifts left and supply shifts right: price definitely falls; quantity is ambiguous.
Drawing the diagram: draw the original D and S, then shift both. Draw versions where one shift is larger, then equal, to see which variable's change is certain.

example.q: During a festival, demand for sweets rises and the price of milk rises at the same time. Predict the effect on sweets.
steps: Both push price up: price definitely rises.
Quantity: demand pushes it up, supply pushes it down → ambiguous.
example.answer: Price rises; quantity may rise, fall or stay the same.

learn.reallife: In a year with rising incomes (demand up) and a good harvest (supply up), the amount of rice sold surely rises, but whether its price rises depends on which effect is stronger.

games.title: Match the simultaneous shift to the certain outcome
Simultaneous shifts
items: If both demand and supply increase, equilibrium quantity must rise.
Both shifts push quantity up.
If both demand and supply increase, equilibrium price must rise.
Price depends on the relative size of the shifts.
If demand rises and supply falls, price must rise.
Both shifts push price up.
If demand falls and supply rises, quantity must fall.

If demand and supply increase by exactly the same amount, price stays the same.

quiz.q: Demand and supply both increase. Which is certain?
quiz.explain: Both shifts raise quantity; their effects on price oppose each other.
quiz.mistake: Assumes price must rise when demand rises

quiz.q: Demand increases and supply decreases. Which is certain?
quiz.explain: Both shifts push price up; their effects on quantity oppose.
quiz.mistake: Thinks quantity must change in a known direction

quiz.q: Demand falls and supply rises. The equilibrium price will:
quiz.explain: Both shifts lower the price.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the price change is ambiguous here

quiz.q: Both demand and supply decrease. The equilibrium quantity will:
quiz.explain: Both shifts reduce quantity.
quiz.mistake: Thinks quantity is ambiguous

quiz.q: Demand and supply both increase, and the increase in demand is greater than the increase in supply. The price will:
quiz.explain: A bigger demand shift dominates the price effect.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the relative sizes

quiz.q: Demand decreases and supply increases by equal amounts. What happens?
quiz.explain: Price falls for sure; with equal-sized opposite shifts, quantity stays the same.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up which variable is certain

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): When demand rises and supply falls, the change in equilibrium quantity cannot be predicted without more information.
Reason (R): The demand shift tends to raise quantity while the supply shift tends to lower it.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Opposing pressures make the net quantity effect depend on the size of the shifts.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the bigger-sounding change always wins

quiz.q: qD = 100 − 2p and qS = 20 + 2p (p* = 20). Demand becomes 120 − 2p and supply becomes 40 + 2p. What is the new equilibrium price?
quiz.explain: 120 − 2p = 40 + 2p → 4p = 80 → p = 20. Equal shifts leave the price unchanged; quantity rises to 80.
quiz.mistake: Assumes price must change

teach.ask: Gappu's forest: more birds want berries, and a drought cuts berry supply. 'What happens to berry prices and sales?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Demand up and supply down: the price surely rises, but sales could go either way!
teach.nudge: Good! Both changes push the price the same way. What about quantity: do they push it the same way?

topics.title: Free entry and exit: long-run equilibrium

learn.hook: A new momo stall makes big profits; within months, five more stalls open on the same street. Profits shrink until no one else wants to join.
points: Note: this section is in the NCERT book; check whether your school examines it this year.
With free entry and exit, super-normal profits attract new firms (supply rises, price falls); losses make firms exit (supply falls, price rises).
In the long run, price settles at the minimum average cost (p = min AC), and each firm earns only normal profit.
Equilibrium number of firms = market quantity demanded at p = min AC ÷ output of each firm at min AC.
If demand shifts, the price returns to min AC; only the market quantity and the number of firms change.

example.q: Each identical firm has min AC = ₹20 at 50 units. Market demand is qD = 1,000 − 10p. Find the long-run price, market quantity and number of firms.

learn.reallife: As more cafés open in a busy college area, prices of a cup of coffee tend towards the level that just covers costs, including the owners' normal profit.

games.title: Adjustment under free entry

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): In the long run, the number of firms changes but the price stays at min AC when demand changes.
Reason (R): Free entry and exit remove any super-normal profit or loss.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

teach.ask: Gappu's nest business is making huge profits, and other birds can freely set up. 'What will happen in the long run?'

teach.nudge: Good! What do other birds do when they see big profits? What happens to the price then?

topics.title: Price ceiling

learn.hook: If the government caps the price of wheat below the market price to help poor families, more people want wheat but farmers offer less. A shortage is born.
points: Price ceiling: a legal maximum price fixed by the government, below the equilibrium price, usually for essential goods (e.g. food grains, kerosene).
At the ceiling price, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied: excess demand (shortage).
Consequences: the government may need rationing (ration cards and fair price shops, as in the Public Distribution System), long queues, and black markets where goods sell above the ceiling.
A ceiling set above the equilibrium price has no effect, since the market price is already lower.
Case analysis, e.g. rent control: tenants gain lower rents, but fewer houses are offered for rent and maintenance suffers.

example.q: qD = 100 − 2p, qS = 20 + 2p (p* = 20). The government fixes a ceiling of ₹15. Find the shortage.

learn.reallife: India's Public Distribution System supplies rice and wheat through fair price shops at prices far below the market, with ration cards deciding who gets how much.

games.title: Consequence of a price ceiling?
items: Long queues
Black market
Rationing with ration cards
Surplus stocks piling up
Shortage of the good
Government buying excess output

games.title: Price ceiling facts
items: An effective price ceiling is set below the equilibrium price.
Otherwise it would not bind.
A price ceiling creates excess supply.
It creates excess demand (shortage).
Black markets may emerge under a price ceiling.
Some buyers pay more to get scarce goods.
Fair price shops are a way of rationing under a ceiling.
They distribute limited supplies.
A ceiling above the equilibrium price causes a shortage.
It has no effect because the market price is lower.

quiz.q: A price ceiling is:
options: A minimum price fixed above equilibrium
A maximum price fixed below equilibrium
quiz.explain: It caps the price below the market level.
quiz.mistake: Confuses ceiling and floor

quiz.q: An effective price ceiling leads to:
quiz.explain: At the low price, buyers want more than sellers offer.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a lower price increases supply

quiz.q: qD = 100 − 2p and qS = 20 + 2p. A ceiling of ₹15 is fixed. What is the shortage?
quiz.explain: qD = 70, qS = 50, shortage = 20.
quiz.mistake: Gives qD or qS instead of the gap

quiz.q: Using qD = 100 − 2p and qS = 20 + 2p, a ceiling of ₹25 is fixed. What happens?
options: No effect, since ₹25 is above the equilibrium price of ₹20
quiz.explain: A ceiling above equilibrium does not bind; the price stays at ₹20.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every ceiling causes a shortage

quiz.q: Which is a likely consequence of a price ceiling?
options: Prices rising above the ceiling legally
quiz.explain: With shortages, some sellers sell illegally at higher prices.
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with a price floor

quiz.q: Ration cards and fair price shops are used under a price ceiling to:
options: Ration the limited supply fairly among consumers
quiz.explain: They distribute scarce goods when price cannot rise.
quiz.mistake: Thinks they are meant to raise prices

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Rent control can reduce the number of houses offered for rent.
Reason (R): A rent ceiling below equilibrium lowers the return to landlords, so quantity supplied falls.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Lower returns discourage landlords from renting out or maintaining houses.
quiz.mistake: Sees only the benefit to tenants

quiz.q: qD = 200 − p and qS = 120 + p (p* = 40). A ceiling of ₹30 is fixed. What is the shortage?
quiz.explain: qD = 170, qS = 150, shortage = 20.
quiz.mistake: Uses equilibrium quantities

teach.ask: Gappu's forest council fixed the berry price at ₹3, below the market's ₹5. 'Now berries vanish fast and some birds sell them secretly for ₹6! Why?'
teach.praise: Tweet! A ceiling below equilibrium causes a shortage, so rationing is needed and black markets appear!
teach.nudge: Good! At ₹3, do more birds want berries or fewer? What happens to supply? What does that gap cause?

topics.title: Price floor

learn.hook: Every season the government announces a minimum support price for wheat. If that price is above the market price, farmers grow more than buyers want, and someone has to buy the extra.
points: Price floor: a legal minimum price fixed by the government, above the equilibrium price.
At the floor price, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded: excess supply (surplus).
Examples: minimum support price (MSP) for crops, which protects farmers' incomes; minimum wage laws in the labour market, which protect workers.
To maintain the floor, the government may buy the surplus (e.g. procurement by the Food Corporation of India, building buffer stocks) or restrict supply.
A floor set below the equilibrium price has no effect, since the market price is already higher.

example.q: qD = 100 − 2p, qS = 20 + 2p (p* = 20). The government fixes a floor of ₹25. Find the surplus the government must buy.

learn.reallife: The Food Corporation of India procures wheat and rice at MSP and stores buffer stocks, which are later used for the Public Distribution System.

games.title: Match the policy to its effect

items.q: Floor ₹30. Government spending to buy the surplus at ₹30?

quiz.q: A price floor is:
options: A maximum price set below equilibrium
A minimum price set above equilibrium
quiz.explain: It guarantees sellers at least this price.
quiz.mistake: Confuses floor with ceiling

quiz.q: An effective price floor results in:
quiz.explain: At the higher price, sellers offer more than buyers want.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a higher price creates shortage

quiz.q: Minimum support price for wheat is an example of:
quiz.explain: It sets a minimum price for farmers above the market level.
quiz.mistake: Thinks support price is a maximum price

quiz.q: qD = 100 − 2p and qS = 20 + 2p. A floor of ₹25 is set. What is the surplus?
quiz.explain: qS = 70, qD = 50, surplus = 20.
quiz.mistake: Gives qS instead of the gap

quiz.q: With the same functions and a floor of ₹30, how much must the government spend to buy the entire surplus at the floor price?
quiz.mistake: Uses total supply instead of the surplus

quiz.q: A minimum wage set above the equilibrium wage in a labour market may cause:
quiz.explain: At the higher wage, more people want work than firms want to hire.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a higher wage raises labour demand

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The government often buys and stores grain when it fixes MSP above the market price.
Reason (R): A price floor above equilibrium creates a surplus that must be absorbed to keep the price from falling.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Without government purchases, the surplus would push the price below the floor.
quiz.mistake: Does not see why procurement is needed

quiz.q: A floor of ₹15 is set when the equilibrium price is ₹20. What happens?
options: No effect; the market price stays ₹20
quiz.explain: A floor below equilibrium does not bind.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every floor causes a surplus

teach.ask: Gappu's forest set a minimum nest price of ₹12, above the market's ₹10. 'Now nests are piling up unsold! What went wrong, and what can we do?'
teach.praise: Tweet! A floor above equilibrium creates a surplus, so the council must buy the extra nests or limit supply!
teach.nudge: Good! At ₹12, do builders supply more or fewer nests? And buyers? What does that gap create?
